title: Introduction to DMAR
text: DMAR general greatly expanded reimagining MBESS package (Kelley, 2007a, Journal Statistical Software; 2007b, Behavior Research Methods). MBESS originally framed Methods Behavioral, Educational, Social Sciences, methods implements became useful far beyond scope; DMAR ships new name make scope expansion explicit. emphasis confidence intervals effect sizes built noncentral sampling distributions, sample size planning power accuracy parameter estimation (AIPE), reliability, factor analysis, critical values used classical inference. DMAR intended serve computational companion Maxwell, Delaney, Kelley’s Designing Experiments Analyzing Data (4th ed., 2027; henceforth MDK), use instruction substantive research. Although package’s origins psychology, questions answers field-specific. Researchers biostatistics (clinical-trial effect size CIs AIPE-based trial sizing), organizational behavior management science (intervention, training, program evaluation), information systems (user-experience /B comparisons; technology-adoption studies), education (instructional effectiveness, longitudinal achievement gains), sociology (program evaluation, attitudinal surveys), methodological literature share three tasks: estimating effect sizes, constructing confidence intervals , planning sample size future studies, power precision estimate. DMAR keeps MBESS philosophy, , insistence effect sizes uncertainty quantified, planning studies accurate estimation rather sufficient power. DMAR changes implementation: uniform snake_case interface, tidy data.frame returns consistently named columns, native ggplot2 visualization, heavier dependencies kept Suggests loaded functions use , test suite checks results published values reference implementations. function families also broadened, particularly ss_power_* family, now covers -subjects, within-subjects, mixed, multilevel designs across chapters MDK.

what: 2. I’m Planning a Study. How Many Subjects Do I Need?
title: Introduction to DMAR
text: Use ss_power_* sufficient power, ss_aipe_* sufficient precision. effect can approached either angle. Confidence level: 95% ss_power_* family spans standard designs covered MDK: one-way ANOVA (ss_power_one_way_anova), factorial ANOVA (ss_power_factorial_anova), repeated measures ANOVA sphericity adjustment (ss_power_rm_anova), split-plot mixed ANOVA (ss_power_split_plot_anova), Pearson correlation (ss_power_r), two-independent-groups standardized mean difference (ss_power_smd), contrasts standardized unstandardized (ss_power_c, ss_power_sc, ss_power_c_ancova, ss_power_contrast), regression coefficients (ss_power_reg_coef), two-level random-intercept models cluster-randomized trials (ss_power_mixed_effects). SEM-style designs, use ss_power_sem(). AIPE counterparts exist correspondingly named effects.
code: # Power-based: per-group n needed for 90% power to detect a contrast among # 4 groups with population means (90, 92, 88, 81) and within-group # variance 144. The contrast compares the average of the first three # groups against the fourth. ss_power_contrast(   c_weights           = c(1/3, 1/3, 1/3, -1),   true_means          = c(90, 92, 88, 81),   true_var_error = 144,   desired_power       = 0.90 ) # AIPE-based: n needed so a 95% CI around a population standardized mean # difference of 0.50 is no wider than 0.30 units (a tight interval). ss_aipe_smd(true_smd = 0.50, conf_level = 0.95, width = 0.30)

code: # Computed by tools/composite_power_reference.R, which runs the code in this # vignette at reps = 10000. Kept as literals because a 10,000-replication # sweep is far too slow to run while the document is being knitted. ref <- list(   marginal   = c(1.0000, 0.8056, 0.9070),   composite  = 0.7126,   product    = 0.7307,   n_seq      = seq(20, 40, by = 2),   comp_seq   = c(0.4837, 0.5695, 0.6251, 0.6909, 0.7310, 0.7734,                  0.8142, 0.8454, 0.8730, 0.8920, 0.9098),   n_comp80   = 32,   threeway   = c(three_way = 0.7909, two_way = 1.0000),   N_try      = c(395, 420, 440, 460),   tw_by_N    = c(0.7909, 0.8161, 0.8298, 0.8479),   N_mc80     = 420 ) composite_power <- function(n, mu, sigma2, reps = 25, alpha = 0.05, seed = 113) {   set.seed(seed)   a <- length(mu); N <- a * n; df <- N - a   tcrit <- qt(1 - alpha / 2, df)   W   <- do.call(cbind, targets)          # the three targeted contrasts   ssq <- colSums(W^2)   cellmeans <- matrix(rep(mu, each = n), nrow = n)   reject <- matrix(FALSE, reps, ncol(W))   for (r in seq_len(reps)) {     y    <- cellmeans + matrix(rnorm(N, 0, sqrt(sigma2)), nrow = n)     ybar <- colMeans(y)     mse  <- sum(sweep(y, 2, ybar)^2) / df          # pooled error variance     psi  <- as.numeric(t(W) %*% ybar)              # contrast estimates     reject[r, ] <- abs(psi / sqrt(mse * ssq / n)) > tcrit   }   list(marginal  = colMeans(reject),        composite = mean(rowSums(reject) == ncol(W)),        product   = prod(colMeans(reject))) }  mc <- composite_power(n_design, mu, sigma2)  data.frame(   row.names = c("smallest_marginal", "product_if_independent", "composite"),   `reps = 25`    = round(c(min(mc$marginal), mc$product, mc$composite), 3),   `reps = 10000` = round(c(min(ref$marginal), ref$product, ref$composite), 3),   check.names = FALSE) #>                        reps = 25 reps = 10000 #> smallest_marginal          0.840        0.806 #> product_if_independent     0.806        0.731 #> composite                  0.800        0.713 bar_df <- data.frame(   quantity = factor(c("Treatment | Human", "Treatment | Machine", "Interaction",                       "Product (independence)", "Composite (all three)"),                     levels = c("Treatment | Human", "Treatment | Machine", "Interaction",                                "Product (independence)", "Composite (all three)")),   power = c(mc$marginal, mc$product, mc$composite),   kind  = c("marginal", "marginal", "marginal", "reference", "composite"))  ggplot(bar_df, aes(quantity, power, fill = kind)) +   geom_col(width = 0.68) +   geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey35") +   geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", power)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.4) +   scale_fill_manual(values = c(marginal = agent_cols[["Machine"]],                                reference = "grey65", composite = accent),                     guide = "none") +   labs(title = "Each targeted effect reaches .80, but not all three jointly",        subtitle = sprintf("At n = %d per cell (N = %d)", n_design, 4 * n_design),        x = NULL, y = "Power") +   ylim(0, 1.05) +   theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8.5))

code: simulate_threeway_power <- function(N, gamma, rho = .2, reps = 25, seed = 113) {   sigma_e <- sqrt(2)   varY_less_M <- bA^2*.25 + bB^2*.25 + bAB^2*.0625 + gamma^2*.0625 + sigma_e^2   betaM <- sqrt(rho^2 * varY_less_M / (1 - rho^2))   set.seed(seed)   hit3 <- hit2 <- logical(reps)   for (r in seq_len(reps)) {     A <- sample(c(-.5, .5), N, TRUE); B <- sample(c(-.5, .5), N, TRUE); M <- rnorm(N)     y <- b0 + bA*A + bB*B + bAB*A*B + betaM*M + gamma*A*B*M + rnorm(N, 0, sigma_e)     cf <- summary(lm(y ~ A * B * M))$coefficients     hit3[r] <- cf["A:B:M", "Pr(>|t|)"] < .05     hit2[r] <- cf["A:B",   "Pr(>|t|)"] < .05   }   c(three_way = mean(hit3), two_way = mean(hit2)) }  mc_small <- simulate_threeway_power(N_3way, gamma = gamma_small)  data.frame(row.names = names(ref$threeway),            `reps = 25`    = round(mc_small, 3),            `reps = 10000` = round(ref$threeway, 3),            check.names = FALSE) #>           reps = 25 reps = 10000 #> three_way      0.88        0.791 #> two_way        1.00        1.000 N_try   <- ref$N_try mc_by_N <- sapply(N_try, function(NN)   simulate_threeway_power(NN, gamma = gamma_small)["three_way"]) N_mc80  <- ref$N_mc80  tw_plot <- rbind(   data.frame(N = N_try, power = ref$tw_by_N, reps = "10000 replications"),   data.frame(N = N_try, power = mc_by_N,     reps = "25 replications"))  ggplot(tw_plot, aes(N, power, color = reps)) +   geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +   geom_vline(xintercept = N_3way, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey55") +   geom_line(linewidth = 1) +   geom_point(size = 2.6) +   scale_color_manual(values = c("10000 replications" = accent,                                 "25 replications" = "grey65"), name = NULL) +   geom_text(data = subset(tw_plot, reps == "10000 replications"),             aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", power)), vjust = -0.9, size = 3.3,             show.legend = FALSE) +   annotate("text", x = N_3way, y = 0.755, angle = 90, vjust = -0.4, size = 3,            color = "grey40", label = sprintf("analytic N = %d", N_3way)) +   labs(title = "Random predictors require a larger sample",        subtitle = "Monte Carlo power for the small three-way interaction (gamma = 0.8)",        x = "Total N", y = "Three-way power (Monte Carlo)") +   ylim(0.72, 0.90)

what: Migration Table: The Renames That Matter
title: Moving From MBESS to DMAR: A Migration Guide and a Tour of the New Methods
text: naming convention DMAR snake_case throughout. Argument names use underscores rather dots (conf_level, conf.level; alpha_level, alpha.level), canonical return tidy data.frame term value columns. table maps -used MBESS calls DMAR equivalents. convention rename : 1. Replace . _ function argument names (ci.smd -> ci_smd, n.1 -> n_1, conf.level -> conf_level). 2. Lowercase abbreviations statistical notation (R.Square -> R2, Mean -> mean, SD -> sd); keep meaningful capitals (R2, N, S, F_value) capital labels variables (X, Y, Z, true_cor_YX). 3. Use p number predictors (MBESS sometimes used K). 4. Use random_predictors (Random.Predictors alias Random.Regressors). 5. Name value role quantity English: true_ population value given planner (delta -> true_smd ss_aipe_smd(), C..V -> true_cv ss_aipe_cv()), supposed_ planning value sensitivity function chooses design . DMAR functions return tidy data.frame term value columns (vignette("dmar_output") describes exceptions). Scripts consumed MBESS’s named-list returns generally need adjust extraction (e.g., $Lower.Conf.Limit.smd becomes $value[$term == "ci_lower"]).

what: The Negative Exponential: Change That Only Decelerates
title: Nonlinear Growth Curves and the Meaning of Their Parameters
text: simplest nonlinear change model negative exponential, also called asymptotic regression (Stevens, 1951): y(t) = alpha + zeta * exp(-gamma * t). Three parameters, three answers: alpha change ends (asymptote), alpha + zeta starts (intercept), gamma fast remaining gap closes. Change fastest first moment decelerates ever ; inflection. three rising curves share start (0) end (1) differ gamma; three falling curves mirror . point curvature parameter: moves fast without touching . simulated sample makes model concrete. Individuals get asymptote, total change, rate; measurements add error:
code: # The six deterministic curves of the illustration in Kelley (2005): # three growth curves that differ only in curvature, and three decay # curves that mirror them. Each curve is its own population of size one, so one # simulator call draws the whole panel. panel <- simulate_longitudinal_negative_exponential(   n_per_group = 1, target_times = seq(0, 10, by = 0.1),   fixed_parameters = list(     c(alpha = 1, zeta = -1, gamma = 0.9),     c(alpha = 1, zeta = -1, gamma = 0.4),     c(alpha = 1, zeta = -1, gamma = 0.2),     c(alpha = 0, zeta =  1, gamma = 1.2),     c(alpha = 0, zeta =  1, gamma = 0.5),     c(alpha = 0, zeta =  1, gamma = 0.3)),   error_variance = 0 ) plot_trajectories(panel, id = "id", time = "time",                   outcome = "true_score", group = "population") set.seed(113) d_ne <- simulate_longitudinal_negative_exponential(   n_per_group = 25, target_times = 0:8,   fixed_parameters = c(alpha = 100, zeta = -80, gamma = 0.5),   random_variances = c(alpha = 25, zeta = 16, gamma = 0.01),   error_variance = 9 ) plot_trajectories(d_ne, id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "y")

title: Nonlinear Growth Curves and the Meaning of Their Parameters
text: Processes floor ceiling need second asymptote. four parameter logistic (Ratkowsky, 1983; Kelley, 2005) y(t) = alpha / (1 + exp(-gamma * (t - beta))) + zeta. new landmark beta, point inflection: moment fastest change. logistic moment always comes exactly half total change, alpha / 2 + zeta; climb away floor mirrors approach ceiling. fourth parameter, zeta, floor , freed fixed zero three parameter logistic intercept modeled quantity. three curves pass inflection point (dot t = 6, y = 50): gamma concentrates change around moment without moving .
code: tt <- seq(0, 12, by = 0.1) curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.5, 0.9, 2), function(g) {   data.frame(t = tt, gamma = g,              y = 80 / (1 + exp(-g * (tt - 6))) + 10) })) curves$gamma <- factor(curves$gamma) ggplot2::ggplot(curves, ggplot2::aes(t, y, color = gamma)) +   ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +   ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = c(10, 90), linetype = "dashed",                       linewidth = 0.3) +   ggplot2::geom_point(data = data.frame(t = 6, y = 50),                       ggplot2::aes(t, y), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2) +   ggplot2::labs(x = "Time", y = "y(t)",                 title = "Logistic change: floor 10, ceiling 90, inflection at t = 6",                 color = "gamma") +   ggplot2::theme_minimal()

what: The Gompertz: S-Shaped Change That Inflects Early
title: Nonlinear Growth Curves and the Meaning of Their Parameters
text: Gompertz curve (Winsor, 1932) also S-shaped, symmetric: y(t) = alpha * exp(-exp(-gamma * (t - beta))) + zeta. inflection pinned alpha / exp(1) + zeta, 36.8 percent total change. Substantively different theory change: rapid early gains, long consolidation. Learning curves often look like . reproduces illustration Kelley (2005): three rising curves share inflection time beta = 2, three falling curves share beta = 3, alpha zeta constant, every curve crosses inflection height, 0.75 / exp(1) + 0.25, 0.526.
code: panel <- simulate_longitudinal_gompertz(   n_per_group = 1, target_times = seq(0, 6, by = 0.05),   fixed_parameters = list(     c(alpha = 0.75, beta = 2, gamma =  1.75, zeta = 0.25),     c(alpha = 0.75, beta = 2, gamma =  1.00, zeta = 0.25),     c(alpha = 0.75, beta = 2, gamma =  0.45, zeta = 0.25),     c(alpha = 0.75, beta = 3, gamma = -0.35, zeta = 0.25),     c(alpha = 0.75, beta = 3, gamma = -0.60, zeta = 0.25),     c(alpha = 0.75, beta = 3, gamma = -2.00, zeta = 0.25)),   error_variance = 0 ) plot_trajectories(panel, id = "id", time = "time",                   outcome = "true_score", group = "population")

what: The Richards Family: The Inflection Becomes a Parameter
title: Nonlinear Growth Curves and the Meaning of Their Parameters
text: Choosing logistic fixes inflection 50 percent total change; choosing Gompertz fixes 36.8 percent. Richards curve (Richards, 1959) makes fraction estimable: y(t) = alpha / (1 + delta * exp(-gamma * (t - beta)))^(1/delta) + zeta. shape parameter delta places inflection ordinate alpha * (1 + delta)^(-1/delta) + zeta. delta = 1 Richards curve logistic; delta approaches 0 Gompertz; larger delta pushes inflection past halfway, shape neither special case can reach. Richards family therefore subsumes others, exactly Guo, Cheng, Kelley (2016) used let network structure move inflection self-replicating malware outbreaks. simulator enforces delta > 0 , delta given -subject variance, refuses draws cross zero rather silently truncating .
code: tt <- seq(0, 12, by = 0.1) rich <- function(delta) 80 / (1 + delta * exp(-0.9 * (tt - 6)))^(1 / delta) + 10 curves <- rbind(   data.frame(t = tt, y = 80 * exp(-exp(-0.9 * (tt - 6))) + 10,              shape = "delta -> 0 (Gompertz)"),   data.frame(t = tt, y = rich(1), shape = "delta = 1 (logistic)"),   data.frame(t = tt, y = rich(3), shape = "delta = 3 (late inflection)") ) ggplot2::ggplot(curves, ggplot2::aes(t, y, color = shape)) +   ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +   ggplot2::labs(x = "Time", y = "y(t)",                 title = "One Richards family, three shapes (same alpha, beta, gamma, zeta)",                 color = "Shape") +   ggplot2::theme_minimal()

code: one_at_a_time <- function(which_var, label) {   set.seed(113)   d <- simulate_longitudinal_logistic(     n_per_group = 20, target_times = seq(0, 12, by = 0.5),     fixed_parameters = c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma = 0.9, zeta = 10),     random_variances = which_var, error_variance = 0   )   d$panel <- label   d } d_all <- rbind(   one_at_a_time(c(zeta = 25),    "Only the floor varies (zeta)"),   one_at_a_time(c(alpha = 100),  "Only the total change varies (alpha)"),   one_at_a_time(c(beta = 1.5),   "Only the timing varies (beta)"),   one_at_a_time(c(gamma = 0.06), "Only the curvature varies (gamma)") ) ggplot2::ggplot(d_all,                 ggplot2::aes(time, true_score, group = id)) +   ggplot2::geom_line(alpha = 0.45, linewidth = 0.4) +   ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 2) +   ggplot2::labs(x = "Time", y = "True score",                 title = "Four sources of individual differences, isolated") +   ggplot2::theme_minimal() set.seed(113) d_mix <- simulate_longitudinal_logistic(   n_per_group = 30, target_times = 0:12,   fixed_parameters = c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma = 0.9, zeta = 10),   random_variances = c(alpha = 36, beta = 1, gamma = 0.01, zeta = 9),   error_variance = 16 ) plot_trajectories(d_mix, id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "y")

what: Nonlinear Versus Polynomial: Why the Parameters Matter
title: Nonlinear Growth Curves and the Meaning of Their Parameters
text: smooth curve can approximated polynomial high enough order, stay linear models? Two reasons, visible one picture. Take deterministic Gompertz curve used Kelley (2005), y(t) = 5 exp(-exp(7 - 1.75 t)), observe t = 0 8, fit polynomials increasing order: ninth-order polynomial tracks curve well. needed ten parameters Gompertz four, one ten answers substantive question: coefficient ceiling, none moment fastest growth. Gompertz parameters theory; polynomial coefficients bookkeeping. second reason appears moment model leaves data. Refit best polynomial observed window, extend time axis: Inside observed window two indistinguishable; past , polynomial rockets top figure Gompertz growth asymptote must . nonlinear model extrapolates theory; polynomial extrapolates arithmetic.
code: t_obs <- seq(0, 8, by = 0.25) y_obs <- 5 * exp(-exp(7 - 1.75 * t_obs)) fits <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 3, 5, 9), function(p) {   data.frame(t = t_obs, order = paste0("order ", p),              y = fitted(lm(y_obs ~ poly(t_obs, p)))) })) truth <- data.frame(t = t_obs, y = y_obs) ggplot2::ggplot(fits, ggplot2::aes(t, y, color = order)) +   ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +   ggplot2::geom_line(data = truth, ggplot2::aes(t, y),                      inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +   ggplot2::labs(x = "Time", y = "y(t)",                 title = "A Gompertz curve (solid) and its polynomial approximations",                 color = "Polynomial") +   ggplot2::theme_minimal() fit9 <- lm(y_obs ~ poly(t_obs, 9, raw = TRUE)) t_new <- seq(0, 12, by = 0.1) pred <- data.frame(   t = t_new,   polynomial = predict(fit9, newdata = data.frame(t_obs = t_new)),   gompertz = 5 * exp(-exp(7 - 1.75 * t_new)) ) long <- rbind(   data.frame(t = pred$t, y = pred$polynomial, model = "9th-order polynomial"),   data.frame(t = pred$t, y = pred$gompertz,  model = "Gompertz") ) ggplot2::ggplot(long, ggplot2::aes(t, y, color = model)) +   ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +   ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 8, linetype = "dashed",                       linewidth = 0.3) +   ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-2, 8)) +   ggplot2::labs(x = "Time", y = "y(t)",                 title = "Beyond the data (dashed line), the polynomial has no theory to hold it",                 color = "Model") +   ggplot2::theme_minimal()

what: DMAR: Design, Measurement, and Analysis in R
title: DMAR: Design, Measurement, and Analysis in R
text: DMAR (Design, Measurement, Analysis R, pronounced “Dee-Mar”) package human-centered research: effect sizes, confidence intervals effect sizes, sample size planning, reliability agreement, mediation analysis (simple mediation model likelihood ratio tests arbitrary indirect effects, moderated mediation probing), equivalence testing, meta-analysis, experimental quasi-experimental designs, repeated measures, model comparison-based inference. draws psychometric statistical traditions reflects methodological applied research program author, Ken Kelley (University Notre Dame). aims methodologically sound useful across psychology, sociology, education, management, marketing, information systems, especially independent dependent variables involve person.

title: DMAR: Design, Measurement, and Analysis in R
text: CRAN release tagged GitHub (v1.0.0 first); releases GitHub copy carries changes next one, listed NEWS. R >= 4.0.0 required. estimation, inference, planning functions return tidy data.frame(term, value) composes naturally dplyr / ggplot2 pipelines broom::tidy() / broom::glance(). Heavier dependencies (e.g., lavaan, lme4, OpenMx) Suggests gated requireNamespace(); install need functions use .

Sample size planning AIPE (accuracy parameter estimation). ss_aipe_*() family covers SMD, R², ω², CV, partial / semipartial r, regression coefficients (standardized unstandardized), ANCOVA contrasts, RMSEA, SEM paths, polynomial change, mixed-effects fixed effects, ICC, reliability, Cliff’s delta, single mean (ss_aipe_mean()), crossed designs units raters (ss_aipe_crossed()), two-phase sampling (ss_aipe_two_phase(), ss_aipe_two_phase_cost()). planners Monte Carlo *_sensitivity() sibling quantifies impact misspecified planning values; ss_aipe_two_phase_sensitivity() also evaluates designs ss_aipe_two_phase_cost(). code: fit <- lme4::lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Subject),                   data = lme4::sleepstudy)  # Marginal R2 is the proportion of variance the fixed effects account for; # conditional R2 adds what the random effects account for, so the gap # between the two is what the subject-level terms buy. R2_mixed_effects(fit) #>  term           value #>  R2_marginal    0.279 #>  R2_conditional 0.799 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # A parametric bootstrap percentile interval for both quantities. Each # replication refits the model. B = 20 keeps the example quick and is # below the 400 a reported interval needs; the option lets it run and # the warning says so. A reported interval deserves the default # B = 1000. The seed makes the limits reproducible and leaves the # caller's generator state as it was. old <- options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) R2_mixed_effects(fit, ci_method = "boot", B = 20, seed = 113) #> Warning: R2_mixed_effects(): B = 20 is below the 400 replications a 95% interval is reported from (10 beyond each limit). The limits are shown because options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) is set. With 20 replications each limit rests on about 0.5 of them and will move from seed to seed; use the result to explore or to demonstrate, and report an interval only from B of at least 400. B, B_used, and B_required are recorded in the result. #>  term                    value #>  R2_marginal             0.279 #>  R2_marginal_ci_lower    0.151 #>  R2_marginal_ci_upper    0.470 #>  R2_conditional          0.799 #>  R2_conditional_ci_lower 0.710 #>  R2_conditional_ci_upper 0.855 #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Bootstrap: 20 replications, 20 used (0 dropped; at least 400 must be requested). code: # 1. Cell means of a 2 x 3 factorial (no covariate): end-of-study IQ in #    the pygmalion expectancy experiment, grades 1 through 3. The grade #    factor is created in the data, not inside the formula. pyg <- subset(pygmalion, grade <= 3) pyg$grade <- factor(pyg$grade) fit <- lm(iq_8 ~ treatment * grade, data = pyg) adjusted_means(fit) #>  treatment grade estimate se    ci_lower ci_upper #>  Control   1     102.378  2.560 97.320   107.435  #>  Bloomer   1     113.714  6.492 100.891  126.537  #>  Control   2     99.761   2.532 94.759   104.763  #>  Bloomer   2     118.500  4.958 108.706  128.294  #>  Control   3     105.475  2.716 100.111  110.839  #>  Bloomer   3     104.308  4.764 94.898   113.717  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # 2. Marginal means of grade, averaging the cell means over treatment. adjusted_means(fit, by = "grade") #>  grade estimate se    ci_lower ci_upper #>  1     108.046  3.489 101.154  114.938  #>  2     109.130  2.784 103.632  114.629  #>  3     104.891  2.742 99.476   110.307  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # 3. An ANCOVA: each adjusted mean holds the covariate, here the pretest #    depression score, at its sample mean. fit_ancova <- lm(bdi_post ~ condition + bdi_pre, data = depression_bdi) adjusted_means(fit_ancova) #>  condition estimate se    ci_lower ci_upper #>  ssri      7.537    1.707 4.028    11.046   #>  placebo   11.985   1.707 8.476    15.493   #>  wait_list 13.978   1.706 10.473   17.484   #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # 4. With unbalanced cells (few bloomers in every grade) the two #    weightings answer different questions. adjusted_means(fit, by = "treatment") #>  treatment estimate se    ci_lower ci_upper #>  Control   102.538  1.504 99.568   105.508  #>  Bloomer   112.174  3.152 105.948  118.400  #>  #> Confidence level: 95% adjusted_means(fit, by = "treatment", weights = "proportional") #>  treatment estimate se    ci_lower ci_upper #>  Control   102.454  1.503 99.485   105.422  #>  Bloomer   112.359  3.131 106.175  118.542  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # Simulate a Gompertz population with individual differences, then # recover both the mean curve and the spread of its parameters. set.seed(113) d <- simulate_longitudinal_gompertz(   n_per_group = 40, target_times = 0:10,   fixed_parameters = c(alpha = 75, beta = 3, gamma = 0.55, zeta = 10),   random_variances = c(alpha = 25, beta = 0.4, gamma = 0.005, zeta = 4),   error_variance = 4 ) analysis_of_change(d, id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "y",                    model = "gompertz") #>  term  estimate se    sd_units var_units #>  alpha 75.041   1.061 6.709    45.007    #>  beta  3.082    0.107 0.674    0.454     #>  gamma 0.557    0.014 0.088    0.008     #>  zeta  10.037   0.529 3.349    11.215     # The same data as a straight-line (order 1) polynomial: the linear # model has nothing to say about floors, ceilings, or timing. analysis_of_change(d, id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "y",                    model = "polynomial", order = 1) #>  term estimate se    sd_units var_units #>  b0   12.917   1.243 7.861    61.795    #>  b1   8.134    0.140 0.887    0.787      # A single unit's trajectory: N = 1 is one fit, with asymptotic # standard errors in place of between-unit spread. one <- d[d$id == levels(d$id)[1], ] analysis_of_change(one, id = NULL, time = "time", outcome = "y",                    model = "gompertz") #>  term  estimate se    sd_units var_units #>  alpha 73.757   2.652 <NA>     <NA>      #>  beta  3.111    0.116 <NA>     <NA>      #>  gamma 0.720    0.073 <NA>     <NA>      #>  zeta  9.817    1.854 <NA>     <NA>       # The proper mixed-effects model, fit simultaneously across units: # nlme::nlme() for a nonlinear curve, lme4::lmer() for the polynomial # (the latter requires lme4 to be installed). analysis_of_change(d, id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "y",                    model = "gompertz", method = "mixed") #>  term  estimate se    sd_units var_units #>  alpha 75.086   1.028 5.636    31.767    #>  beta  3.063    0.113 0.698    0.487     #>  gamma 0.549    0.013 0.065    0.004     #>  zeta  9.804    0.448 1.874    3.512     analysis_of_change(d, id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "y",                    model = "polynomial", order = 1,                    method = "mixed") #>  term estimate se    sd_units var_units #>  b0   12.917   1.193 5.966    35.593    #>  b1   8.134    0.135 0.339    0.115

code: # Both fits ask for the Wald interval and skip the effect size block, # since the likelihood ratio test needs neither and each costs refits. fit1 <- mlmr(t6_paragraph_comprehension ~ t5_general_information,              data = holzinger_swineford, ci_method = "wald",              effect_sizes = FALSE) fit2 <- mlmr(t6_paragraph_comprehension ~ t5_general_information +                t9_word_meaning,              data = holzinger_swineford, ci_method = "wald",              effect_sizes = FALSE) anova(fit1, fit2) #> Likelihood ratio test for nested mlmr fits #> Model 2: t6_paragraph_comprehension ~ t5_general_information + t9_word_meaning #> Model 1: t6_paragraph_comprehension ~ t5_general_information #>         Df    AIC    BIC Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)     #> Model 2  0 5601.5 5634.9  0.00                                   #> Model 1  1 5661.3 5691.0 61.78      61.78       1   3.84e-15 *** #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Because every # bin lower edge is at or above zero, this is the mean # absolute error rather than the mean error itself. wmean_obs <- with(bessel_errors,                   sum(observed * midpoint) / sum(observed)) wmean_exp <- with(bessel_errors,                   sum(expected * midpoint) / sum(expected)) c(observed = wmean_obs, expected_under_normal = wmean_exp) #>              observed expected_under_normal  #>             0.1770000             0.1746667   # Weighted variance and standard deviation of the absolute # error, using bin midpoints as plug-in values for the # individual observations. wvar_obs <- with(bessel_errors,                  sum(observed * (midpoint - wmean_obs)^2) /                  (sum(observed) - 1)) c(weighted_variance = wvar_obs,   weighted_sd       = sqrt(wvar_obs)) #> weighted_variance       weighted_sd  #>        0.02084047        0.14436228   # Side-by-side bar plot of observed and expected counts. # Bessel's normal-model expectation tracks the empirical # distribution closely except in the long right tail, where # Bradley's three largest errors (counts 3, 1, 1) exceed what # the normal model predicts. op <- par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2)) barplot(rbind(bessel_errors$observed, bessel_errors$expected),         beside    = TRUE,         names.arg = sprintf("%.1f-%.1f",                             bessel_errors$lower,                             bessel_errors$upper),         legend.text = c("Observed (Bradley)",                         "Expected under normal model"),         args.legend = list(x = "topright", bty = "n"),         xlab = "Absolute error (seconds of arc)",         ylab = "Frequency",         main = "Bessel (1818) on Bradley's 300 stellar positions")  par(op)

code: # Nine items: one general factor and three orthogonal group factors. set.seed(113) n <- 600 g <- rnorm(n); grp <- list(rnorm(n), rnorm(n), rnorm(n)) X <- vapply(1:9, function(i)   0.5 * g + 0.5 * grp[[ceiling(i / 3)]] + sqrt(0.5) * rnorm(n), numeric(n)) colnames(X) <- paste0("x", 1:9) model <- "g  =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8 + x9           f1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3           f2 =~ x4 + x5 + x6           f3 =~ x7 + x8 + x9" fit <- lavaan::cfa(model, data = as.data.frame(X),                    orthogonal = TRUE, std.lv = TRUE) bifactor_indices(fit) #>  factor ECV   omega omega_H omega_HS PUC   H     #>  g      0.547 0.858 0.673   <NA>     0.750 0.769 #>  f1     0.609 0.727 <NA>    0.280    <NA>  0.412 #>  f2     0.543 0.756 <NA>    0.345    <NA>  0.477 #>  f3     0.490 0.743 <NA>    0.377    <NA>  0.506 #>  #> Denominator: composite variance implied by the fitted model #>  #> For a group factor, ECV is the general factor's share of the common variance of that factor's items (one minus it is the group factor's share), and omega is the reliability of their total score #> H is the index of Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016), which counts the other factors' common variance as uncorrelated error; title: The Bryant-Paulson Generalized Studentized Range Distribution — bryant_paulson
code: # Critical value from the worked example of Bryant and Bruvold (1980): # k = 6 panels, p = 1 covariate, nu = 14 error df, alpha = .05. The quantile # is found by inverting the distribution function with uniroot; it is 4.83, # the entry in Table 1 of Bryant and Paulson (1976). qbryant_paulson(0.95, n_covariates = 1, n_groups = 6, df = 14) #> [1] 4.829856  # The ordinary Tukey value (ignoring that the covariate is random and # estimated) is smaller, 4.64, so it yields intervals that are too narrow: qtukey(0.95, nmeans = 6, df = 14) #> [1] 4.638538  # How much too narrow: the Bryant-Paulson area beyond the Tukey value is the # familywise error rate Tukey's method actually delivers in this design. # With no covariate the two distributions coincide, so the area is .0499, # the nominal .05 up to the rounding of 4.64 itself. Each additional random # covariate carries more estimation uncertainty, stretches the distribution # to the right, and pushes the rate up, to .063, .076, and .091. pbryant_paulson(4.64, n_covariates = 0:3, n_groups = 6, df = 14,                 lower_tail = FALSE) #> [1] 0.04990724 0.06273456 0.07633320 0.09054790  # The p = 0 entry above is exactly the ordinary studentized range: ptukey(4.64, nmeans = 6, df = 14, lower.tail = FALSE) #> [1] 0.04990724

title: Confidence Interval for the Population Squared Multiple Correlation Coefficient — ci_R2
text: Constructs confidence interval population squared multiple correlation coefficient \(\rho^2\) inverting sampling distribution sample \(R^2\). confidence interval population value \(\rho^2\); required input corresponding sample value, observed sample squared multiple correlation coefficient \(R^2\) (, equivalently, observed F-statistic degrees freedom). right choice sampling distribution, right interval, depends whether predictors treated random draws joint multivariate normal distribution (default typical case behavioral, educational, social sciences) fixed design (planned dosing levels, factorial covariates, etc.). function selects sampling distribution via random_predictors inverts corresponding noncentral distribution; construction regression analog noncentral distribution based CI standardized effect size (Steiger & Fouladi, 1992; Kelley, 2007).

title: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for the Bifactor Indices — ci_bifactor_indices
code: # The nine-item bifactor model of ?bifactor_indices: one general factor # and three orthogonal group factors, simulated so that resamples give # proper solutions and the example runs quickly. (The 15-test # Holzinger and Swineford model of Details gives an improper solution # in a fifth of its resamples, each of which took seconds to fit.) set.seed(113) n <- 600 g <- rnorm(n); grp <- list(rnorm(n), rnorm(n), rnorm(n)) X <- vapply(1:9, function(i)   0.5 * g + 0.5 * grp[[ceiling(i / 3)]] + sqrt(0.5) * rnorm(n), numeric(n)) colnames(X) <- paste0("x", 1:9) model <- "g  =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8 + x9           f1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3           f2 =~ x4 + x5 + x6           f3 =~ x7 + x8 + x9" fit <- lavaan::cfa(model, data = as.data.frame(X),                    orthogonal = TRUE, std.lv = TRUE)  # Every replication refits the bifactor model. B = 10 keeps the # example quick and is below the 400 a reported interval needs; the # option lets it run and the warning says so. A reported interval # deserves the default B = 1000. A resample whose solution is improper # is set aside, and the warning and the printed lines count it. old <- options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) ci <- ci_bifactor_indices(fit, B = 10, seed = 113) #> Warning: ci_bifactor_indices(): B = 10 is below the 400 replications a 95% interval is reported from (10 beyond each limit). The limits are shown because options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) is set. With 10 replications each limit rests on about 0.3 of them and will move from seed to seed; use the result to explore or to demonstrate, and report an interval only from B of at least 400. title: Confidence Interval for a Contrast in a Fixed Effects ANOVA — ci_c
code: # Here is a four group example. Suppose that the means of groups 1--4 are 2, 4, 9, # and 13, respectively. Further, let the error variance be .64 and thus the standard # deviation would be .80 (note we use the standard deviation in the function, not the # variance). The contrast of interest here is the average of groups 1 and 4 versus the # average of groups 2 and 3. ci_c(means = c(2, 4, 9, 13), s_anova = .80, c_weights = c(.5, -.5, -.5, .5), n_per_group = c(3, 3, 3, 3), N = 12, conf_level = .95) #>  term     value  #>  ci_lower -0.065 #>  contrast 1.000  #>  ci_upper 2.065  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Here is an example with two groups. ci_c(means = c(1.6, 0), s_anova = .80, c_weights = c(1, -1), n_per_group = c(10, 10), N = 20, conf_level = .95) #>  term     value #>  ci_lower 0.848 #>  contrast 1.600 #>  ci_upper 2.352 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # An example given by Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley (2027) : # 20 subjects of mild hypertensives are assigned to one of four treatments: drug # therapy, biofeedback, dietary modification, and a treatment combining all the # three previous treatments. Subjects' blood pressure is measured two weeks # after the termination of treatment. Now we want to form a 95% level # confidence interval for the difference in blood pressure between subjects # who received drug treatment and those who received biofeedback treatment  ## Drug group's mean = 94; group size=4 ## Biofeedback group's mean = 91; group size=6 ## Diet group's mean = 92; group size=5 ## Combination group's mean = 83; group size=5 ## Mean Square Within (i.e., 'error_variance') = 67.375  ci_c(means = c(94, 91, 92, 83), s_anova = sqrt(67.375), c_weights = c(1, -1, 0, 0), n_per_group = c(4, 6, 5, 5), N = 20, conf_level = .95) #>  term     value  #>  ci_lower -8.232 #>  contrast 3.000  #>  ci_upper 14.232 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley (2027) offer an example that 30 depressive # individuals are randomly assigned to three groups, 10 in each, and ANCOVA # is performed on the posttest scores using the participants' pretest # scores as the covariate. The means of pretest scores of group 1 to 3 are # 17, 17.7, and 17.4, respectively, and the adjusted means of groups 1 to 3 # are 7.5, 12, and 14, respectively. The error variance in ANCOVA is 29, # and the sum of squares within groups from ANOVA on the covariate is 752.5.  # To obtain the confidence interval for adjusted mean of group 1 versus group 2: ci_c_ancova(adj_means = c(7.5, 12, 14), s_ancova = sqrt(29),             c_weights = c(1, -1, 0), n_per_group = 10,             cov_means = c(17, 17.7, 17.4), SSwithin_x = 752.5) #>  term     value  #>  ci_lower -9.458 #>  contrast -4.500 #>  ci_upper 0.458  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # That interval is the right one for a single contrast planned in advance. # For the family of all three pairwise comparisons of the adjusted means, # with coverage that holds simultaneously across the family, select # procedure = "bryant_paulson"; the call is forwarded to ci_c_ancova_bp(). # The simultaneous limits are wider, which is the price of the family # statement: group 1 against group 2 runs from -10.61 to 1.61, where the # single planned contrast above ran from -9.46 to 0.46. ci_c_ancova(adj_means = c(7.5, 12, 14), s_ancova = sqrt(29), n_per_group = 10,             procedure = "bryant_paulson") #>  contrast          estimate ci_lower ci_upper #>  group_1 - group_2 -4.500   -10.607  1.607    #>  group_1 - group_3 -6.500   -12.607  -0.393   #>  group_2 - group_3 -2.000   -8.107   4.107    #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # Bryant and Bruvold (1980) worked example: 6 panels, 1 covariate, nu = 14, # ANCOVA error MS = 0.01326. Here the design is a randomized block with # s = 4 blocks, so the per-group size for the adjusted-mean SE is 4 and the # error df (14) must be supplied directly. The multiplier for these # intervals is a Bryant-Paulson quantile, which has no closed form; it is # obtained by inverting the distribution function with a root search. adj <- c(3.595, 3.619, 4.102, 4.515, 4.618, 4.876) bp <- ci_c_ancova_bp(adj_means = adj, s_ancova = sqrt(0.01326),                      n_per_group = 4, n_covariates = 1, df = 14) bp #>  contrast          estimate ci_lower ci_upper #>  group_1 - group_2 -0.024   -0.302   0.254    #>  group_1 - group_3 -0.507   -0.785   -0.229   #>  group_1 - group_4 -0.920   -1.198   -0.642   #>  group_1 - group_5 -1.023   -1.301   -0.745   #>  group_1 - group_6 -1.281   -1.559   -1.003   #>  group_2 - group_3 -0.483   -0.761   -0.205   #>  group_2 - group_4 -0.896   -1.174   -0.618   #>  group_2 - group_5 -0.999   -1.277   -0.721   #>  group_2 - group_6 -1.257   -1.535   -0.979   #>  group_3 - group_4 -0.413   -0.691   -0.135   #>  group_3 - group_5 -0.516   -0.794   -0.238   #>  group_3 - group_6 -0.774   -1.052   -0.496   #>  group_4 - group_5 -0.103   -0.381   0.175    #>  group_4 - group_6 -0.361   -0.639   -0.083   #>  group_5 - group_6 -0.258   -0.536   0.020    #>  #> Confidence level: 95% # The multiplier is 4.83 and every pairwise critical difference is 0.278, # matching the paper; the 15 intervals hold jointly at the 95 percent level. # The multiplier is kept on the result, so the critical difference can be # rebuilt by hand as q * s_ancova * sqrt(1/n): attr(bp, "critical_value") #> [1] 4.829856 attr(bp, "critical_value") * sqrt(0.01326) * sqrt(1 / 4) #> [1] 0.278084  # A complex contrast (say panels 1 and 2 against panels 3 through 6) is # requested by passing its weights to c_weights, together with # contrast_type = "allowance", the all-contrasts form of Eq. (2.4) of # Bryant and Bruvold. code: # Shrout and Fleiss (1979, Table 2): four judges each rated the same # six targets. ratings <- matrix(c( 9, 2, 5, 8,                      6, 1, 3, 2,                      8, 4, 6, 8,                      7, 1, 2, 6,                     10, 5, 6, 9,                      6, 2, 4, 7),                   nrow = 6, byrow = TRUE) fit <- ci_crossed(ratings) fit #>  term         value #>  ci_lower     1.827 #>  grand_mean   5.292 #>  ci_upper     8.756 #>  se           1.334 #>  df           4.837 #>  var_unit     2.556 #>  var_rater    5.244 #>  var_residual 1.019 #>  n_units      6     #>  n_raters     4     #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # The judges differ a great deal in leniency, and with only four of # them the interval for the mean over the population of judges is wide. # Treating these four judges as the only ones of interest ignores that # variability; the interval from the six target means is much narrower. t.test(rowMeans(ratings))$conf.int #> [1] 3.532362 7.050972 #> attr(,"conf.level") #> [1] 0.95  # The variance components are planning values for a larger study, here # one whose 95% interval for the mean is no wider than 2 points. v <- setNames(fit$value, fit$term) ss_aipe_crossed(true_var_unit = v[["var_unit"]], true_var_rater = v[["var_rater"]],                 true_var_residual = v[["var_residual"]], width = 2) #>  term               value  #>  necessary_n_units  22     #>  necessary_n_raters 40     #>  total_judgments    880    #>  cost               880    #>  expected_width     1.997  #>  df                 55.903 #>  rater_floor        20.146 #>  true_var_unit      2.556  #>  true_var_rater     5.244  #>  true_var_residual  1.019  #>  width              2      #>  conf_level         0.950  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # The raw drinks_per_week outcome of the drinks_trial data: the arms hold # 37, 32, and 19 patients, fewer than the roughly 50 per group below # which Games-Howell runs slightly liberal, and the Standard arm's # variance is more than three times that of either CRA arm. ci_dunnett_t3(drinks_trial$drinks_per_week, drinks_trial$treatment) #>  contrast                    mean_difference se     df     t_value ci_lower #>  CRA - Standard              -24.474         20.108 56.392 -1.217  -73.898  #>  CRA + Disulfiram - Standard -24.690         22.363 53.210 -1.104  -79.753  #>  CRA + Disulfiram - CRA      -0.216          17.178 35.653 -0.013  -43.164  #>  ci_upper p_adjusted #>  24.950   0.5366     #>  30.373   0.6135     #>  42.732   1.0000     #>  #> Confidence level: 95%, simultaneous interval (Dunnett's T3)  # A fitted one-way model may be passed instead of the two vectors. ci_dunnett_t3(aov(drinks_per_week ~ treatment, data = drinks_trial)) #>  contrast                    mean_difference se     df     t_value ci_lower #>  CRA - Standard              -24.474         20.108 56.392 -1.217  -73.898  #>  CRA + Disulfiram - Standard -24.690         22.363 53.210 -1.104  -79.753  #>  CRA + Disulfiram - CRA      -0.216          17.178 35.653 -0.013  -43.164  #>  ci_upper p_adjusted #>  24.950   0.5366     #>  30.373   0.6135     #>  42.732   1.0000     #>  #> Confidence level: 95%, simultaneous interval (Dunnett's T3)  # Each half-width is the studentized maximum modulus critical value for # the three comparisons, at that pair's degrees of freedom, times the # pair's standard error. t3 <- ci_dunnett_t3(drinks_trial$drinks_per_week, drinks_trial$treatment) t3$ci_upper[1] - t3$mean_difference[1] #> [1] 49.42394 cv_smm(alpha_level = .05, df = t3$df[1], n_comparisons = 3)$value * t3$se[1] #> [1] 49.42394

text: Asymptotic distribution. multivariate normality eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 > \lambda_2 \ge \cdots \ge \lambda_p\), sample eigenvalues \(\hat\lambda_j\) asymptotically independent approximately normal mean \(\lambda_j\) variance \(2 \lambda_j^2 / (N - 1)\) eigenvalues simple (well-separated) (Anderson, 2003, Theorem 13.3.1; Muirhead, 1982, Section 9.7). asymptotic CI therefore $$\hat\lambda_j   \cdot \exp\!\left(\pm z_{1 - \alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{2}{N - 1}}\right),$$ multiplicative scale (equivalently, Wald CI \(\log \lambda_j\) variance \(2/(N - 1)\)). log scale natural variance-stabilizing transformation eigenvalue. Caveats. asymptotic CI assumes well-separated population eigenvalues. largest two eigenvalues close, sample eigenvalue exhibits "repulsion" phenomenon CI biased (typically narrow). Diagnostic: \(\hat\lambda_1 / \hat\lambda_2\) close 1, asymptotic CI relied upon; bootstrap preferable.

code: # 1. The F interface. Bargmann's (1970) example, used in turn by #    Venables (1975), Fleishman (1980), and Steiger (2004): a one-way #    ANOVA with five groups of 11 and an observed F of 11.221 on 4 and #    50 df, at 90%. F determines the partial value, which in a one-way #    design is the total. ci_eta_squared(F_value = 11.221, df_effect = 4, df_error = 50, N = 55,                estimand = "partial", conf_level = 0.90) #>  effect  eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower #>  overall 0.473               0.261                        #>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N  #>  0.565                        11.221  4         50       55 #>  #> Confidence level: 90%  # 2. One-way ANOVA from a fitted model: mean IQ gain differs across #    the six grades of the pygmalion data (N = 310). The total and the #    partial value coincide, and so do their intervals. fit_one <- aov(iq_gain ~ factor(grade), data = pygmalion) ci_eta_squared(fit_one) #>  effect        eta_squared_total eta_squared_total_ci_lower #>  factor(grade) 0.118             0.048                      #>  eta_squared_total_ci_upper eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower #>  0.176                      0.118               0.048                        #>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N   #>  0.176                        8.159   5         304      310 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # 3. Two-factor ANOVA for the manipulated expectancy treatment and the #    measured grade classification (pygmalion data, N = 310). The #    treatment by grade interaction is weak here (F = 1.19), so the #    additive model is used. The totals are reported without limits. fit_additive <- aov(iq_8 ~ treatment + factor(grade), data = pygmalion) ci_eta_squared(fit_additive) #>  effect        eta_squared_total eta_squared_total_ci_lower #>  treatment     0.020             <NA>                       #>  factor(grade) 0.043             <NA>                       #>  eta_squared_total_ci_upper eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower #>  <NA>                       0.021               0.001                        #>  <NA>                       0.044               0.001                        #>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N   #>  0.062                        6.519   1         303      310 #>  0.082                        2.787   5         303      310 #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> NA eta_squared_total limits: No confidence interval is formed for the total eta squared of an effect in a design with other effects or with an Error() term: the noncentral F interval from the effect's F is an interval for the partial value, and the total depends as well on the other effects of the design (see the Details of ?ci_eta_squared).  # 4. Within-subjects ANOVA. The partial value's interval is computed #    against the within-subjects error stratum, named in 'stratum'. set.seed(113) n <- 20 rm_data <- data.frame(   subject = factor(rep(seq_len(n), each = 3)),   time    = factor(rep(c("Pre", "Mid", "Post"), n),                    levels = c("Pre", "Mid", "Post")),   y       = rnorm(n, sd = 1.5)[rep(seq_len(n), each = 3)] +             0.7 * rep(1:3, n) + rnorm(n * 3, sd = 1.2) ) fit_rm <- aov(y ~ time + Error(subject/time), data = rm_data) ci_eta_squared(fit_rm, estimand = "partial") #>  effect eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower #>  time   0.231               0.023                        #>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper stratum      F_value df_effect df_error N  #>  0.417                        subject:time 5.701   2         38       60 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # 5. The size with which the limits are converted. The interaction of #    the 2 by 7 design with four observations per cell analyzed by #    Steiger (2004, p. 171), F = 2.50 on 6 and 42 df, at 90%: the #    total sample size of 56 gives the interval for the population #    partial eta squared, and 6 + 42 + 1 = 49 gives the limits that #    Smithson (2001) reports for the same F. ci_eta_squared(F_value = 2.50, df_effect = 6, df_error = 42, N = 56,                estimand = "partial", conf_level = 0.90) #>  effect  eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower #>  overall 0.263               0.008                        #>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N  #>  0.316                        2.500   6         42       56 #>  #> Confidence level: 90% ci_eta_squared(F_value = 2.50, df_effect = 6, df_error = 42, N = 49,                estimand = "partial", conf_level = 0.90) #>  effect  eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower #>  overall 0.263               0.009                        #>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N  #>  0.346                        2.500   6         42       49 #>  #> Confidence level: 90%  # 6. A within-subjects F from a report: the three IQ occasions of the #    pygmalion data, F(2, 618) = 83.11 for 310 children. N is the #    620 degrees of freedom of the occasion stratum, not 930 rows. ci_eta_squared(F_value = 83.11, df_effect = 2, df_error = 618, N = 620,                estimand = "partial") #>  effect  eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower #>  overall 0.212               0.157                        #>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N   #>  0.265                        83.110  2         618      620 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # The pygmalion expectancy experiment: treatment is manipulated, while # grade is a measured classification, so grade belongs in the denominator. pyg <- pygmalion pyg$grade <- factor(pyg$grade) fit <- aov(iq_8 ~ treatment * grade, data = pyg)  # The default returns the point estimate and leaves the limits NA, because # both interval methods are approximations. ci_eta_squared_generalized(fit, observed = "grade") #> No CI computed (method = 'none'). Set method = 'parametric' for an approximate noncentral F transformation, or method = 'bootstrap' for a residual bootstrap (requires a fitted model). Both methods are approximate; see ?ci_eta_squared_generalized. #>  effect          eta_squared_generalized ci_lower ci_upper method #>  treatment       0.020                   <NA>     <NA>     none   #>  grade           0.044                   <NA>     <NA>     none   #>  treatment:grade 0.019                   <NA>     <NA>     none    # The parametric approximation maps a noncentral F interval for the focal # effect through the observed sums of squares. Warnings mark the method as # preliminary and report that the interaction's lower limit is clamped at # 0; treat the limits accordingly. ci_eta_squared_generalized(fit, observed = "grade", method = "parametric") #> Warning: Parametric CI uses an approximate transformation that maps the partial eta squared CI through the observed sums of squares for measured factors. Coverage properties have not been broadly validated; results should be treated as preliminary and independently evaluated. #> Warning: The observed F_value is below the alpha_lower critical value of the central F-distribution, so the lower confidence limit on generalized eta squared is 0. #>  effect          eta_squared_generalized ci_lower ci_upper method     #>  treatment       0.020                   0.001    0.058    parametric #>  grade           0.044                   0.001    0.081    parametric #>  treatment:grade 0.019                   0.000    0.041    parametric #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # The third option is a residual bootstrap, which refits the model once per # replication. B = 100 keeps the example quick and is below the 1000 the # function requires; the option lets it run and the warning says so. A # reported interval deserves B = 10000 or more. The seed makes the # interval reproducible and leaves the random number stream of the # surrounding session as it was. old <- options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) ci_eta_squared_generalized(fit, observed = "grade",                            method = "bootstrap", B = 100, seed = 113) #> Warning: Bootstrap CI resamples the fitted model's residuals nonparametrically (B = 100). Coverage has not been broadly validated for generalized eta squared; results should be treated as preliminary. #> Warning: ci_eta_squared_generalized(): B = 100 is below the 1000 replications a 95% interval is reported from (10 beyond each limit). The limits are shown because options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) is set. With 100 replications each limit rests on about 2.5 of them and will move from seed to seed; use the result to explore or to demonstrate, and report an interval only from B of at least 1000. B, B_used, and B_required are recorded in the result. #>  effect          eta_squared_generalized ci_lower ci_upper method    #>  treatment       0.020                   0.001    0.059    bootstrap #>  grade           0.044                   0.022    0.108    bootstrap #>  treatment:grade 0.019                   0.007    0.083    bootstrap #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Bootstrap: 100 replications, 100 used (0 dropped; at least 1000 must be requested). Exploratory: below the number required for a reported interval. options(old)  # The parametric treatment row from summary statistics, as an ANOVA table # reports them: the sums of squares of treatment, of its error term (the # residual), and of the measured sources in its denominator (grade and # the treatment by grade interaction), with the degrees of freedom and # the number of children for the interval. tab <- anova(fit) ci_eta_squared_generalized(   SS_effect   = tab["treatment", "Sum Sq"],   SS_observed = tab[c("grade", "treatment:grade"), "Sum Sq"],   SS_error    = tab["Residuals", "Sum Sq"],   df_effect   = tab["treatment", "Df"], df_error = tab["Residuals", "Df"],   N = nobs(fit), method = "parametric") #> Warning: Parametric CI uses an approximate transformation that maps the partial eta squared CI through the observed sums of squares for measured factors. Coverage properties have not been broadly validated; results should be treated as preliminary and independently evaluated. #>  effect  eta_squared_generalized ci_lower ci_upper method     #>  overall 0.020                   0.001    0.058    parametric #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Within-subjects ANOVA. The parametric CI uses each effect's own stratum # and converts its limits with that stratum's size. set.seed(113) n <- 20 rm_data <- data.frame(   subject = factor(rep(seq_len(n), each = 3)),   time    = factor(rep(c("Pre", "Mid", "Post"), n),                    levels = c("Pre", "Mid", "Post")),   y       = rnorm(n, sd = 1.5)[rep(seq_len(n), each = 3)] +             0.7 * rep(1:3, n) + rnorm(n * 3, sd = 1.2) ) fit_rm <- aov(y ~ time + Error(subject/time), data = rm_data) ci_eta_squared_generalized(fit_rm, method = "parametric") #> Warning: Parametric CI uses an approximate transformation that maps the partial eta squared CI through the observed sums of squares for measured factors. Coverage properties have not been broadly validated; results should be treated as preliminary and independently evaluated. #>  effect eta_squared_generalized stratum      ci_lower ci_upper method     #>  time   0.097                   subject:time 0.008    0.203    parametric #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # The raw drinks_per_week outcome of the drinks_trial data: the # Standard arm's variance is more than three times that of either CRA # arm, so the pooled error term Tukey's HSD relies on is questionable. ci_games_howell(drinks_trial$drinks_per_week, drinks_trial$treatment) #>  contrast                    mean_difference se     df     q_statistic ci_lower #>  CRA - Standard              -24.474         14.219 56.392 -1.721      -72.876  #>  CRA + Disulfiram - Standard -24.690         15.813 53.210 -1.561      -78.608  #>  CRA + Disulfiram - CRA      -0.216          12.146 35.653 -0.018      -42.221  #>  ci_upper p_adjusted #>  23.929   0.4481     #>  29.228   0.5158     #>  41.788   0.9999     #>  #> Confidence level: 95%, simultaneous interval (Games-Howell)  # A fitted one-way model may be passed instead of the two vectors. ci_games_howell(aov(drinks_per_week ~ treatment, data = drinks_trial)) #>  contrast                    mean_difference se     df     q_statistic ci_lower #>  CRA - Standard              -24.474         14.219 56.392 -1.721      -72.876  #>  CRA + Disulfiram - Standard -24.690         15.813 53.210 -1.561      -78.608  #>  CRA + Disulfiram - CRA      -0.216          12.146 35.653 -0.018      -42.221  #>  ci_upper p_adjusted #>  23.929   0.4481     #>  29.228   0.5158     #>  41.788   0.9999     #>  #> Confidence level: 95%, simultaneous interval (Games-Howell)  # With two groups the procedure is Welch's t test, so the limits agree; # the trial's two enrollment cohorts give a two-group comparison. ci_games_howell(drinks_trial$drinks_per_week, drinks_trial$cohort)$ci_lower #> [1] -48.36926 -t.test(drinks_per_week ~ cohort, data = drinks_trial)$conf.int[2] #> [1] -48.36926

title: Confidence Interval for the Squared Mahalanobis Distance — ci_mahalanobis
text: Definition. \(p\)-vector \(\mathbf{x}\) drawn multivariate normal mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\), Mahalanobis's (1936) squared distance reference vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_0\) (argument null_mean one-sample case) $$\Delta^2 = (\boldsymbol{\mu} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_0)^\top                   \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}                   (\boldsymbol{\mu} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_0).$$ two-sample case population distance groups \(\Delta^2 = (\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2)^\top                  \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}                  (\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2)\), assuming common covariance. corresponding sample estimates plug sample means sample (pooled) covariance quadratic form. Link Hotelling's \(T^2\). Hotelling's (1931) \(T^2\) statistic \(T^2 = n D^2\) (one sample) \(T^2 = \{n_1 n_2 / (n_1 + n_2)\} D^2\) (two samples). multivariate normality $$\frac{n_1 + n_2 - p - 1}{(n_1 + n_2 - 2)\,p}\,T^2 \sim         F'\!\left(p,\, n_1 + n_2 - p - 1,\;                   \lambda = \frac{n_1 n_2}{n_1 + n_2}\,\Delta^2\right)$$ two-sample case, analogously \(\{(n - p)/[(n-1)p]\}\,T^2 \sim F'(p, n-p, n\Delta^2)\) one-sample case (see Anderson, 2003, Section 5.2). Confidence interval. CI \(\Delta^2\) obtained inverting distributional results (Reiser, 2001): CI noncentrality parameter \(\lambda\) constructed via ci_nc_F mapped back \(\Delta^2\) \(\Delta^2 = \lambda\,(n_1 + n_2)/(n_1 n_2)\) (two sample) \(\Delta^2 = \lambda / n\) (one sample). observed \(F\) lower-tail critical value central F-distribution requested confidence level, lower CI \(\lambda\) (hence \(\Delta^2\)) clamped zero, keeping ci_nc_F convention. Bias. plug-estimator \(D^2\) upward biased \(\Delta^2\); CI function exact \(\Delta^2\) multivariate normality reflects bias structure correctly, point estimate reported standard plug-\(D^2\).

title: Confidence Interval for the Squared Mahalanobis Distance — ci_mahalanobis
code: # Two-sample distance between the two schools of the holzinger_swineford #     data on a four-test cognitive battery. battery <- c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t4_lozenges",              "t6_paragraph_comprehension") g1 <- as.matrix(holzinger_swineford[   holzinger_swineford$school == "Grant-White", battery]) g2 <- as.matrix(holzinger_swineford[   holzinger_swineford$school == "Pasteur", battery]) ci_mahalanobis(group_1 = g1, group_2 = g2) #>  sample_type D2    ci_lower ci_upper F_value df_1 df_2 n_1 n_2 p #>  two-sample  0.608 0.259    0.975    11.314  4    296  145 156 4 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # One-sample distance: how far is the Grant-White centroid from a #     reference vector of (29, 24, 18, 9)? ci_mahalanobis(group_1 = g1, null_mean = c(29, 24, 18, 9)) #>  sample_type D2    ci_lower ci_upper F_value df_1 df_2 n_1 n_2  p #>  one-sample  0.289 0.110    0.474    10.248  4    141  145 <NA> 4 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Pre-computed D^2 (no raw data needed): the two-school distance, #     reproduced from reported summaries. ci_mahalanobis(D2 = 0.608, n_1 = 145, n_2 = 156, p = 4) #>  sample_type D2    ci_lower ci_upper F_value df_1 df_2 n_1 n_2 p #>  two-sample  0.608 0.259    0.974    11.308  4    296  145 156 4 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

title: Confidence Interval for Omega Squared (Effect Size for ANOVA) — ci_omega_squared
code: # 1. The F interface. Bargmann's (1970) example, used in turn by #    Venables (1975), Fleishman (1980), and Steiger (2004): a one-way #    ANOVA with five groups of 11 and an observed F of 11.221 on 4 and #    50 df, at 95% and at 90%. F determines the partial value, which in #    a one-way design is the total. ci_omega_squared(F_value = 11.221, df_effect = 4, df_error = 50, N = 55,                  estimand = "partial") #>  effect  omega_squared_partial omega_squared_partial_ci_lower #>  overall 0.426                 0.226                          #>  omega_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N  #>  0.587                          11.221  4         50       55 #>  #> Confidence level: 95% ci_omega_squared(F_value = 11.221, df_effect = 4, df_error = 50, N = 55,                  estimand = "partial", conf_level = 0.90) #>  effect  omega_squared_partial omega_squared_partial_ci_lower #>  overall 0.426                 0.261                          #>  omega_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N  #>  0.565                          11.221  4         50       55 #>  #> Confidence level: 90%  # 2. One-way ANOVA from a fitted model: mean IQ gain differs across #    the six grades of the pygmalion data (N = 310). fit_one <- aov(iq_gain ~ factor(grade), data = pygmalion) ci_omega_squared(fit_one) #>  effect        omega_squared_total omega_squared_total_ci_lower #>  factor(grade) 0.104               0.048                        #>  omega_squared_total_ci_upper omega_squared_partial #>  0.176                        0.104                 #>  omega_squared_partial_ci_lower omega_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value #>  0.048                          0.176                          8.159   #>  df_effect df_error N   #>  5         304      310 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # 3. Two-factor ANOVA for the manipulated expectancy treatment and the #    measured grade classification (pygmalion data, N = 310). The #    treatment by grade interaction is weak here (F = 1.19), so the #    additive model is used. fit_additive <- aov(iq_8 ~ treatment + factor(grade), data = pygmalion) ci_omega_squared(fit_additive) #>  effect        omega_squared_total omega_squared_total_ci_lower #>  treatment     0.017               <NA>                         #>  factor(grade) 0.028               <NA>                         #>  omega_squared_total_ci_upper omega_squared_partial #>  <NA>                         0.017                 #>  <NA>                         0.028                 #>  omega_squared_partial_ci_lower omega_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value #>  0.001                          0.062                          6.519   #>  0.001                          0.082                          2.787   #>  df_effect df_error N   #>  1         303      310 #>  5         303      310 #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> NA omega_squared_total limits: No confidence interval is formed for the total omega squared of an effect in a design with other effects or with an Error() term: the noncentral F interval from the effect's F is an interval for the partial value, and the total depends as well on the other effects of the design (see the Details of ?ci_omega_squared).

code: # Liver scan data from McNeil, Keeler, and Adelstein (1975), the # example of Nam (1997, p. 1427): 344 patients classified as positive # or negative by scan (x) and by pathology (y). Only the 32 and 27 # patients on whom the two disagree inform the difference in the # positive rates. liver <- matrix(c(231, 27, 32, 54), nrow = 2,                 dimnames = list(scan = c("positive", "negative"),                                 pathology = c("positive", "negative"))) liver #>           pathology #> scan       positive negative #>   positive      231       32 #>   negative       27       54 ci_proportion_paired(n_10 = liver["positive", "negative"],                      n_01 = liver["negative", "positive"],                      N = sum(liver)) #>  term       value  #>  ci_lower   -0.030 #>  difference 0.015  #>  ci_upper   0.059  #>  n_10       32     #>  n_01       27     #>  N          344    #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # From raw outcomes: two judges assign the same 200 cases to one of # three diagnoses. diagnosis_agreement holds one row per cell of their # agreement table, so repeating each row by its frequency gives one row # per case. How much more often does Judge A (x) than Judge B (y) # diagnose a personality disorder? cases <- diagnosis_agreement[rep(seq_len(nrow(diagnosis_agreement)),                                  diagnosis_agreement$frequency), ] ci_proportion_paired(x = cases$judge_a == "Personality disorder",                      y = cases$judge_b == "Personality disorder") #>  term       value #>  ci_lower   0.036 #>  difference 0.100 #>  ci_upper   0.166 #>  n_10       32    #>  n_01       12    #>  N          200   #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # When the two conditions agree on all 40 units, the Wald interval has # zero width, as though the difference were known exactly; the score # interval still reflects how few units were observed. ci_proportion_paired(n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, N = 40) #>  term       value  #>  ci_lower   -0.088 #>  difference 0.000  #>  ci_upper   0.088  #>  n_10       0      #>  n_01       0      #>  N          40     #>  #> Confidence level: 95% ci_proportion_paired(n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, N = 40, method = "wald") #>  term       value #>  ci_lower   0.000 #>  difference 0.000 #>  ci_upper   0.000 #>  n_10       0     #>  n_01       0     #>  N          40    #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

title: Confidence Interval for the Ratio of Two Independent Means — ci_ratio_of_means
code: # Drinks per week among the homeless alcohol-dependent adults of # drinks_trial: the mean under the community reinforcement approach (CRA) # relative to the mean under standard treatment. The group variances are # not assumed equal. drinks <- drinks_trial$drinks_per_week cra <- drinks[drinks_trial$treatment == "CRA"] standard <- drinks[drinks_trial$treatment == "Standard"] ci_ratio_of_means(cra, standard) #>  term           value  #>  ci_lower       0.116  #>  ratio          0.521  #>  ci_upper       1.865  #>  excluded_lower <NA>   #>  excluded_upper <NA>   #>  mean_1         26.636 #>  mean_2         51.110 #>  mean_baseline  <NA>   #>  se_1           9.982  #>  se_2           17.456 #>  se_baseline    <NA>   #>  t_denominator  2.928  #>  df             36     #>  n_1            32     #>  n_2            37     #>  n_baseline     <NA>   #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Fieller confidence set: a bounded interval.  # The drinking counts are strongly skewed, so the response ratio interval # and a BCa bootstrap interval are worth setting beside Fieller's; # B = 2000 keeps the example quick, and a reported interval deserves the # default B = 10000. ci_ratio_of_means(cra, standard, ci_method = "log") #>  term           value  #>  ci_lower       0.189  #>  ratio          0.521  #>  ci_upper       1.435  #>  excluded_lower <NA>   #>  excluded_upper <NA>   #>  mean_1         26.636 #>  mean_2         51.110 #>  mean_baseline  <NA>   #>  se_1           9.982  #>  se_2           17.456 #>  se_baseline    <NA>   #>  t_denominator  2.928  #>  df             36     #>  n_1            32     #>  n_2            37     #>  n_baseline     <NA>   #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Log ratio interval: a bounded interval. ci_ratio_of_means(cra, standard, ci_method = "bca", B = 2000, seed = 113) #>  term           value  #>  ci_lower       0.156  #>  ratio          0.521  #>  ci_upper       1.276  #>  excluded_lower <NA>   #>  excluded_upper <NA>   #>  mean_1         26.636 #>  mean_2         51.110 #>  mean_baseline  <NA>   #>  se_1           9.982  #>  se_2           17.456 #>  se_baseline    <NA>   #>  t_denominator  2.928  #>  df             36     #>  n_1            32     #>  n_2            37     #>  n_baseline     <NA>   #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> BCa bootstrap interval: a bounded interval. #>  #> Bootstrap: 2000 replications, 2000 used (0 dropped; at least 2000 must be requested)  # From the summary statistics a paper reports, with pooled variances. ci_ratio_of_means(mean_1 = 104, sd_1 = 14, n_1 = 40,                   mean_2 = 96, sd_2 = 15, n_2 = 42, var_equal = TRUE) #>  term           value   #>  ci_lower       1.016   #>  ratio          1.083   #>  ci_upper       1.155   #>  excluded_lower <NA>    #>  excluded_upper <NA>    #>  mean_1         104.000 #>  mean_2         96.000  #>  mean_baseline  <NA>    #>  se_1           2.296   #>  se_2           2.241   #>  se_baseline    <NA>    #>  t_denominator  42.845  #>  df             80      #>  n_1            40      #>  n_2            42      #>  n_baseline     <NA>    #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Fieller confidence set: a bounded interval.  # A three-arm trial reported as summary statistics: the fraction of the # reference arm's advantage over placebo that the new arm retains. ci_ratio_of_means(mean_1 = 60.1, sd_1 = 12.2, n_1 = 60,                   mean_2 = 62.4, sd_2 = 10.1, n_2 = 60,                   mean_baseline = 50.3, sd_baseline = 9.8,                   n_baseline = 60) #>  term           value   #>  ci_lower       0.512   #>  ratio          0.810   #>  ci_upper       1.171   #>  excluded_lower <NA>    #>  excluded_upper <NA>    #>  mean_1         60.100  #>  mean_2         62.400  #>  mean_baseline  50.300  #>  se_1           1.575   #>  se_2           1.304   #>  se_baseline    1.265   #>  t_denominator  6.660   #>  df             117.893 #>  n_1            60      #>  n_2            60      #>  n_baseline     60      #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Fieller confidence set: a bounded interval.  # A three-arm trial: the fraction of the reference treatment's advantage # over placebo that a new treatment retains, with a one-sided 95 percent # lower bound. Noninferiority at a retained fraction f holds for every f # below the lower limit. set.seed(113) placebo <- rnorm(60, mean = 50, sd = 10) reference <- rnorm(60, mean = 62, sd = 10) new_drug <- rnorm(60, mean = 60, sd = 12) ci_ratio_of_means(new_drug, reference, baseline = placebo,                   alpha_lower = 0.05, alpha_upper = 0) #>  term           value   #>  ci_lower       0.357   #>  ratio          0.678   #>  ci_upper       Inf     #>  excluded_lower <NA>    #>  excluded_upper <NA>    #>  mean_1         57.699  #>  mean_2         60.465  #>  mean_baseline  51.864  #>  se_1           1.353   #>  se_2           1.359   #>  se_baseline    1.312   #>  t_denominator  4.553   #>  df             117.855 #>  n_1            60      #>  n_2            60      #>  n_baseline     60      #>  #> Confidence level: 95% (one-sided: the lower limit is the 95% lower confidence bound, with tail area 0.05 below it and none above the upper limit) #>  #> Fieller confidence set: an interval unbounded above.

code: # Depressive symptoms at the end of treatment relative to the start, # for the ten participants given the SSRI: the ratio of the posttest # mean to the pretest mean of the Beck Depression Inventory. ssri <- depression_bdi[depression_bdi$condition == "ssri", ] ci_ratio_of_means_paired(ssri$bdi_post, ssri$bdi_pre) #>  term           value  #>  ci_lower       0.218  #>  ratio          0.429  #>  ci_upper       0.632  #>  excluded_lower <NA>   #>  excluded_upper <NA>   #>  mean_1         7.300  #>  mean_2         17.000 #>  mean_baseline  <NA>   #>  se_numerator   1.693  #>  se_denominator 1.291  #>  r              0.442  #>  t_denominator  13.168 #>  df             9      #>  N              10     #>  n_clusters     <NA>   #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Fieller confidence set: a bounded interval.  # Fieller's (1954, p. 180) example, the ratio of the mean effects of two # hypnotic drugs given to the same ten patients, from his summary # statistics (variances of the means 0.3201 and 0.4009, covariance # 0.2848). Its denominator's t is 3.68, so the set is a bounded interval # at 95 percent, the complement of an interval at 99.5 percent, and the # whole line at 99.9 percent, as Fieller reported. drug_a_sd <- sqrt(10 * 0.3201) drug_b_sd <- sqrt(10 * 0.4009) r_ab <- 0.2848 / sqrt(0.3201 * 0.4009) ci_ratio_of_means_paired(mean_1 = 0.75, sd_1 = drug_a_sd, mean_2 = 2.33,                          sd_2 = drug_b_sd, r = r_ab, N = 10) #>  term           value  #>  ci_lower       -0.485 #>  ratio          0.322  #>  ci_upper       0.657  #>  excluded_lower <NA>   #>  excluded_upper <NA>   #>  mean_1         0.750  #>  mean_2         2.330  #>  mean_baseline  <NA>   #>  se_numerator   0.566  #>  se_denominator 0.633  #>  r              0.795  #>  t_denominator  3.680  #>  df             9      #>  N              10     #>  n_clusters     <NA>   #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Fieller confidence set: a bounded interval. ci_ratio_of_means_paired(mean_1 = 0.75, sd_1 = drug_a_sd, mean_2 = 2.33,                          sd_2 = drug_b_sd, r = r_ab, N = 10,                          conf_level = 0.995) #>  term           value   #>  ci_lower       -Inf    #>  ratio          0.322   #>  ci_upper       Inf     #>  excluded_lower 0.896   #>  excluded_upper 147.018 #>  mean_1         0.750   #>  mean_2         2.330   #>  mean_baseline  <NA>    #>  se_numerator   0.566   #>  se_denominator 0.633   #>  r              0.795   #>  t_denominator  3.680   #>  df             9       #>  N              10      #>  n_clusters     <NA>    #>  #> Confidence level: 99.5% #>  #> Fieller confidence set: the complement of an interval, every value except those strictly between excluded_lower and excluded_upper. The set is unbounded because |t_denominator| does not exceed the critical value. ci_ratio_of_means_paired(mean_1 = 0.75, sd_1 = drug_a_sd, mean_2 = 2.33,                          sd_2 = drug_b_sd, r = r_ab, N = 10,                          conf_level = 0.999) #>  term           value #>  ci_lower       -Inf  #>  ratio          0.322 #>  ci_upper       Inf   #>  excluded_lower <NA>  #>  excluded_upper <NA>  #>  mean_1         0.750 #>  mean_2         2.330 #>  mean_baseline  <NA>  #>  se_numerator   0.566 #>  se_denominator 0.633 #>  r              0.795 #>  t_denominator  3.680 #>  df             9     #>  N              10    #>  n_clusters     <NA>  #>  #> Confidence level: 99.9% #>  #> Fieller confidence set: the whole line; no value of the ratio is excluded at this level. The set is unbounded because |t_denominator| does not exceed the critical value.  # A retained fraction: a candidate procedure, a reference procedure, and # a trivial baseline scored on the same 300 items, which come from 60 # topics of five items each. The ratio is the share of the reference's # gain over the baseline that the candidate keeps, with a one-sided # 95 percent lower bound and topics as clusters. set.seed(113) topic <- rep(1:60, each = 5) topic_effect <- rnorm(60, sd = 0.08)[topic] trivial <- 0.20 + topic_effect + rnorm(300, sd = 0.10) reference <- trivial + 0.15 + rnorm(300, sd = 0.10) candidate <- trivial + 0.13 + rnorm(300, sd = 0.10) ci_ratio_of_means_paired(candidate, reference, baseline = trivial,                          cluster = topic, alpha_lower = 0.05,                          alpha_upper = 0) #>  term           value  #>  ci_lower       0.725  #>  ratio          0.800  #>  ci_upper       Inf    #>  excluded_lower <NA>   #>  excluded_upper <NA>   #>  mean_1         0.338  #>  mean_2         0.371  #>  mean_baseline  0.208  #>  se_numerator   0.007  #>  se_denominator 0.006  #>  r              0.109  #>  t_denominator  28.365 #>  df             59     #>  N              300    #>  n_clusters     60     #>  #> Confidence level: 95% (one-sided: the lower limit is the 95% lower confidence bound, with tail area 0.05 below it and none above the upper limit) #>  #> Fieller confidence set: an interval unbounded above.  # A percentile bootstrap interval for the SSRI ratio; B = 2000 keeps the # example quick, and a reported interval deserves the default B = 10000. ci_ratio_of_means_paired(ssri$bdi_post, ssri$bdi_pre,                          ci_method = "percentile", B = 2000, seed = 113) #>  term           value  #>  ci_lower       0.253  #>  ratio          0.429  #>  ci_upper       0.588  #>  excluded_lower <NA>   #>  excluded_upper <NA>   #>  mean_1         7.300  #>  mean_2         17.000 #>  mean_baseline  <NA>   #>  se_numerator   1.693  #>  se_denominator 1.291  #>  r              0.442  #>  t_denominator  13.168 #>  df             9      #>  N              10     #>  n_clusters     <NA>   #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Percentile bootstrap interval: a bounded interval. #>  #> Bootstrap: 2000 replications, 2000 used (0 dropped; at least 400 must be requested)
