title: Confidence Interval for a Standardized Contrast in ANCOVA With One Covariate — ci_sc_ancova
code: # Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley (2027) offer an example that 30 depressive # individuals are randomly assigned to three groups, 10 in each, and ANCOVA # is performed on the posttest scores using the participants' pretest # scores as the covariate. The means of pretest scores of group 1, 2, and 3 are # 17, 17.7, and 17.4, respectively, whereas the adjusted means of groups 1, 2, and 3 # are 7.5, 12, and 14, respectively. The error variance in ANCOVA is 29 and thus # 5.385165 is the error standard deviation, with the sum of squares within groups # from an ANOVA on the covariate is 752.5.  # To obtained the confidence interval for the standardized adjusted mean difference # between group 1 and 2, using the ANCOVA error standard deviation: ci_sc_ancova(adj_means = c(7.5, 12, 14), s_ancova = 5.385165, c_weights = c(1, -1, 0),              n_per_group = 10, cov_means = c(17, 17.7, 17.4), SSwithin_x = 752.5) #>  term         value  #>  ci_lower     -1.735 #>  std_contrast -0.836 #>  ci_upper     0.078  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Or, with less error in rounding: ci_sc_ancova(adj_means = c(7.54, 11.98, 13.98), s_ancova = 5.393, c_weights = c(-1, 0, 1),              n_per_group = 10, cov_means = c(17, 17.7, 17.4), SSwithin_x = 752.5) #>  term         value #>  ci_lower     0.249 #>  std_contrast 1.194 #>  ci_upper     2.119 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Now, using the standard deviation from ANOVA (and not ANCOVA as above), we have: ci_sc_ancova(adj_means = c(7.54, 11.98, 13.98), s_anova = 6.294, s_ancova = 5.393,              c_weights = c(-1, 0, 1),n_per_group = 10, cov_means = c(17, 17.7, 17.4),              SSwithin_x = 752.5, standardizer = "s_anova", conf_level = .95) #>  term         value #>  ci_lower     0.214 #>  std_contrast 1.023 #>  ci_upper     1.815 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Recovering SSwithin_x from a covariate ANOVA F when a report does not print # it directly (see the Details section). This example follows Lai and Kelley # (2012): three groups of sizes 19, 18, and 19 have covariate means 60.08, # 57.08, and 57.97, and the one-way ANOVA on the covariate reports F = 0.756. cov_means_ex  <- c(60.08, 57.08, 57.97) n_ex          <- c(19, 18, 19) grand_x       <- sum(n_ex * cov_means_ex) / sum(n_ex) ss_between_x  <- sum(n_ex * (cov_means_ex - grand_x)^2) ms_between_x  <- ss_between_x / (length(n_ex) - 1) ms_within_x   <- ms_between_x / 0.756 SSwithin_x_ex <- ms_within_x * (sum(n_ex) - length(n_ex))  ci_sc_ancova(adj_means = c(63.88, 62.39, 56.48), s_ancova = 20.267,              c_weights = c(0.5, 0.5, -1), n_per_group = n_ex, cov_means = cov_means_ex,              SSwithin_x = SSwithin_x_ex) #>  term         value  #>  ci_lower     -0.230 #>  std_contrast 0.328  #>  ci_upper     0.884  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # 1. All pairwise contrasts among the six marketing panels of the #    test_market data via the default: fit <- lm(brand_movement ~ panel, data = test_market) ci_scheffe(fit) #>  contrast estimate se    F_value ci_lower ci_upper p_adjusted #>  2 - 1    0.110    0.380 0.017   -1.305   1.525    0.9999     #>  3 - 1    0.685    0.380 0.650   -0.730   2.100    0.6652     #>  4 - 1    0.870    0.380 1.049   -0.545   2.285    0.4201     #>  5 - 1    1.245    0.380 2.147   -0.170   2.660    0.1061     #>  6 - 1    1.295    0.380 2.323   -0.120   2.710    0.0855     #>  3 - 2    0.575    0.380 0.458   -0.840   1.990    0.8021     #>  4 - 2    0.760    0.380 0.800   -0.655   2.175    0.5639     #>  5 - 2    1.135    0.380 1.785   -0.280   2.550    0.1668     #>  6 - 2    1.185    0.380 1.945   -0.230   2.600    0.1364     #>  4 - 3    0.185    0.380 0.047   -1.230   1.600    0.9984     #>  5 - 3    0.560    0.380 0.434   -0.855   1.975    0.8186     #>  6 - 3    0.610    0.380 0.516   -0.805   2.025    0.7611     #>  5 - 4    0.375    0.380 0.195   -1.040   1.790    0.9605     #>  6 - 4    0.425    0.380 0.250   -0.990   1.840    0.9342     #>  6 - 5    0.050    0.380 0.003   -1.365   1.465    1.0000     #>  #> Confidence level: 95%, simultaneous interval (Scheffe)  # 2. A contrast chosen after inspecting the means: the two panels with #    the highest brand movement (5 and 6) against the two with the #    lowest (1 and 2). The Scheffe coverage holds for a contrast picked #    this way, and the interval still excludes zero even though none of #    the pairwise intervals above does. cmat <- matrix(c(-0.5, -0.5, 0, 0, 0.5, 0.5), nrow = 6,                dimnames = list(levels(test_market$panel),                                "panels 5,6 - panels 1,2")) ci_scheffe(fit, contrasts = cmat) #>  contrast                estimate se    F_value ci_lower ci_upper p_adjusted #>  panels 5,6 - panels 1,2 1.215    0.269 4.090   0.215    2.215    0.0117     #>  #> Confidence level: 95%, simultaneous interval (Scheffe)

code: ## Bargmann (1970) gave an example of a one-way ANOVA with an observed ## F value of 11.2213 on 4 and 50 degrees of freedom, which Venables (1975), ## Fleishman (1980), and Steiger (2004) used in turn. Steiger describes it ## as five groups of 11 and reports F as 11.221, the value used here. ## The exact confidence interval for the square root of the signal-to-noise ratio of that example:  ci_srsnr(F_value = 11.221, df_1 = 4, df_2 = 50, N = 55) #>  term     value #>  ci_lower 0.541 #>  ci_upper 1.193 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  ci_srsnr(F_value = 11.221, df_1 = 4, df_2 = 50, N = 55, conf_level = .90) #>  term     value #>  ci_lower 0.594 #>  ci_upper 1.141 #>  #> Confidence level: 90%  ci_srsnr(F_value = 11.221, df_1 = 4, df_2 = 50, N = 55, alpha_lower = .02, alpha_upper = .03) #>  term     value #>  ci_lower 0.525 #>  ci_upper 1.180 #>  #> Confidence level: 95% (unequal tail areas: 0.02 below the lower limit, 0.03 above the upper limit)  # The interval from the summaries of an observed one-way design: the # group means, the pooled within-group mean square, and the group sizes # of the three arms of drinks_trial. The F route gives the same interval # for the same data. fit <- stats::lm(log_drinks ~ treatment, data = drinks_trial) ci_srsnr(means = tapply(drinks_trial$log_drinks, drinks_trial$treatment, mean),          var_within = sum(stats::residuals(fit)^2) / stats::df.residual(fit),          n_per_group = as.vector(table(drinks_trial$treatment))) #>  term     value #>  ci_lower 0.050 #>  ci_upper 0.510 #>  #> Confidence level: 95% ci_srsnr(F_value = stats::anova(fit)[1, "F value"], df_1 = 2, df_2 = 85, N = 88) #>  term     value #>  ci_lower 0.050 #>  ci_upper 0.510 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # A hypothetical interval: with population means of 94, 91, 92, and 83, a # within-group variance of 67.375, and 20 per group, the interval a study # would report if its summaries equaled these values. It is not the # expected interval of that study. ci_srsnr(means = c(94, 91, 92, 83), var_within = 67.375, n_per_group = 20) #>  term     value #>  ci_lower 0.238 #>  ci_upper 0.722 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # 1. Two groups of different sizes, no ties: set.seed(113) a <- rnorm(30, mean = 0, sd = 1) b <- rnorm(40, mean = 0.5, sd = 1) cliff_delta(a, b) #>  term            value  #>  cliff_delta     -0.223 #>  ci_lower        -0.470 #>  ci_upper        0.056  #>  var_cliff_delta 0.019  #>  p_y1_greater    0.388  #>  p_y1_less       0.612  #>  p_tied          0.000  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # 2. With ties (ordinal data): o1 <- c(1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5) o2 <- c(2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5) cliff_delta(o1, o2) #>  term            value  #>  cliff_delta     -0.403 #>  ci_lower        -0.776 #>  ci_upper        0.179  #>  var_cliff_delta 0.067  #>  p_y1_greater    0.194  #>  p_y1_less       0.597  #>  p_tied          0.208  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # 3. Robust to right skew. Cliff's delta on the raw, untransformed #    drinking outcome from the Smith, Meyers, and Delaney (1998) #    trial, comparing the Community Reinforcement Approach (CRA) #    against standard care. Because the statistic uses only ranks it #    needs no normalizing transformation of the heavily skewed #    outcome, unlike the standardized mean difference. data(drinks_trial) cra <- drinks_trial$drinks_per_week[drinks_trial$treatment == "CRA"] std <- drinks_trial$drinks_per_week[drinks_trial$treatment == "Standard"] cliff_delta(cra, std) #>  term            value  #>  cliff_delta     -0.300 #>  ci_lower        -0.535 #>  ci_upper        -0.021 #>  var_cliff_delta 0.018  #>  p_y1_greater    0.293  #>  p_y1_less       0.593  #>  p_tied          0.114  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # 4. An ordinal response is supplied as an ordered factor with its #    levels stated from lowest to highest. The unordered factors #    rating_1 and rating_2 themselves are refused, with a message that #    says why: their codes follow the alphabetical order of the labels #    (high, low, mid). rating_1 <- factor(c("low", "mid", "high", "high")) rating_2 <- factor(c("low", "low", "mid", "high")) lev <- c("low", "mid", "high") cliff_delta(factor(rating_1, levels = lev, ordered = TRUE),             factor(rating_2, levels = lev, ordered = TRUE)) #>  term            value  #>  cliff_delta     0.312  #>  ci_lower        -0.517 #>  ci_upper        0.839  #>  var_cliff_delta 0.170  #>  p_y1_greater    0.500  #>  p_y1_less       0.188  #>  p_tied          0.312  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # 5. Completely separated groups: the estimated variance is 0, the two #    limits equal the estimate, and a warning says that they are not a #    confidence interval and gives the limit of Feng and Cliff (2004). separated <- cliff_delta(6:10, 1:5) #> Warning: cliff_delta(): the groups are completely separated (|delta| = 1), so the estimated variance is 0. Both confidence limits are reported equal to the estimate (1, 1). They are not a confidence interval with the stated coverage: the variance estimate is built from how much the comparisons differ from one observation to the next, and in a sample with no overlap they do not differ at all. That describes this sample, not the population. A population with some overlap often produces a sample with none when the samples are small (here 5 and 5 observations), so the limits must not be read as showing that the population value is 1. For this case Feng and Cliff (2004, Equation 8) give the limit (n_b - z^2) / (n_b + z^2) for delta, with n_b the smaller group size and z the normal quantile of the level: 0.131 here at the 95% level, with the other limit 1. Report the estimate with the sample sizes and say that the groups did not overlap; the randomization test (randomization_test()) gives a p-value that remains valid here. separated #>  term            value #>  cliff_delta     1.000 #>  ci_lower        1.000 #>  ci_upper        1.000 #>  var_cliff_delta 0.000 #>  p_y1_greater    1.000 #>  p_y1_less       0.000 #>  p_tied          0.000 #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Limits are not a confidence interval: the estimated variance is 0. results_sentence(separated) #> [1] "cliff_delta = 1.00 (no confidence interval: the groups are completely separated, so the estimated variance is 0)"

At full precision, this f plans a balanced study of # 40, ten per group, for power .80 at the .05 level, as the article does. f_kim <- cohen_f(means = c(18.4, 22.2, 25.1, 32.1), var_within = 8.6^2) f_kim #>  term    value #>  cohen_f 0.583 ss_power_one_way_anova(a = 4, true_f = f_kim$value, desired_power = .80) #>  term              value  #>  necessary_N       40     #>  n_per_group       10     #>  a                 4      #>  noncentral_f_parm 13.603 #>  actual_power      0.847   # Cohen (1988, p. 277) places seven population means over half a # within-population standard deviation, one at each end and five at the # midpoint, and gives f as .13 (.267 times .5, his Equation 8.2.8). cohen_f(means = c(-.25, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, .25), var_within = 1) #>  term    value #>  cohen_f 0.134  # The plug-in value from the summaries of an observed one-way design # with unequal groups: the group means, the pooled within-group mean # square, and the group sizes of the three arms of drinks_trial. fit <- stats::lm(log_drinks ~ treatment, data = drinks_trial) cohen_f(means = tapply(drinks_trial$log_drinks, drinks_trial$treatment, mean),         var_within = sum(stats::residuals(fit)^2) / stats::df.residual(fit),         n_per_group = as.vector(table(drinks_trial$treatment))) #>  term    value #>  cohen_f 0.311  # The sample eta squared of the same fit gives a larger plug-in value, # by the factor sqrt(N / (N - k)) = sqrt(88 / 85) (see Details). ss <- stats::anova(fit)[["Sum Sq"]] cohen_f(eta_squared = ss[1] / sum(ss)) #>  term    value #>  cohen_f 0.317  # From eta squared, and from the two standard deviations: cohen_f(eta_squared = .10) #>  term    value #>  cohen_f 0.333 cohen_f(sd_means = 4, sd_within = 8) #>  term    value #>  cohen_f 0.500

title: Cohen's Kappa Coefficient of Inter-Rater Agreement — cohen_kappa
code: # --------------------------------------------------------------------- # Cohen (1968, Table 1): two judges assign N = 200 cases to three # diagnostic categories. The table ships as the diagnosis_agreement # data set in the paper's own layout, Judge B in rows and Judge A in # columns, carrying Cohen's per-cell disagreement weights, observed # proportions, and chance-expected proportions. data(diagnosis_agreement) tab <- xtabs(frequency ~ judge_b + judge_a, data = diagnosis_agreement) v   <- unclass(xtabs(disagreement_weight ~ judge_b + judge_a,                      data = diagnosis_agreement)) tab #>                       judge_a #> judge_b                Personality disorder Neurosis Psychosis #>   Personality disorder                   88       10         2 #>   Neurosis                               14       40         6 #>   Psychosis                              18       10        12  # Unweighted kappa, all disagreements equal (Cohen's Formula 4): .492. cohen_kappa(table = tab) #>  weights    kappa se    ci_lower ci_upper z_value p_value  N   n_categories #>  unweighted 0.492 0.051 0.392    0.591    9.637   < 0.0001 200 3            #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # A percentile bootstrap interval for the same table, which expands # it to its 200 paired ratings and resamples the subjects. The point # estimate and the asymptotic standard error are unchanged; only the # interval is read off the bootstrap distribution. B = 2000 keeps the # example quick; a reported interval deserves the default B = 10000. cohen_kappa(table = tab, ci_method = "percentile", B = 2000,             seed = 113) #>  weights    kappa se    ci_lower ci_upper z_value p_value  N   n_categories #>  unweighted 0.492 0.051 0.387    0.592    9.637   < 0.0001 200 3            #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Bootstrap: 2000 replications, 2000 used (0 dropped; at least 400 must be requested)  # Cohen's ratio-scaled disagreement weights: a neurosis-psychosis # confusion (weight 6) is six times as grave as a personality # disorder-neurosis confusion (weight 1). Weighted kappa = .348, # smaller than the unweighted .492: these judges disagree less than # chance expectation where it matters little and at about the chance # level where it matters most. res <- cohen_kappa(table = tab, weights = v,                    weight_scaling = "disagreement") res #>  weights             kappa se    ci_lower ci_upper z_value p_value  N   #>  custom_disagreement 0.348 0.076 0.200    0.496    4.607   < 0.0001 200 #>  n_categories #>  3            #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # The per-cell quantities of Cohen's Table 1 travel with the result: # observed and chance-expected proportions and both weight scalings. attr(res, "cells") #>                rater_1              rater_2 observed_proportion #> 1 Personality disorder Personality disorder                0.44 #> 2 Personality disorder             Neurosis                0.05 #> 3 Personality disorder            Psychosis                0.01 #> 4             Neurosis Personality disorder                0.07 #> 5             Neurosis             Neurosis                0.20 #> 6             Neurosis            Psychosis                0.03 #> 7            Psychosis Personality disorder                0.09 #> 8            Psychosis             Neurosis                0.05 #> 9            Psychosis            Psychosis                0.06 #>   expected_proportion    weight disagreement_weight #> 1                0.30 1.0000000                   0 #> 2                0.15 0.8333333                   1 #> 3                0.05 0.5000000                   3 #> 4                0.18 0.8333333                   1 #> 5                0.09 1.0000000                   0 #> 6                0.03 0.0000000                   6 #> 7                0.12 0.5000000                   3 #> 8                0.06 0.0000000                   6 #> 9                0.02 1.0000000                   0  # Interchanging the 6 and 1 weights reverses the story: kappa_w = .574. v_swap <- v v_swap[v == 6] <- 1 v_swap[v == 1] <- 6 cohen_kappa(table = tab, weights = v_swap,             weight_scaling = "disagreement") #>  weights             kappa se    ci_lower ci_upper z_value p_value  N   #>  custom_disagreement 0.574 0.055 0.465    0.682    10.373  < 0.0001 200 #>  n_categories #>  3            #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Cohen's own Table 1 arithmetic (his Formulas 8, 10, and 13), # computed straight from the data set's per-cell columns and # reproduced for the historical record. The function reports the # Fleiss-Cohen-Everitt (1969) standard error, which superseded # Formulas 10 and 13. q_o <- with(diagnosis_agreement,             sum(disagreement_weight * observed_proportion))   # = .90 q_c <- with(diagnosis_agreement,             sum(disagreement_weight * expected_proportion))   # = 1.38 1 - q_o / q_c                          # kappa_w = .348   (Formula 8) #> [1] 0.3478261 v2_o <- with(diagnosis_agreement,              sum(disagreement_weight^2 * observed_proportion)) v2_c <- with(diagnosis_agreement,              sum(disagreement_weight^2 * expected_proportion)) sqrt((v2_o - q_o^2) / (200 * q_c^2))   # = .0901   (Formula 10) #> [1] 0.09007104 sqrt((v2_c - q_c^2) / (200 * q_c^2))   # = .0916   (Formula 13) #> [1] 0.09159718 (1 - q_o / q_c) + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * 0.0901  # 95% CI [.171, .524] #> [1] 0.1712333 0.5244188 (1 - q_o / q_c) / 0.0916               # z = 3.80, p < .001 #> [1] 3.797228  # Cohen's validity reinterpretation: Judge A is a diagnostic panel # (the criterion), Judge B a computer diagnosis (the predictor), and # the weights are asymmetric because the two directions of a # confusion carry different costs. Oriented to the table's layout # (rows = Judge B = computer, columns = Judge A = panel), the weights # below reproduce Cohen's published quantities: sum(v * p_o) = .86, # sum(v * p_c) = 1.33, kappa_w = .353, with his Formulas 10 and 13 # giving .0887 and .0915. The weighted kappa vignette works this # example in full, including the orientation of the paper's printed # weight display relative to these values. v_validity <- matrix(   c(0, 1, 2,     1, 0, 2,     4, 6, 0), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE) cohen_kappa(table = tab, weights = v_validity,             weight_scaling = "disagreement") #>  weights             kappa se    ci_lower ci_upper z_value p_value  N   #>  custom_disagreement 0.353 0.063 0.231    0.476    5.640   < 0.0001 200 #>  n_categories #>  3            #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # --------------------------------------------------------------------- # Raw rater vectors and ordinal categories (quadratic agreement # weights, e.g., Likert-style severity). set.seed(113) x <- sample(1:5, 100, replace = TRUE) y <- pmin(pmax(x + sample(-1:1, 100, replace = TRUE), 1), 5) cohen_kappa(x, y, weights = "quadratic") #>  weights   kappa se    ci_lower ci_upper z_value p_value  N   n_categories #>  quadratic 0.850 0.020 0.810    0.890    41.469  < 0.0001 100 5            #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # Visual, textual, and speed composites of the nine Holzinger and # Swineford tests in the primary set, each the mean of three tests. hs <- holzinger_swineford scores <- data.frame(   visual  = rowMeans(hs[c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes",                           "t4_lozenges")]),   textual = rowMeans(hs[c("t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence",                           "t9_word_meaning")]),   speed   = rowMeans(hs[c("t10_addition", "t12_counting_groups_of_dots",                           "t13_straight_and_curved_capitals")])) R <- stats::cor(scores)  # The smallest positive correlation as the proxy marker; the pair that # supplied it (textual with speed) is adjusted to zero. Visual with # speed shows the interval and the test parting near the boundary: the # interval includes zero while the p-value is below .05. common_method_adjusted_r(R, N = nrow(scores)) #>  marker_r variable_1 variable_2 r     estimate ci_lower ci_upper t_value df  #>  0.237    visual     textual    0.312 0.098    -0.041   0.227    1.700   298 #>  0.237    visual     speed      0.326 0.116    -0.021   0.244    2.022   298 #>  0.237    textual    speed      0.237 0.000    -0.144   0.136    0.000   298 #>  p_value #>  0.0901  #>  0.0440  #>  1.0000  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # A grid of marker correlations, from no adjustment to a large one. grid <- common_method_adjusted_r(R, N = nrow(scores),                                  marker_r = c(0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3)) grid[grid$variable_1 == "visual" & grid$variable_2 == "textual", ] #>  marker_r variable_1 variable_2 r     estimate ci_lower ci_upper t_value df  #>  0.000    visual     textual    0.312 0.312    0.206    0.411    5.670   298 #>  0.100    visual     textual    0.312 0.236    0.118    0.345    4.185   298 #>  0.200    visual     textual    0.312 0.140    0.008    0.263    2.442   298 #>  0.300    visual     textual    0.312 0.017    -0.134   0.158    0.298   298 #>  p_value  #>  < 0.0001 #>  < 0.0001 #>  0.0152   #>  0.7662   #>  #> Confidence level: 95% attr(grid, "adjusted")[["0.2"]] #>            visual   textual     speed #> visual  1.0000000 0.1400825 0.1575495 #> textual 0.1400825 1.0000000 0.0466276 #> speed   0.1575495 0.0466276 1.0000000

code: # An observed correlation of .30 between measures with reliabilities .80 # and .70 corresponds to a construct-level correlation of about .40. correction_for_attenuation(r = 0.30, reliability_x = 0.80, reliability_y = 0.70) #>  term                  value #>  correlation_observed  0.300 #>  correlation_corrected 0.401 #>  reliability_x         0.800 #>  reliability_y         0.700  # With the sample size, the corrected interval comes along. correction_for_attenuation(r = 0.30, reliability_x = 0.80, reliability_y = 0.70,                     N = 120) #>  term                  value #>  correlation_observed  0.300 #>  correlation_corrected 0.401 #>  ci_lower              0.171 #>  ci_upper              0.608 #>  reliability_x         0.800 #>  reliability_y         0.700 #>  N                     120   #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Correct one side only (error-free criterion). correction_for_attenuation(r = 0.30, reliability_x = 0.80, reliability_y = 1) #>  term                  value #>  correlation_observed  0.300 #>  correlation_corrected 0.335 #>  reliability_x         0.800 #>  reliability_y         1      # The two routes to the construct-level correlation, on the same data # (requires lavaan). Two congeneric scales of three items each whose # latent variables correlate .50: set.seed(113) n <- 400 fx <- rnorm(n); fy <- 0.5 * fx + sqrt(1 - 0.25) * rnorm(n) lam <- c(.8, .7, .6) items <- data.frame(   x1 = lam[1] * fx + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(1 - lam[1]^2)),   x2 = lam[2] * fx + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(1 - lam[2]^2)),   x3 = lam[3] * fx + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(1 - lam[3]^2)),   y1 = lam[1] * fy + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(1 - lam[1]^2)),   y2 = lam[2] * fy + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(1 - lam[2]^2)),   y3 = lam[3] * fy + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(1 - lam[3]^2)))  # Route 1, summary statistics: omega reliabilities into the formula. x_score <- rowMeans(items[, 1:3]); y_score <- rowMeans(items[, 4:6]) om_x <- reliability_omega(data = items[, 1:3])$value[1] #> Robust omega is reported without a confidence interval by default because its interval is bootstrap based. Request it with ci_method = "percentile" (or "bca"); B = 10000 replications is the default when you do. om_y <- reliability_omega(data = items[, 4:6])$value[1] #> Robust omega is reported without a confidence interval by default because its interval is bootstrap based. Request it with ci_method = "percentile" (or "bca"); B = 10000 replications is the default when you do. correction_for_attenuation(r = cor(x_score, y_score),                            reliability_x = om_x, reliability_y = om_y,                            N = n) #>  term                  value #>  correlation_observed  0.307 #>  correlation_corrected 0.413 #>  ci_lower              0.290 #>  ci_upper              0.529 #>  reliability_x         0.760 #>  reliability_y         0.725 #>  N                     400   #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Route 2, the factor model: the latent correlation estimated directly. fit <- lavaan::cfa("X =~ x1 + x2 + x3\nY =~ y1 + y2 + y3",                    data = items, std.lv = TRUE) lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit)[   lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit)$op == "~~" &   lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit)$lhs == "X" &   lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit)$rhs == "Y", ] #>    lhs op rhs  est    se     z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper #> 15   X ~~   Y 0.43 0.056 7.661      0     0.32    0.539

title: Formatted Correlation Matrix With p-values and Confidence Intervals — correlations_test
code: # Worked example using four cognitive tests from the holzinger_swineford # data (301 children in two schools). The goal of # correlations_test() is to produce a formatted correlation matrix that # reports, for every variable pair, the correlation, its two-sided # p-value, a confidence interval on the population correlation, and the # pairwise sample size. See Kelley (2007) and Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley # (2027, Chapter 9) for discussion of why effect sizes should be # accompanied by confidence intervals. hs_tests <- holzinger_swineford[, c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes",                                     "t4_lozenges",                                     "t6_paragraph_comprehension")]  # Pearson correlations (the default). Each lower-triangle cell stacks r, # the two-sided p-value, the 95\% confidence interval (Fisher's Z # transformation; Fisher, 1915, 1921), and the pairwise N. correlations_test(hs_tests) #> Correlations (Pearson, 95% CI) #>  #>                             t1_visual_perception          t2_cubes                      t4_lozenges                   t6_paragraph_comprehension     #> ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #> t1_visual_perception        -                                                                                                                        #>                                                                                                                                                      #>                                                                                                                                                      #>                                                                                                                                                      #>  #> t2_cubes                    .30                           -                                                                                          #>                             p < .0001                                                                                                                #>                             [.19, .40]                                                                                                               #>                             N = 301                                                                                                                  #>  #> t4_lozenges                 .44                           .34                           -                                                            #>                             p < .0001                     p < .0001                                                                                  #>                             [.34, .53]                    [.24, .44]                                                                                 #>                             N = 301                       N = 301                                                                                    #>  #> t6_paragraph_comprehension  .37                           .15                           .16                           -                              #>                             p < .0001                     p = .0079                     p = .0058                                                    #>                             [.27, .47]                    [.04, .26]                    [.05, .27]                                                   #>                             N = 301                       N = 301                       N = 301                                                      #>   # Add significance stars and an explanatory footnote. correlations_test(hs_tests, stars = TRUE) #> Correlations (Pearson, 95% CI) #>  #>                             t1_visual_perception          t2_cubes                      t4_lozenges                   t6_paragraph_comprehension     #> ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #> t1_visual_perception        -                                                                                                                        #>                                                                                                                                                      #>                                                                                                                                                      #>                                                                                                                                                      #>  #> t2_cubes                    .30***                        -                                                                                          #>                             p < .0001                                                                                                                #>                             [.19, .40]                                                                                                               #>                             N = 301                                                                                                                  #>  #> t4_lozenges                 .44***                        .34***                        -                                                            #>                             p < .0001                     p < .0001                                                                                  #>                             [.34, .53]                    [.24, .44]                                                                                 #>                             N = 301                       N = 301                                                                                    #>  #> t6_paragraph_comprehension  .37***                        .15**                         .16**                         -                              #>                             p < .0001                     p = .0079                     p = .0058                                                    #>                             [.27, .47]                    [.04, .26]                    [.05, .27]                                                   #>                             N = 301                       N = 301                       N = 301                                                      #>  #> Note. * p < .05, ** p < .01, *** p < .001.  # Spearman correlations at a 99\% confidence level. The interval uses # Bonett and Wright's (2000) Fisher's Z standard error # sqrt((1 + r^2/2) / (n - 3)), which corrects the plain Fisher interval # for the heavier tails of Spearman's sampling distribution. correlations_test(hs_tests, method = "spearman", conf_level = 0.99) #> Correlations (Spearman, 99% CI) #>  #>                             t1_visual_perception          t2_cubes                      t4_lozenges                   t6_paragraph_comprehension     #> ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #> t1_visual_perception        -                                                                                                                        #>                                                                                                                                                      #>                                                                                                                                                      #>                                                                                                                                                      #>  #> t2_cubes                    .28                           -                                                                                          #>                             p < .0001                                                                                                                #>                             [.14, .42]                                                                                                               #>                             N = 301                                                                                                                  #>  #> t4_lozenges                 .44                           .32                           -                                                            #>                             p < .0001                     p < .0001                                                                                  #>                             [.31, .56]                    [.18, .45]                                                                                 #>                             N = 301                       N = 301                                                                                    #>  #> t6_paragraph_comprehension  .38                           .19                           .15                           -                              #>                             p < .0001                     p = .0007                     p = .0105                                                    #>                             [.24, .50]                    [.05, .33]                    [-.00, .29]                                                  #>                             N = 301                       N = 301                       N = 301                                                      #>   # Kendall's tau, also using Bonett and Wright's (2000) Fisher's Z standard # error sqrt(0.437 / (n - 4)). Kendall is often preferred over Spearman # for small samples and for samples with many tied ranks, and these # integer test scores carry many ties. correlations_test(hs_tests, method = "kendall") #> Correlations (Kendall, 95% CI) #>  #>                             t1_visual_perception          t2_cubes                      t4_lozenges                   t6_paragraph_comprehension     #> ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #> t1_visual_perception        -                                                                                                                        #>                                                                                                                                                      #>                                                                                                                                                      #>                                                                                                                                                      #>  #> t2_cubes                    .21                           -                                                                                          #>                             p < .0001                                                                                                                #>                             [.13, .28]                                                                                                               #>                             N = 301                                                                                                                  #>  #> t4_lozenges                 .32                           .23                           -                                                            #>                             p < .0001                     p < .0001                                                                                  #>                             [.25, .38]                    [.15, .30]                                                                                 #>                             N = 301                       N = 301                                                                                    #>  #> t6_paragraph_comprehension  .28                           .14                           .10                           -                              #>                             p < .0001                     p = .0007                     p = .0104                                                    #>                             [.21, .34]                    [.07, .21]                    [.03, .18]                                                   #>                             N = 301                       N = 301                       N = 301                                                      #>   # Save a formatted HTML table that opens directly in a browser # (then copy into Word). No pandoc required. tmp_html <- tempfile(fileext = ".html") correlations_test(hs_tests, stars = TRUE, format = "html", file = tmp_html)

code: # The six spatial tests of the Holzinger and Swineford data. The revised # paper form board (t25) and flags (t26) tests were given only at # Grant-White, so the 156 Pasteur pupils are missing both of them. spatial <- c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t3_paper_form_board",              "t4_lozenges", "t25_paper_form_board_r", "t26_flags") em <- cov_fiml(holzinger_swineford[spatial]) em$N #> [1] 301 em$N_complete #> [1] 145 em$patterns #> [1] 2 round(stats::cov2cor(em$S), 2) #>                        t1_visual_perception t2_cubes t3_paper_form_board #> t1_visual_perception                   1.00     0.30                0.37 #> t2_cubes                               0.30     1.00                0.24 #> t3_paper_form_board                    0.37     0.24                1.00 #> t4_lozenges                            0.44     0.34                0.31 #> t25_paper_form_board_r                 0.40     0.33                0.41 #> t26_flags                              0.47     0.21                0.31 #>                        t4_lozenges t25_paper_form_board_r t26_flags #> t1_visual_perception          0.44                   0.40      0.47 #> t2_cubes                      0.34                   0.33      0.21 #> t3_paper_form_board           0.31                   0.41      0.31 #> t4_lozenges                   1.00                   0.31      0.49 #> t25_paper_form_board_r        0.31                   1.00      0.30 #> t26_flags                     0.49                   0.30      1.00  # Listwise deletion would keep the 145 Grant-White pupils alone and # estimate every correlation from them. round(stats::cor(holzinger_swineford[spatial], use = "complete.obs"), 2) #>                        t1_visual_perception t2_cubes t3_paper_form_board #> t1_visual_perception                   1.00     0.33                0.37 #> t2_cubes                               0.33     1.00                0.19 #> t3_paper_form_board                    0.37     0.19                1.00 #> t4_lozenges                            0.45     0.42                0.37 #> t25_paper_form_board_r                 0.40     0.31                0.40 #> t26_flags                              0.47     0.23                0.33 #>                        t4_lozenges t25_paper_form_board_r t26_flags #> t1_visual_perception          0.45                   0.40      0.47 #> t2_cubes                      0.42                   0.31      0.23 #> t3_paper_form_board           0.37                   0.40      0.33 #> t4_lozenges                   1.00                   0.33      0.47 #> t25_paper_form_board_r        0.33                   1.00      0.30 #> t26_flags                     0.47                   0.30      1.00  # Values missing at random given a variable that is not analyzed: word # meaning (t9) goes missing more often for pupils who scored high on # general information (t5). The two visual tests say little about those # pupils, so without t5 the mean of t9 stays near that of the pupils who # took it; named as an auxiliary, t5 recovers most of the difference. set.seed(113) d <- holzinger_swineford[c("t1_visual_perception", "t4_lozenges",                            "t9_word_meaning", "t5_general_information")] z <- as.numeric(scale(d$t5_general_information)) p_missing <- stats::plogis(-0.5 + 2 * z) d$t9_word_meaning[stats::runif(nrow(d)) < p_missing] <- NA without_aux <- cov_fiml(d[1:3]) with_aux <- cov_fiml(d, aux = "t5_general_information") rbind(without_aux = without_aux$mu, with_aux = with_aux$mu,       full_data = colMeans(holzinger_swineford[names(d)[1:3]])) #>             t1_visual_perception t4_lozenges t9_word_meaning #> without_aux             29.61462    18.00332        12.42404 #> with_aux                29.61462    18.00332        14.66152 #> full_data               29.61462    18.00332        15.29900

code: # Population model with all parameters fixed to their values: two factors, # three indicators each, and a structural path of 0.5 from the first # factor to the second. pop_model <- "   f1 =~ 1*y1 + 0.8*y2 + 0.8*y3   f2 =~ 1*y4 + 0.8*y5 + 0.8*y6   f2 ~ 0.5*f1   f1 ~~ 1*f1   f2 ~~ 0.75*f2   y1 ~~ 0.5*y1; y2 ~~ 0.5*y2; y3 ~~ 0.5*y3   y4 ~~ 0.5*y4; y5 ~~ 0.5*y5; y6 ~~ 0.5*y6 " cov_sem(pop_model)$sigma_theta #>     y1   y2   y3  y4   y5   y6 #> y1 1.5 0.80 0.80 0.5 0.40 0.40 #> y2 0.8 1.14 0.64 0.4 0.32 0.32 #> y3 0.8 0.64 1.14 0.4 0.32 0.32 #> y4 0.5 0.40 0.40 1.5 0.80 0.80 #> y5 0.4 0.32 0.32 0.8 1.14 0.64 #> y6 0.4 0.32 0.32 0.8 0.64 1.14  # A population model with a mean structure: a linear latent growth curve # over four waves. The intercepts and latent means are fixed too, and # mu_theta carries the model implied wave means, which start at 5.0 and # rise by 0.3 per wave. pop_lgm <- "   i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4   s =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 3*t4   i ~~ 1*i   s ~~ 0.2*s   i ~~ -0.15*s   t1 ~~ 0.5*t1; t2 ~~ 0.5*t2; t3 ~~ 0.5*t3; t4 ~~ 0.5*t4   t1 ~ 0*1; t2 ~ 0*1; t3 ~ 0*1; t4 ~ 0*1   i ~ 5*1   s ~ 0.3*1 " cov_sem(pop_lgm)$mu_theta #>  t1  t2  t3  t4  #> 5.0 5.3 5.6 5.9

title: Provides the Critical Value for the Bryant–Paulson ANCOVA Multiple-Comparison Procedure — cv_bryant_paulson
code: # Multiple comparisons of adjusted means in ANCOVA (the setting of Maxwell, # Delaney, and Kelley, 2027, Chapter 9), using the worked example of Bryant # and Bruvold (1980): 6 panels, 1 random covariate, 14 error df, # alpha_level = .05. The single-step value is the multiplier for simultaneous # confidence intervals on the pairwise differences of adjusted means. With a # covariate present there is no closed form for it: the Bryant-Paulson # distribution function is integrated numerically and then inverted. The # value is 4.83, the entry in Table 1 of Bryant and Paulson (1976) and the # multiplier behind the simultaneous intervals of the 1980 worked example. cv_bryant_paulson(alpha_level = .05, df = 14, n_groups = 6, n_covariates = 1) #>  term     value area_less area_greater #>  upper_cv 4.830 0.950     0.050         # With no covariates the reference distribution is the ordinary studentized # range, which base R supplies directly. The critical value is then sqrt(2) # times the Tukey HSD critical value. cv_bryant_paulson(alpha_level = .05, df = 14, n_groups = 6, n_covariates = 0)$value #> [1] 4.638538 sqrt(2) * cv_tukey_hsd(alpha_level = .05, df = 14, n_groups = 6)$value #> [1] 4.638538  # The stepwise Duncan multiple-range significant range comes from # procedure = "duncan". With n_covariates = 0 it reduces to Duncan's (1955) # own significant studentized range, 3.37 for a stretch of 6 groups on 14 # error degrees of freedom. cv_bryant_paulson(alpha_level = .05, df = 14, n_groups = 6, n_covariates = 0,                   procedure = "duncan") #>  term     value area_less area_greater #>  upper_cv 3.371 <NA>      <NA>         # One random covariate raises that range to 3.50, the entry in Table 2 of # Bryant and Bruvold (1980). Being stepwise, the value is a running maximum # of Bryant-Paulson quantiles, one inverted for every stretch from 2 to 6 # groups at that stretch's own protection level; the package tests check # the full sequence against the paper's Section 4 example. cv_bryant_paulson(alpha_level = .05, df = 14, n_groups = 6, n_covariates = 1,                   procedure = "duncan") #>  term     value area_less area_greater #>  upper_cv 3.496 <NA>      <NA>

title: Kish's Design Effect (DEFF), DEFT, and the Effective Sample Size — design_effect
text: Definition (Kish, 1965). clustered sample per-cluster sizes \(m_1, m_2, \ldots, m_K\) intraclass correlation \(\rho\), design effect variance mean $$\mathrm{DEFF} \;=\; 1 + (\bar m^{*} - 1) \rho,$$ \(\bar m^{*} = \sum_k m_k^2 / \sum_k m_k\) design-weighted average cluster size (Kish, 1965, eq. 5.4; sometimes called "Kish weighted average" "effective cluster size"). equal cluster sizes \(m_k = m\), reduces classroom form \(1 + (m - 1)\rho\). DEFT square root DEFF inflation factor standard error mean (whereas DEFF inflates variance). Effective sample size. number observations simple random sample yield standard error clustered sample $$N_{\mathrm{eff}} \;=\; N / \mathrm{DEFF} \;=\; N / \mathrm{DEFT}^2,$$ \(N = \sum_k m_k\) total observations. empty singleton clusters reported separately. mixed-effects / multilevel modeling, clusters zero observations carry information (dropped fitting), clusters one observation contribute \(N\) fixed-effect estimate contribute nothing estimation random-effect variance within-cluster residual. Hox et al. (2017) note singleton-heavy designs design effect close 1 even moderate \(\rho\) weighted cluster size small. output reports counts empty singleton clusters user can see glance much nominal sample size carries clustering information. fitted lmerMod object available, typical workflow extract icc via icc_lmer per-cluster sample sizes via table(cluster_id), pass design_effect(); see second example.

code: # von Hippel's (2016, p. 432) worked example: a simple regression with # n = 25 cases, an intercept and a slope (k = 2), and half of the # information about the slope missing. df_missing(0.5, N = 25, k = 2) #>  term        df     df_unbounded fmi   N  k df_complete at_floor #>  parameter_1 10.500 10.500       0.500 25 2 <NA>        FALSE    #>  #> Degrees of freedom: von Hippel's (2016, Eq. 31) effective sample size rule, #> N(1 - fmi) - k, bounded below at 3 df_missing(0.5, df_complete = 23, method = "complete_df") #>  term        df     df_unbounded fmi   N    k    df_complete at_floor #>  parameter_1 10.615 10.615       0.500 <NA> <NA> 23          FALSE    #>  #> Degrees of freedom: von Hippel's (2016, Eq. 32) complete data rule, #> df_complete (1 - fmi) (df_complete + 1) / (df_complete + 3), bounded below at 3  # Each parameter gets the degrees of freedom of its own FMI. With no # missing information the effective sample size rule returns the # complete data degrees of freedom, N - k = 23; near an FMI of 1 the # floor of 3 takes over. df_missing(c(slope = 0.5, intercept = 0.1, complete = 0, sparse = 0.95),            N = 25, k = 2) #>  term      df     df_unbounded fmi   N  k df_complete at_floor #>  slope     10.500 10.500       0.500 25 2 <NA>        FALSE    #>  intercept 20.500 20.500       0.100 25 2 <NA>        FALSE    #>  complete  23     23           0.000 25 2 <NA>        FALSE    #>  sparse    3      -0.750       0.950 25 2 <NA>         TRUE    #>  #> Degrees of freedom: von Hippel's (2016, Eq. 31) effective sample size rule, #> N(1 - fmi) - k, bounded below at 3  # A regression whose outcome is observed for only the 145 Grant-White # students of 301: t26_flags is missing for every Pasteur student. mlmr() # fits it by full information maximum likelihood (with the Wald interval, # whose normal quantile the t reference replaces, and without the effect # size refits, which this example does not use), and # fraction_missing_information() gives each slope's FMI with the N behind # it, so its rows go to df_missing() as they are; k = 3 counts the two # slopes and the intercept. fit <- mlmr(t26_flags ~ t1_visual_perception + t4_lozenges,             data = holzinger_swineford, ci_method = "wald",             effect_sizes = FALSE) fmi <- fraction_missing_information(fit) slopes <- fmi[fmi$op == "~", ] dfs <- df_missing(slopes, k = 3) dfs #>  term                             df      df_unbounded fmi   N   k df_complete #>  t26_flags ~ t1_visual_perception 136.521 136.521      0.536 301 3 <NA>        #>  t26_flags ~ t4_lozenges          118.008 118.008      0.598 301 3 <NA>        #>  at_floor #>  FALSE    #>  FALSE    #>  #> Degrees of freedom: von Hippel's (2016, Eq. 31) effective sample size rule, #> N(1 - fmi) - k, bounded below at 3  # The t interval keeps the FIML estimate and standard error and replaces # the normal quantile. With more than a hundred effective cases the # change is small; it matters when the effective sample size is small. est <- coef(fit)[-1] se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))[-1] crit <- qt(0.975, dfs$df) data.frame(term = names(est), df = dfs$df,            t_ci_lower = est - crit * se, t_ci_upper = est + crit * se,            normal_ci_lower = est - qnorm(0.975) * se,            normal_ci_upper = est + qnorm(0.975) * se, row.names = NULL) #>                   term       df t_ci_lower t_ci_upper normal_ci_lower #> 1 t1_visual_perception 136.5211  0.1988930  0.5693348       0.2005348 #> 2          t4_lozenges 118.0076  0.1735529  0.4819296       0.1751340 #>   normal_ci_upper #> 1       0.5676930 #> 2       0.4803484

code: x <- ci_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50)  # A knitr_kable that keeps every column, ready for a report. as_kable(x) #>  #>  #> Table: Confidence level: 95% #>  #> |term     |value | #> |:--------|:-----| #> |ci_lower |0.101 | #> |smd      |0.500 | #> |ci_upper |0.897 |  # The sentence an author writes in a results section. results_sentence(x, label = "Cohen's d") #> [1] "Cohen's d = 0.50, 95% CI [0.10, 0.90]"  # Wide tables (one interval per row) work the same way. results_sentence(ci_R2(R2 = 0.25, N = 100, p = 5)) #> [1] "R2 = 0.25, 95% CI [0.08, 0.37]"  # So does one row of a tidy() result, here the same interval. results_sentence(generics::tidy(x)) #> [1] "smd = 0.50, 95% CI [0.10, 0.90]"  # A table that holds an interval in rows named for its estimate: the # RMSEA of a model with chi square 85.3 on 24 df and N = 301, with its # 90 percent interval (the default level of every RMSEA interval), and # then gamma hat. fm <- sem_fit_measures(chisq = 85.3, df = 24, N = 301, p = 9) results_sentence(fm, label = "RMSEA", digits = 3) #> [1] "RMSEA = 0.092, 90% CI [0.072, 0.114]" results_sentence(fm, term = "gamma_hat", digits = 3) #> [1] "gamma_hat = 0.957, 90% CI [0.935, 0.973]"

title: Printing for DMAR Result Tables — dmar_tbl
code: # Every DMAR estimation function returns a table that prints this way. x <- ci_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50) x                       # rounded for reading, to three decimal places #>  term     value #>  ci_lower 0.101 #>  smd      0.500 #>  ci_upper 0.897 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # The stored numbers keep full precision; only the display rounds. x$value[x$term == "smd"] #> [1] 0.5 print(x, digits = 8)    # ask the display for more decimal places #>  term     value      #>  ci_lower 0.10058571 #>  smd      0.50000000 #>  ci_upper 0.89694143 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Pull a single number out, exactly as you would from a data frame. x$value[x$term == "ci_upper"] #> [1] 0.8969414  # The broom verbs give the programmer-friendly wide and summary views. generics::tidy(x) #>   term estimate  ci_lower  ci_upper conf_level #> 1  smd      0.5 0.1005857 0.8969414       0.95 generics::glance(x) #>   term estimate  ci_lower  ci_upper conf_level #> 1  smd      0.5 0.1005857 0.8969414       0.95  # The same display rules apply to a wide table, one with several typed # columns, for example an effect size with its confidence interval per # effect. ci_eta_squared(aov(iq_8 ~ treatment, data = pygmalion)) #>  effect    eta_squared_total eta_squared_total_ci_lower #>  treatment 0.020             0.001                      #>  eta_squared_total_ci_upper eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower #>  0.061                      0.020               0.001                        #>  eta_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N   #>  0.061                        6.335   1         308      310 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Stacking two tables computed at different confidence levels gives an # ordinary data frame, because no one confidence level describes every # row. The tidy() rows keep each level in a column. x_90 <- ci_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50, conf_level = 0.90) class(rbind(x, x_90)) #> [1] "data.frame" rbind(generics::tidy(x), generics::tidy(x_90)) #>   term estimate  ci_lower  ci_upper conf_level #> 1  smd      0.5 0.1005857 0.8969414       0.95 #> 2  smd      0.5 0.1645872 0.8329100       0.90

a 1.665520  0.62193264 2.709108 1.976750e-03       0.95  games_howell #> 2 c - a 2.809851  1.61418391 4.005519 3.511181e-05       0.95  games_howell #> 3 c - b 1.144331 -0.01274098 2.301403 5.283057e-02       0.95  games_howell #>   p_adjustment #> 1 games_howell #> 2 games_howell #> 3 games_howell generics::glance(gh) #>   n_contrasts conf_level ci_adjustment p_adjustment #> 1           3       0.95  games_howell games_howell  # A set of contrasts: tidy() keeps both the unadjusted and the # adjusted p-value, and glance() names the adjustment that produced # the second of them. fit <- aov(bdi_post ~ condition, data = depression_bdi) ct <- contrast_test(fit, contrasts = "pairwise", adjust = "tukey") generics::tidy(ct) #>                  term estimate   ci_lower  ci_upper statistic df    p_value #> 1      placebo - ssri      4.9 -2.0793312 11.879331 1.7407322 27 0.09311706 #> 2    wait_list - ssri      6.7 -0.2793312 13.679331 2.3801849 27 0.02462568 #> 3 wait_list - placebo      1.8 -5.1793312  8.779331 0.6394526 27 0.52791718 #>   p_adjusted conf_level ci_adjustment p_adjustment #> 1  0.2088175       0.95         tukey        tukey #> 2  0.0617362       0.95         tukey        tukey #> 3  0.7998146       0.95         tukey        tukey generics::glance(ct) #>   n_contrasts adjust var_equal p_adjusted_min conf_level ci_adjustment #> 1           3  tukey      TRUE      0.0617362       0.95         tukey #>   p_adjustment #> 1        tukey  # A sample size planner: tidy() gives the size and the power it buys, # glance() adds the planning inputs that produced them. plan <- ss_power_smd(true_smd = 0.5, desired_power = 0.80) generics::tidy(plan) #>          term estimate     power #> 1 sample_size       64 0.8014596 generics::glance(plan) #>          term estimate     power noncentral_t_parm true_smd desired_power #> 1 sample_size       64 0.8014596          2.828427      0.5           0.8 #>   alpha_level tails #> 1        0.05     2

code: # Liver scan data from McNeil, Keeler, and Adelstein (1975), the # example of Nam (1997, p. 1427): 344 patients classified by scan (x) # and by pathology (y), 32 positive by scan only and 27 by pathology # only. Does the scan understate the rate of disease by less than five # percentage points? That is a noninferiority question, so only # prop_diff_lower is given, and the rows that would need an upper bound # are NA. z_lower is the score statistic Nam reports, 2.795; the table # rounds it for display and stores the full value. res <- equivalence_proportion_paired(n_10 = 32, n_01 = 27, N = 344,                                      prop_diff_lower = 0.05) res #>  term             value  #>  difference       0.015  #>  n_10             32     #>  n_01             27     #>  N                344    #>  z_lower          2.795  #>  z_upper          <NA>   #>  p_lower          0.0026 #>  p_upper          <NA>   #>  p_tost           <NA>   #>  p_noninferiority 0.0026 #>  ci_lower         -0.023 #>  ci_upper         0.052  #>  prop_diff_lower  -0.050 #>  prop_diff_upper  <NA>   #>  equivalent       <NA>   #>  noninferior      1      #>  superior         <NA>   #>  inferior         0      #>  nonsuperior      <NA>   #>  #> Confidence level: 90% res$value[res$term == "z_lower"] #> [1] 2.795403 attr(res, "verdict") #> [1] "Noninferior"  # Agreement within five points in both directions is a stronger # claim. The interval rules out a shortfall of five points but not an # excess of five, so the verdict is noninferiority only. res <- equivalence_proportion_paired(n_10 = 32, n_01 = 27, N = 344,                                      prop_diff_lower = 0.05,                                      prop_diff_upper = 0.05) attr(res, "verdict") #> [1] "Noninferior only"  # A short form (x) and the full form (y) of a screening scale given to # the same 400 respondents: 38 screen positive on the short form only # and 52 on the full form only. A shortfall of five points is not ruled # out, but an excess of five is. res <- equivalence_proportion_paired(n_10 = 38, n_01 = 52, N = 400,                                      prop_diff_lower = 0.05,                                      prop_diff_upper = 0.05) res #>  term             value  #>  difference       -0.035 #>  n_10             38     #>  n_01             52     #>  N                400    #>  z_lower          0.632  #>  z_upper          -3.498 #>  p_lower          0.2636 #>  p_upper          0.0002 #>  p_tost           0.2636 #>  p_noninferiority 0.2636 #>  ci_lower         -0.074 #>  ci_upper         0.004  #>  prop_diff_lower  -0.050 #>  prop_diff_upper  0.050  #>  equivalent       0      #>  noninferior      0      #>  superior         0      #>  inferior         0      #>  nonsuperior      1      #>  #> Confidence level: 90% attr(res, "verdict") #> [1] "Not relevantly superior only"

code: # 1. Fitted model with `observed`. In the pygmalion expectancy #        experiment, treatment is manipulated while grade is a measured #        classification, so grade's variance stays in the denominator. pyg <- pygmalion pyg$grade <- factor(pyg$grade) fit <- aov(iq_8 ~ treatment * grade, data = pyg) eta_squared_generalized(fit, observed = "grade") #>            effect eta_squared_generalized #> 1       treatment              0.02015391 #> 2           grade              0.04396181 #> 3 treatment:grade              0.01872564  # 2. Raw sums of squares. eta_squared_generalized(SS_effect = 100, SS_observed = c(40, 30),                         SS_error = 200) #>    effect eta_squared_generalized #> 1 overall               0.2702703  # 3. Raw F-values and degrees of freedom. eta_squared_generalized(F_effect = 6.0, df_effect = 2,                         F_observed = c(2.5, 1.8),                         df_observed = c(1, 2), df_error = 50) #>    effect eta_squared_generalized #> 1 overall               0.1762115  # 4. Within-subjects (repeated measures) ANOVA. The denominator #        automatically includes the subject-level variance plus the #        within-subjects error, following Bakeman (2005). set.seed(113) n <- 20 rm_data <- data.frame(   subject = factor(rep(seq_len(n), each = 3)),   time    = factor(rep(c("Pre", "Mid", "Post"), n),                    levels = c("Pre", "Mid", "Post")),   y       = rnorm(n, sd = 1.5)[rep(seq_len(n), each = 3)] +             0.7 * rep(1:3, n) + rnorm(n * 3, sd = 1.2) ) fit_rm <- aov(y ~ time + Error(subject/time), data = rm_data) eta_squared_generalized(fit_rm) #>   effect eta_squared_generalized      stratum #> 1   time              0.09652627 subject:time  # 5. Mixed design with a measured between-subjects factor. Treat #        'group' as observed; its SS stays in the denominator for #        'time' and the 'group:time' interaction. set.seed(113) n_per_group <- 10 n <- n_per_group * 2 mixed_data <- data.frame(   subject = factor(rep(seq_len(n), each = 3)),   group   = factor(rep(c("Treatment", "Control"), each = 3 * n_per_group)),   time    = factor(rep(c("Pre", "Mid", "Post"), n),                    levels = c("Pre", "Mid", "Post")),   y       = rnorm(n, sd = 1)[rep(seq_len(n), each = 3)] +             0.5 * rep(1:3, n) + rnorm(n * 3, sd = 1) ) fit_mixed <- aov(y ~ group * time + Error(subject/time), data = mixed_data) eta_squared_generalized(fit_mixed, observed = "group") #>       effect eta_squared_generalized      stratum #> 1      group              0.01108528      subject #> 2       time              0.09101617 subject:time #> 3 group:time              0.01120063 subject:time

Derivation. scores normal within group common variance, observed t-statistic \(t = \hat d \sqrt{n_1 n_2 / (n_1 + n_2)}\) follows noncentral t distribution \(\mathit{df} = n_1 + n_2 - 2\) degrees freedom noncentrality parameter \(\lambda = \delta \sqrt{n_1 n_2 / (n_1 + n_2)}\). expected value noncentral t variate equals \(\lambda / J(\mathit{df})\) (Johnson, Kotz, & Balakrishnan, 1995, Section 31.3), \(\mathrm{E}[\hat d] = \mathrm{E}[t] / \sqrt{n_1 n_2 / (n_1 + n_2)} =   \delta / J(\mathit{df})\). bias \(\mathrm{E}[\hat d] - \delta =   \delta\,(1 - J)/J\) positive \(\delta > 0\). Magnitude correction. \(J(\mathit{df}) \approx 1 - 3/(4\,\mathit{df} - 1)\) leading order (Hedges & Olkin, 1985, p.\ 81). \(\delta = 0.5\), \(n_1 = n_2 = 10\) (\(\mathit{df} = 18\)), \(J \approx 0.957\), \(\mathrm{E}[\hat d] \approx 0.522\) upward bias 4%. \(n_1 = n_2 = 50\) bias 1%; \(n_1 = n_2 = 5\) (small samples) exceeds 10%. code: items <- c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t4_lozenges",            "t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence", "t9_word_meaning") # Congruence compares loadings alone, so the two fits leave out the # standard errors, tests, and intervals (point_estimates_only = TRUE). oblimin <- fa_exploratory(holzinger_swineford, nfactors = 2, items = items,                           seed = 113, point_estimates_only = TRUE) geomin <- fa_exploratory(holzinger_swineford, nfactors = 2, items = items,                          rotation = "geomin", seed = 113,                          point_estimates_only = TRUE)  # The same two factors under two rotations, compared by their pattern # loadings and then by their structure loadings. factor_congruence(oblimin, geomin) #> Tucker's congruence coefficients: 6 items; x has 2 factors, y has 2 #> x and y: fa_exploratory() tables (standardized pattern loadings) #>  #>  factor_x factor_y congruence reflected next_largest #>  f1       f1       0.999      FALSE     0.118        #>  f2       f2       0.999      FALSE     0.025        #> (congruence: the coefficient of each pair, after reflection; reflected: whether the factor of y was reflected to match; next_largest: the largest absolute coefficient of the row's factor with any factor of the other solution other than its partner) #>  #> Matching: the one-to-one assignment of y's factors to x's that maximizes the sum of the absolute coefficients; 2 pairs, 0 factors of y reflected. #>  #> Congruence matrix (rows: the factors of x; columns: the factors of y; before matching and reflection): #>       f1    f2 #> f1 0.999 0.118 #> f2 0.025 0.999 factor_congruence(oblimin, geomin, loadings = "structure") #> Tucker's congruence coefficients: 6 items; x has 2 factors, y has 2 #> x and y: fa_exploratory() tables (standardized structure loadings) #>  #>  factor_x factor_y congruence reflected next_largest #>  f1       f1       0.998      FALSE     0.639        #>  f2       f2       1.000      FALSE     0.569        #> (congruence: the coefficient of each pair, after reflection; reflected: whether the factor of y was reflected to match; next_largest: the largest absolute coefficient of the row's factor with any factor of the other solution other than its partner) #>  #> Matching: the one-to-one assignment of y's factors to x's that maximizes the sum of the absolute coefficients; 2 pairs, 0 factors of y reflected. #>  #> Congruence matrix (rows: the factors of x; columns: the factors of y; before matching and reflection): #>       f1    f2 #> f1 0.998 0.639 #> f2 0.569 1.000  # A loading matrix and a copy with its items in reverse order, its # factors listed the other way around, and one factor reflected: # matching recovers the pairing and the sign. L <- matrix(c(0.7, 0.6, 0.8, 0.1, 0.0, 0.2,               0.1, 0.2, 0.0, 0.7, 0.8, 0.6), ncol = 2,             dimnames = list(paste0("item_", 1:6), c("A", "B"))) L_copy <- L[6:1, c("B", "A")] L_copy[, "A"] <- -L_copy[, "A"] matched <- factor_congruence(L, L_copy) matched #> Tucker's congruence coefficients: 6 items; x has 2 factors, y has 2 #> x and y: loading matrices (as supplied) #>  #>  factor_x factor_y congruence reflected next_largest #>  A        A        1.000       TRUE     0.247        #>  B        B        1.000      FALSE     0.247        #> (congruence: the coefficient of each pair, after reflection; reflected: whether the factor of y was reflected to match; next_largest: the largest absolute coefficient of the row's factor with any factor of the other solution other than its partner) #>  #> Matching: the one-to-one assignment of y's factors to x's that maximizes the sum of the absolute coefficients; 2 pairs, 1 factor of y reflected. #>  #> Congruence matrix (rows: the factors of x; columns: the factors of y; before matching and reflection): #>       B      A #> A 0.247 -1.000 #> B 1.000 -0.247 attr(matched, "loadings_aligned") #>          A   B #> item_1 0.7 0.1 #> item_2 0.6 0.2 #> item_3 0.8 0.0 #> item_4 0.1 0.7 #> item_5 0.0 0.8 #> item_6 0.2 0.6  # Paired by position instead, the coefficients keep their signs. factor_congruence(L, L_copy, match = "order") #> Tucker's congruence coefficients: 6 items; x has 2 factors, y has 2 #> x and y: loading matrices (as supplied) #>  #>  factor_x factor_y congruence reflected next_largest #>  A        B        0.247      FALSE     1.000        #>  B        A        -0.247     FALSE     1.000        #> (congruence: the coefficient of each pair, signed; reflected: whether the factor of y was reflected to match; next_largest: the largest absolute coefficient of the row's factor with any factor of the other solution other than its partner) #>  #> Matching: by position, column j of y with column j of x; before any component is removed it is 0.164). #>  #> Confidence level: 90% #>  #> No cutoff is applied and no count is chosen: the count is a judgment that combines the fit of each model, the difference tests, the information criteria, the eigenvalues against their reference, and the MAP with theory and the interpretability of the rotated solutions, which fa_exploratory() gives at a chosen count. Each model's interval and p-values condition on its own count, and the criterion weights are conditional on the set of proper counts compared.

code: # An unbalanced two-factor design: IQ gain in the pygmalion expectancy # experiment, by treatment and by lower (grades 1 and 2) versus upper # (grades 3 through 6) grades, where the expectancy effect concentrated # in the lower grades. The cell sizes are unequal, so the Types differ. pyg <- pygmalion pyg$grade_band <- factor(ifelse(pyg$grade <= 2, "lower", "upper")) factorial_anova(iq_gain ~ treatment * grade_band, data = pyg) #>  effect               SS        df  F_value p_value eta_squared_partial #>  treatment            1505.059  1   8.244   0.0044  0.026               #>  grade_band           1829.890  1   10.023  0.0017  0.032               #>  treatment:grade_band 1115.315  1   6.109   0.0140  0.020               #>  Residuals            55867.220 306 <NA>    <NA>    <NA>                #>  eta_squared_partial_ci_lower eta_squared_partial_ci_upper #>  0.003                        0.070                        #>  0.005                        0.079                        #>  0.001                        0.060                        #>  <NA>                         <NA>                         #>  omega_squared_partial omega_squared_partial_ci_lower #>  0.023                 0.003                          #>  0.028                 0.005                          #>  0.016                 0.001                          #>  <NA>                  <NA>                           #>  omega_squared_partial_ci_upper #>  0.070                          #>  0.079                          #>  0.060                          #>  <NA>                           #>  #> Sum of squares: Type III #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # The same design under Type II (adjusts each main effect for the other # main effect, but not for the interaction). text: \(n_{ij}\) = number raters assigned subject \(\) category \(j\), \(\sum_j n_{ij} = m\) every \(\), define marginal proportion category \(j\) \(p_j = \sum_i n_{ij} / (Nm)\), per-subject agreement $$P_i = \frac{1}{m(m-1)}\Bigl(\sum_j n_{ij}^2 - m\Bigr).$$ Fleiss's kappa $$\hat\kappa_F = \frac{\bar P - P_e}{1 - P_e}, \qquad                     \bar P = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i P_i, \qquad                     P_e = \sum_j p_j^2.$$ Standard error. Two variances involved, variance \(\hat\kappa_F\) \(H_0\!: \kappa = 0\) variance nonzero value. test agreement uses null variance Fleiss, Nee, Landis (1979, Equation 12), corrected standard errors given Fleiss (1971), $$\mathrm{Var}_0(\hat\kappa_F) = \frac{2\,\bigl(P_e + P_e^2 - 2\sum_j p_j^3\bigr)}{N\,m\,(m-1)\,(1-P_e)^2},$$ reported \(z\) statistic p-value come . Fleiss (1971) Table 1 example gives \(z = 17.65\), matching irr::kappam.fleiss. confidence interval instead uses linearization variance Gwet (2008, Section 6), consistent estimated \(\hat\kappa_F\): subject \(\) contributes influence value \(\kappa_i^\ast\) (Gwet's Equations 34 35), \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\kappa_F) = \sum_i (\kappa_i^\ast - \hat\kappa_F)^2 / \{N(N-1)\}\), Gwet's Equation 33 sampling fraction set zero. (Gwet derives variance multiple-rater pi statistic, estimator Fleiss's kappa.) Wald confidence interval \(\hat\kappa_F \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}\), upper limit truncated 1. Each row of `ratings` gives, for one # subject, the count of raters who chose each category (rows sum to 6). # kappa = 0.430, matching Fleiss (1971). fleiss_1971 <- matrix(c(   0, 0, 0, 6, 0,   0, 3, 0, 0, 3,   0, 1, 4, 0, 1,   0, 0, 0, 0, 6,   0, 3, 0, 3, 0,   2, 0, 4, 0, 0,   0, 0, 4, 0, 2,   2, 0, 3, 1, 0,   2, 0, 0, 4, 0,   0, 0, 0, 0, 6,   1, 0, 0, 5, 0,   1, 1, 0, 4, 0,   0, 3, 3, 0, 0,   1, 0, 0, 5, 0,   0, 2, 0, 3, 1,   0, 0, 5, 0, 1,   3, 0, 0, 1, 2,   5, 1, 0, 0, 0,   0, 2, 0, 4, 0,   1, 0, 2, 0, 3,   0, 0, 0, 0, 6,   0, 1, 0, 5, 0,   0, 2, 0, 1, 3,   2, 0, 0, 4, 0,   1, 0, 0, 4, 1,   0, 5, 0, 1, 0,   4, 0, 0, 0, 2,   0, 2, 0, 4, 0,   1, 0, 5, 0, 0,   0, 0, 0, 0, 6 ), nrow = 30, byrow = TRUE) fleiss_kappa(fleiss_1971) #>  kappa se    ci_lower ci_upper z_value p_value  n_subjects n_raters #>  0.430 0.054 0.324    0.536    17.652  < 0.0001 30         6        #>  n_categories #>  5            #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # A percentile bootstrap interval, which resamples the subjects (rows) # with replacement and recomputes kappa on each resample. B = 2000 keeps the example quick; a reported # interval deserves the default B = 10000. fleiss_kappa(fleiss_1971, ci_method = "percentile", B = 2000,              seed = 113) #>  kappa se    ci_lower ci_upper z_value p_value  n_subjects n_raters #>  0.430 0.054 0.316    0.532    17.652  < 0.0001 30         6        #>  n_categories #>  5            #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Bootstrap: 2000 replications, 2000 used (0 dropped; at least 400 must be requested)

title: Gwet's AC1 and AC2 Chance-Corrected Agreement Coefficients — gwet_ac
text: Coefficient. $$\widehat{\mathrm{AC}} \;=\; \frac{p_a - p_e}{1 - p_e},$$ identical Cohen's \(\kappa\) structure different chance-correction \(p_e\): $$p_e \;=\; \frac{T_w}{Q (Q - 1)} \sum_{k = 1}^{Q} \pi_k (1 - \pi_k),$$ \(\pi_k\) mean within-unit proportion category \(k\), \(Q\) number categories, \(T_w\) sum entries weight matrix. nominal data unit weights (AC1), \(T_w = Q\) \(p_e\) reduces \((1 / (Q - 1)) \sum_k \pi_k (1 - \pi_k)\). AC \(\kappa\). \(\kappa\) can near zero even raters agree almost every unit trait rare common ("kappa paradox"; Feinstein & Cicchetti, 1990). Gwet's AC keeps chance-correction logic uses less extreme reference distribution. Variance. SE Gwet's (2008) linearization variance, $$\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mathrm{AC}}) \;=\;   \frac{1 - f}{n (n - 1)} \sum_i (\widehat{\mathrm{AC}}_i^{*}   - \widehat{\mathrm{AC}})^2,$$ \(\widehat{\mathrm{AC}}_i^{*}\) \(\)th unit's influence value, combining agreement chance-term contributions, \(n\) number units, \(f\) sampling fraction (\(0\) infinite target population). interval \(\widehat{\mathrm{AC}} \pm t_{1 - \alpha / 2,\, n - 1} \mathit{SE}\), upper limit truncated \(1\). quantities match Gwet's (2014) reference software.

title: Holzinger and Swineford (1939) Factor Analysis Study — holzinger_swineford
text: Karl John Holzinger (1893 1954) quantitative psychologist University Chicago one central figures first generation factor analysis. spent 1922 1923 academic year working Charles Spearman University College London, absorbing Spearman's two-factor theory intelligence, later developed bi-factor model extension theory. bi-factor model posits single general intelligence factor runs tests, plus several group factors capture residual correlation among substantively related subgroups tests, uncorrelated general factor. bifactor model later psychometric work (see fa_bifactor) structure. Frances Swineford Holzinger's research collaborator University Chicago coauthor much applied work. 1939 monograph reports study pupils seventh eighth grade classrooms two Chicago elementary schools, Pasteur Grant-White. Two schools used deliberately, stability bi-factor solution assessed fitting model school comparing results. 26 tests designed span five hypothesized ability domains: Spatial: tests 1 4 (visual perception, cubes,     paper form board, lozenges), tests 25 (revised paper     form board) 26 (flags) administered     Grant-White sample experimental substitutes tests 3     4. Verbal: tests 5 9 (general information,     paragraph comprehension, sentence completion, word     classification, word meaning). Mental speed: tests 10 13 (addition, code,     counting groups dots, straight curved capitals). Memory: tests 14 19 (word recognition, number     recognition, figure recognition, object-number, number-figure,     figure-word). Reasoning arithmetic: tests 20 24     (deduction, numerical puzzles, problem reasoning, series     completion, Woody-McCall mixed fundamentals). Holzinger Swineford concluded bi-factor solution reasonably stable across two schools, supporting substantive interpretation general factor together group factors. data far outlived original purpose. Jöreskog (1969) used 9-test subset drawn Grant-White sample (n = 145) introduce confirmatory maximum likelihood factor analysis; nine tests, schools per-item-rescaled form, shipped HolzingerSwineford1939 lavaan package, whose confirmatory factor analysis example (?lavaan::cfa) uses . complete 26-test data shipped support wider range analyses, including comparisons spatial, verbal, speed, memory, reasoning ability blocks multiple group analyses across Pasteur Grant-White schools. values holzinger_swineford corrected version data, identical 26 test cells MBESS::HS MBESS version 4.9.3 onward psychTools::holzinger.raw. older version data, approximately 53 cell values later corrected, continues circulate HS.data sem package HS.ability.data OpenMx package; byte-identical snapshots taken MBESS version 4.6.0 prior correction. corrections concentrated memory reasoning tests, largest cluster t20_deduction (15 cells, including number sign flips reflect corrected guessing-penalty adjustment).

ICC(2,k): two-way random model, average \(k\) raters,     absolute agreement. ICC(3,1): two-way mixed model, single rater, consistency.     Raters fixed (ones interest); rates differences     mean across raters penalized. ICC(3,k): two-way mixed model, average \(k\) raters,     consistency. code: # Twenty groups of six, with a group-level standard deviation of 0.7 on # top of within-group noise with a standard deviation of 1, so the data # generating ICC is 0.7^2 / (0.7^2 + 1) = 0.329. The estimate below comes # with a wide interval: 20 clusters is not many, and the interval is what # keeps that fact visible. set.seed(113) n_grp <- 20; n_per <- 6 grp <- factor(rep(1:n_grp, each = n_per)) y   <- rnorm(n_grp * n_per, 0, 1) + rep(rnorm(n_grp, 0, 0.7), each = n_per) d <- data.frame(y, grp) fit <- lme4::lmer(y ~ 1 + (1 | grp), data = d) icc_lmer(fit) #>  term                 value #>  icc                  0.174 #>  sigma2_between       0.248 #>  sigma2_within        1.177 #>  total_variance       1.425 #>  ci_lower             0.017 #>  ci_upper             0.377 #>  n_clusters           20    #>  average_cluster_size 6     #>  #> Confidence level: 95%
