title: Coefficient Omega (McDonald) With a Confidence Interval — reliability_omega
code: set.seed(113) J <- 6 loadings <- seq(0.5, 0.8, length.out = J) eta <- rnorm(200) errors <- matrix(rnorm(200 * J), 200, J) %*% diag(sqrt(1 - loadings^2)) items <- sweep(matrix(rep(eta, J), 200, J), 2, loadings, `*`) + errors colnames(items) <- paste0("y", seq_len(J))  # Default: robust omega, point estimate only (no bootstrap is run # unless requested; a message names the call that produces the # recommended interval). reliability_omega(data = items) #> Robust omega is reported without a confidence interval by default because its interval is bootstrap based. Request it with ci_method = "percentile" (or "bca"); B = 10000 replications is the default when you do. #>  term       value #>  estimate   0.821 #>  se         <NA>  #>  ci_lower   <NA>  #>  ci_upper   <NA>  #>  conf_level 0.950 #>  N          200   #>  N_complete 200   #>  n_items    6     #>  #> Denominator: observed composite variance (robust omega) #> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.043 (y2 with y5)  # The closed-form standard errors are derived under the model implied # ratio, so with the observed denominator the interval comes from a # bootstrap, which refits the single factor model once per # replication. B = 10 keeps the example quick and is below the 400 a # reported interval needs; the option lets it run and the warning says # so. A reported interval deserves the default B = 10000, an accuracy # choice rather than a formality (see Details). The percentile # interval is what Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) recommend for # this coefficient, with ci_method = "bca" as the alternative, and # seed makes the interval reproducible. old <- options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) reliability_omega(data = items, ci_method = "percentile", B = 10,                   seed = 113) #> Warning: reliability_omega(): B = 10 is below the 400 replications a 95% interval is reported from (10 beyond each limit). The limits are shown because options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) is set. With 10 replications each limit rests on about 0.3 of them and will move from seed to seed; use the result to explore or to demonstrate, and report an interval only from B of at least 400. B, B_used, and B_required are recorded in the result. #>  term       value #>  estimate   0.821 #>  se         0.016 #>  ci_lower   0.794 #>  ci_upper   0.840 #>  conf_level 0.950 #>  N          200   #>  N_complete 200   #>  n_items    6     #>  #> Denominator: observed composite variance (robust omega) #> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.043 (y2 with y5) #>  #> Bootstrap: 10 replications attempted, 10 returned a value; at least 400 are required for a reported interval. Exploratory: below the number required for a reported interval options(old)  # Model implied denominator with its closed-form robust ML interval, # whose limits are formed on the logit scale; ci_method = "mlr" gives # limits formed on the scale of omega. reliability_omega(data = items, denominator = "model_implied") #>  term       value #>  estimate   0.820 #>  se         0.019 #>  ci_lower   0.779 #>  ci_upper   0.854 #>  conf_level 0.950 #>  N          200   #>  N_complete 200   #>  n_items    6     #>  #> Denominator: composite variance implied by the fitted model #> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.043 (y2 with y5)  # Two further routes into the same coefficient. The first works from # the summary statistics a paper reports, a covariance matrix and its # sample size, with the maximum likelihood interval that summary # input supports. reliability_omega(S = cov(items), N = 200,                   denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml") #>  term       value #>  estimate   0.820 #>  se         0.020 #>  ci_lower   0.781 #>  ci_upper   0.858 #>  conf_level 0.950 #>  N          200   #>  N_complete 200   #>  n_items    6     #>  #> Denominator: composite variance implied by the fitted model #> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.043 (y2 with y5)  # How much would a t reference lengthen that interval? On 30 degrees of # freedom, an arbitrary small value chosen to show the effect, the # limits move out a little; the line under the table says so. reliability_omega(S = cov(items), N = 200,                   denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml",                   wald_df = 30) #>  term       value #>  estimate   0.820 #>  se         0.020 #>  ci_lower   0.780 #>  ci_upper   0.860 #>  conf_level 0.950 #>  N          200   #>  N_complete 200   #>  n_items    6     #>  #> Wald interval: t reference on 30 degrees of freedom (wald_df), in place of the normal #>  #> Denominator: composite variance implied by the fitted model #> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.043 (y2 with y5)  # The second is full information maximum likelihood with an auxiliary # variable, where missingness on y2 depends on an auxiliary z (missing # at random given z). Supplying aux implies missing = "fiml"; the # N_complete row shows how many rows listwise deletion would have # kept. With values missing, the interval can also refer to a t # distribution on degrees of freedom taken from omega's own fraction of # missing information, here in the fit that carries z (the calibration # study behind the rule had no auxiliary variable, so this case rests # on analogy; see Details); the line under the table gives N, the FMI, # and the degrees of freedom that result. The rule is calibrated for # limits on the scale of omega, so the interval here is the "mlr" one. z <- eta + rnorm(200, sd = 0.5) d <- data.frame(items, z = z) d$y2[runif(200) < plogis(-1 + 1.5 * as.numeric(scale(z)))] <- NA reliability_omega(data = d, aux = "z", denominator = "model_implied",                   wald_df = "missing_information") #>  term       value #>  estimate   0.819 #>  se         0.020 #>  ci_lower   0.780 #>  ci_upper   0.859 #>  conf_level 0.950 #>  N          200   #>  N_complete 140   #>  n_items    6     #>  #> Wald interval: t reference on 187.3 degrees of freedom, from von Hippel's (2016) max(3, N(1 - FMI) - 1) with N = 200 and FMI = 0.05845 (wald_df = "missing_information"), in place of the normal #>  #> The FMI degrees-of-freedom rule is approximate. Its calibration study admitted data sets that the affine-collapse screening sets aside, so coverage under that screening has not been established. See the method's help for its scope and conditional evidence. #>  #> Denominator: composite variance implied by the fitted model #> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.075 (y2 with y5)  # Two-stage estimation instead: z enters only the first stage, where the # means and covariances are estimated, and the interval uses the robust # two-stage standard error, its limits again formed on the logit scale. reliability_omega(data = d, aux = "z", missing = "two_stage",                   denominator = "model_implied") #>  term       value #>  estimate   0.819 #>  se         0.020 #>  ci_lower   0.776 #>  ci_upper   0.855 #>  conf_level 0.950 #>  N          200   #>  N_complete 140   #>  n_items    6     #>  #> Denominator: composite variance implied by the fitted model #> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.070 (y2 with y5)

title: Categorical Omega for Ordered-Categorical Items, With a Confidence Interval — reliability_omega_categorical
code: set.seed(113) # The mixed-skew design of Green and Yang (2009, Table 1): four items # loading 0.8 on one factor, each cut into five categories, two piled # into the top category and two into the bottom. Their population # categorical omega for this design is 0.716. N <- 1000 p_top <- c(.011, .027, .047, .118, .797) cut_top <- c(-Inf, qnorm(cumsum(p_top)[-5]), Inf) cut_bottom <- c(-Inf, qnorm(cumsum(rev(p_top))[-5]), Inf) latent <- outer(rnorm(N), rep(0.8, 4)) +           matrix(rnorm(N * 4, sd = 0.6), N, 4) items <- cbind(y1 = cut(latent[, 1], cut_top, labels = FALSE),                y2 = cut(latent[, 2], cut_top, labels = FALSE),                y3 = cut(latent[, 3], cut_bottom, labels = FALSE),                y4 = cut(latent[, 4], cut_bottom, labels = FALSE))  # Categorical omega as Green and Yang defined it: the total variance # of the summed categories comes from the correlations the fitted # single-factor model reproduces. reliability_omega_categorical(data = items, denominator = "model_implied") #> Categorical omega is reported without a confidence interval by default because its interval is bootstrap based. Request it with ci_method = "bca" (the recommended method) or "percentile"; B = 10000 replications is the default when you do. #>  term       value #>  estimate   0.714 #>  se         <NA>  #>  ci_lower   <NA>  #>  ci_upper   <NA>  #>  conf_level 0.950 #>  N          1000  #>  N_complete 1000  #>  n_items    4     #>  #> Denominator: variance of the summed categories from the model implied polychoric correlations (Green & Yang, 2009) #> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: 0.028 (y1 with y4)  # The default, categorical omega as Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) # computed and recommended it: the total variance comes from the # unrestricted polychoric correlations. The single factor holds in # this design, so the two agree to within about 0.01; they part ways # as the model misfits. reliability_omega_categorical(data = items) #> Categorical omega is reported without a confidence interval by default because its interval is bootstrap based. Request it with ci_method = "bca" (the recommended method) or "percentile"; B = 10000 replications is the default when you do. #>  term       value #>  estimate   0.720 #>  se         <NA>  #>  ci_lower   <NA>  #>  ci_upper   <NA>  #>  conf_level 0.950 #>  N          1000  #>  N_complete 1000  #>  n_items    4     #>  #> Denominator: variance of the summed categories from the unrestricted polychoric correlations (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016) #> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: 0.028 (y1 with y4)  # The same sum score with the items treated as continuous. Robust # omega falls far below 0.716 here, because items whose categories # pile up at opposite ends relate to the factor far from linearly, # which is the case Green and Yang designed their coefficient for. reliability_omega(data = items) #> Robust omega is reported without a confidence interval by default because its interval is bootstrap based. Request it with ci_method = "percentile" (or "bca"); B = 10000 replications is the default when you do. #>  term       value #>  estimate   0.549 #>  se         <NA>  #>  ci_lower   <NA>  #>  ci_upper   <NA>  #>  conf_level 0.950 #>  N          1000  #>  N_complete 1000  #>  n_items    4     #>  #> Denominator: observed composite variance (robust omega) #> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: 0.283 (y3 with y4)  # The same items with values missing at random: respondents low on y1 # and y2 leave y3 and y4 unanswered more often. Listwise deletion, the # default, keeps only the complete rows, and here that leaves too # little: the few respondents who determine the correlation of a # top-piled item with a bottom-piled one (one to five of the 1000 for # each pair) stand low on y1 and y2, the complete rows keep none of # them for y2 with y3 or for y1 with y4, and the correlations left do # not identify the loadings, so a call with the default stops and says # so (see Details). z <- as.numeric(scale(items[, "y1"] + items[, "y2"])) items_mar <- items items_mar[runif(N) < plogis(-1.5 - 1.2 * z), "y3"] <- NA items_mar[runif(N) < plogis(-1.5 - 1.2 * z), "y4"] <- NA  # Pairwise deletion estimates each polychoric correlation from the rows # that observe both items, so every row contributes. It still assumes # values missing completely at random, as listwise deletion does. # Multiple imputation, which assumes only that they are missing at # random, takes longer than an example here can (see Details). reliability_omega_categorical(data = items_mar,                               denominator = "model_implied",                               missing = "pairwise") #> The data do not determine the polychoric correlation of y2 and y3 (the bivariate table has empty cells). The model implied denominator does not need it, and the correlations the data do determine identify the single-factor loadings; its residual correlation is reported as NA. #> Categorical omega is reported without a confidence interval by default because its interval is bootstrap based. Use the default of 1000 or more in an # analysis. d <- holzinger_swineford[c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t4_lozenges",                            "t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence",                            "t9_word_meaning", "t5_general_information")] set.seed(113) drop <- runif(nrow(d)) < plogis((d$t5_general_information - 30) / 10) - 0.35 d[drop, c("t2_cubes", "t7_sentence")] <- NA fit <- lavaan::cfa(   "visual  =~ t1_visual_perception + t2_cubes + t4_lozenges    textual =~ t6_paragraph_comprehension + t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning",   data = d, missing = "ml", std.lv = TRUE, aux = "t5_general_information") #> lavaan NOTE:   #>    auxiliary (aux) variable(s) added to the model as saturated correlates  #>    (estimated with FIML and hidden from the output): t5_general_information #> Warning: lavaan->lav_object_post_check():   #>    the covariance matrix of the residuals of the observed variables (theta)  #>    is not positive definite; use lavInspect(fit, "theta") to investigate. old <- options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) sem_exact_fit_bootstrap(fit, B = 10, seed = 113) #> Warning: sem_exact_fit_bootstrap(): B = 10 is below the 100 replications a Monte Carlo p-value is reported from (100 for a Monte Carlo p-value). The p-value is shown because options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) is set. With 10 replications it will move from seed to seed; use the result to explore or to demonstrate, and report a p-value only from B of at least 100. B, B_used, and B_required are recorded in the result. #>  term                 value    #>  chi_square           23.859   #>  df                   8        #>  p_chi_square         0.0024   #>  p_bootstrap          < 0.0001 #>  p_bootstrap_ci_lower 0.0000   #>  p_bootstrap_ci_upper 0.2775   #>  bootstrap_mean       6.604    #>  B                    10       #>  B_used               10       #>  B_improper           0        #>  B_failed             0        #>  N                    301      #>  n_groups             1        #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Transformation: incomplete data, one matrix for every pattern (Savalei & Yuan, 2009); the statistic is the standard likelihood ratio statistic under FIML #> Bootstrap: B = 10 samples, 10 used; p_bootstrap is the share of used statistics at least the observed one, with the Wilson interval for its Monte Carlo error at 95 percent. Exploratory: below the 100 samples a reported p-value needs #> Sample size: N = 301 in 1 group options(old)

code: # 1. 2 x 2 randomized design, single covariate. set.seed(113) design_2x2 <- expand.grid(A = factor(1:2), B = factor(1:2)) design_2x2$true_mean_Y <- c(50, 60, 55, 65)   # cell means in expand.grid order  d1 <- simulate_ancova_factorial_data(   a            = 2, b = 2,   true_mean_Y  = design_2x2$true_mean_Y,   true_mean_X  = matrix(10, nrow = 4, ncol = 1),  # constant covariate mean   true_sd_Y      = 8,   true_sd_X      = 3,   true_cor_YX  = 0.40,   n_per_cell   = 30 ) aggregate(y ~ A + B, data = d1, FUN = mean) #>   A B        y #> 1 1 1 48.65943 #> 2 2 1 60.48404 #> 3 1 2 58.24399 #> 4 2 2 65.81071  # 2. 3 x 2 nonrandomized design with two covariates and unequal n. set.seed(113) a <- 3; b <- 2; q <- 2 n_cells <- a * b d2 <- simulate_ancova_factorial_data(   a            = a, b = b,   n_covariates = q,   true_mean_Y  = c(50, 55, 60,  52, 58, 64),   true_mean_X  = matrix(c(10, 11, 12,  9, 10, 11,                            5,  6,  7,  4,  5,  6),                          nrow = n_cells, ncol = q),   true_sd_Y      = 8,   true_sd_X      = c(3, 2),   true_cor_YX  = c(0.40, 0.25),   true_cor_XX  = matrix(c(1,   0.3,                           0.3, 1),                         nrow = 2),   n_per_cell   = c(30, 25, 20,  35, 30, 25),   randomized   = FALSE ) head(d2) #>   A B        x1         x2        y #> 1 1 1 13.254525  8.5360960 50.29890 #> 2 1 1 11.325283  4.5916342 61.15584 #> 3 1 1  9.805804  6.4857128 56.11123 #> 4 1 1  8.257290 -0.4105572 39.99210 #> 5 1 1 10.668032  5.1076307 45.26514 #> 6 1 1  4.298724  3.7604657 36.75722  # 3. 2 x 2 x 2 randomized design with one covariate. set.seed(113) d3 <- simulate_ancova_factorial_data(   a       = 2, b = 2, c = 2,   true_mean_Y = c(50, 55, 52, 57,  53, 58, 55, 60),  # 8 cells in A-fastest order   true_mean_X = matrix(10, nrow = 8, ncol = 1),   true_sd_Y = 8,   true_sd_X = 3,   true_cor_YX = 0.40,   n_per_cell = 25 ) table(d3$A, d3$B, d3$C)  # 25 per cell, 200 total #> , ,  = 1 #>  #>     #>      1  2 #>   1 25 25 #>   2 25 25 #>  #> , ,  = 2 #>  #>     #>      1  2 #>   1 25 25 #>   2 25 25 #>

title: Simulate Data From a Gompertz Change (Growth) Model — simulate_longitudinal_gompertz
code: # The six-curve illustration from Kelley (2005): alpha = 0.75 and # zeta = 0.25 throughout, so every curve crosses its inflection at # the same height, 0.75 / exp(1) + 0.25, about 0.526. The three # rising curves share the inflection time beta = 2 and differ only # in curvature; the three falling curves share beta = 3. Each curve # is its own population of size one, so a single call draws the whole panel. panel <- simulate_longitudinal_gompertz(   n_per_group = 1, target_times = seq(0, 6, by = 0.1),   fixed_parameters = list(     c(alpha = 0.75, beta = 2, gamma =  1.75, zeta = 0.25),     c(alpha = 0.75, beta = 2, gamma =  1.00, zeta = 0.25),     c(alpha = 0.75, beta = 2, gamma =  0.45, zeta = 0.25),     c(alpha = 0.75, beta = 3, gamma = -0.35, zeta = 0.25),     c(alpha = 0.75, beta = 3, gamma = -0.60, zeta = 0.25),     c(alpha = 0.75, beta = 3, gamma = -2.00, zeta = 0.25)),   error_variance = 0 ) plot_trajectories(panel, id = "id", time = "time",                   outcome = "true_score", group = "population")   # Individual differences in a single parameter: only the inflection # time varies (a named entry leaves every other variance at zero), # so every trajectory shares the floor and the ceiling but reaches # its fastest growth at its own moment. set.seed(113) d_beta <- simulate_longitudinal_gompertz(   n_per_group = 25, target_times = seq(0, 8, by = 0.5),   fixed_parameters = c(alpha = 75, beta = 3, gamma = 0.55, zeta = 10),   random_variances = c(beta = 0.8), error_variance = 0 ) plot_trajectories(d_beta, id = "id", time = "time",                   outcome = "true_score")   # Individual differences in every parameter at once, plus level-one # error: the realistic sampling model. set.seed(113) d <- simulate_longitudinal_gompertz(   n_per_group = 30, target_times = 0:12,   fixed_parameters = c(alpha = 75, beta = 3, gamma = 0.55, zeta = 10),   random_variances = c(alpha = 36, beta = 0.8, gamma = 0.01, zeta = 9),   error_variance = 16 ) plot_trajectories(d, id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "y")

title: Simulate Data From a Logistic Change (Growth) Model — simulate_longitudinal_logistic
code: # A six-curve panel in the style of the growth-curve illustrations # in Kelley (2005): floor 10 and ceiling 90 throughout, so every # curve crosses its inflection at the same height (50, half the # total change). The rising curves share beta = 6 and differ only in # curvature; the falling curves mirror them. Each curve is its own population # of size one, so a single call draws the whole panel. panel <- simulate_longitudinal_logistic(   n_per_group = 1, target_times = seq(0, 12, by = 0.1),   fixed_parameters = list(     c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma =  2.0, zeta = 10),     c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma =  0.9, zeta = 10),     c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma =  0.5, zeta = 10),     c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma = -0.5, zeta = 10),     c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma = -0.9, zeta = 10),     c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma = -2.0, zeta = 10)),   error_variance = 0 ) plot_trajectories(panel, id = "id", time = "time",                   outcome = "true_score", group = "population")   # Individual differences in a single parameter: only the inflection # time varies (a named entry leaves the other variances at zero), so # every learner shares the floor and the ceiling but hits fastest # growth on a different week. set.seed(113) d_beta <- simulate_longitudinal_logistic(   n_per_group = 25, target_times = seq(0, 12, by = 0.5),   fixed_parameters = c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma = 0.9, zeta = 10),   random_variances = c(beta = 1.2), error_variance = 0 ) plot_trajectories(d_beta, id = "id", time = "time",                   outcome = "true_score")   # Unit-specific measurement times: each child is tested at their own # ages, drawn uniformly between 40 and 90 weeks with five to nine # visits each, rather than on one shared schedule. set.seed(113) d_ages <- simulate_longitudinal_logistic(   n_per_group = 12, time_range = c(40, 90), n_occasions = c(5, 9),   fixed_parameters = c(alpha = 80, beta = 65, gamma = 0.15, zeta = 10),   random_variances = c(beta = 16), error_variance = 4 ) plot_trajectories(d_ages, id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "y")   # Individual differences in every parameter, plus level-one error: # skill acquisition from a floor near 10 to a ceiling near 90, # fastest around week 6. set.seed(113) d <- simulate_longitudinal_logistic(   n_per_group = 30, target_times = 0:12,   fixed_parameters = c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma = 0.9, zeta = 10),   random_variances = c(alpha = 36, beta = 1, gamma = 0.01, zeta = 9),   error_variance = 16 ) plot_trajectories(d, id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "y")

title: Simulate Data From a Negative Exponential (Asymptotic Regression) Change Model — simulate_longitudinal_negative_exponential
code: # The six-curve illustration from Kelley (2005): three growth curves # (intercept 0, asymptote 1) that differ only in curvature, and # three decay curves (intercept 1, asymptote 0) that mirror them. # Each curve is its own population of size one, so a single call draws the # whole panel. panel <- simulate_longitudinal_negative_exponential(   n_per_group = 1, target_times = seq(0, 10, by = 0.1),   fixed_parameters = list(     c(alpha = 1, zeta = -1, gamma = 0.9),     c(alpha = 1, zeta = -1, gamma = 0.4),     c(alpha = 1, zeta = -1, gamma = 0.2),     c(alpha = 0, zeta =  1, gamma = 1.2),     c(alpha = 0, zeta =  1, gamma = 0.5),     c(alpha = 0, zeta =  1, gamma = 0.3)),   error_variance = 0 ) plot_trajectories(panel, id = "id", time = "time",                   outcome = "true_score", group = "population")   # Individual differences in a single parameter: only the curvature # varies (a named entry leaves the other variances at zero), so all # trajectories share their start and their destination but close the # gap at their own rates. set.seed(113) d_gamma <- simulate_longitudinal_negative_exponential(   n_per_group = 25, target_times = seq(0, 8, by = 0.5),   fixed_parameters = c(alpha = 100, zeta = -80, gamma = 0.5),   random_variances = c(gamma = 0.02), error_variance = 0 ) plot_trajectories(d_gamma, id = "id", time = "time",                   outcome = "true_score")   # Individual differences in every parameter, plus level-one error: # vocabulary learning that starts near 20 words (phi = alpha + zeta), # climbs toward an asymptote near 100, and closes about 40% of the # remaining gap per month (gamma = 0.5). set.seed(113) d <- simulate_longitudinal_negative_exponential(   n_per_group = 30, target_times = 0:8,   fixed_parameters = c(alpha = 100, zeta = -80, gamma = 0.5),   random_variances = c(alpha = 25, zeta = 16, gamma = 0.01),   error_variance = 9 ) head(d) #>     id population occasion target_time time true_score        y #> 1 u001          1        1           0    0   14.93417 12.42780 #> 2 u001          1        2           1    1   55.25373 53.94814 #> 3 u001          1        3           2    2   76.61122 76.80784 #> 4 u001          1        4           3    3   87.92441 86.11628 #> 5 u001          1        5           4    4   93.91707 87.91651 #> 6 u001          1        6           5    5   97.09142 98.29619 plot_trajectories(d, id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "y")

title: Simulate Data From a Polynomial Change (Growth) Model — simulate_longitudinal_polynomial
code: # 1. One population of linear growers with a random intercept and a random slope, #    measured yearly for four years (five occasions), with the level-one #    error set directly. set.seed(113) d <- simulate_longitudinal_polynomial(   n_per_group        = 50,   target_times       = 0:4,   fixed_coefficients = c(10, 1.5),          # intercept 10, slope 1.5 per year   random_variances   = c(4, 0.25),          # var(intercept) = 4, var(slope) = .25   error_variance     = 1 ) head(d) #>   id population occasion target_time time true_score         y #> 1  1          1        1           0    0   9.733291  9.084685 #> 2  1          1        2           1    1  11.773957 11.949644 #> 3  1          1        3           2    2  13.814622 13.610660 #> 4  1          1        4           3    3  15.855288 15.918206 #> 5  1          1        5           4    4  17.895953 17.911464 #> 6  2          1        1           0    0   7.249557  8.428662  # 2. Two populations that differ only in their slope (a treatment that changes #    the rate of growth). Pass a list of coefficient vectors, one per population. set.seed(113) two <- simulate_longitudinal_polynomial(   n_per_group        = c(40, 40),   target_times       = 0:4,   fixed_coefficients = list(control = c(10, 1.0), treatment = c(10, 1.8)),   random_variances   = c(4, 0.25),   error_variance     = 1 ) aggregate(y ~ population + occasion, data = two, FUN = mean) #>    population occasion        y #> 1           1        1  9.77354 #> 2           2        1 10.34420 #> 3           1        2 10.66252 #> 4           2        2 12.11865 #> 5           1        3 11.38262 #> 6           2        3 14.02571 #> 7           1        4 12.39497 #> 8           2        4 15.66385 #> 9           1        5 13.34494 #> 10          2        5 17.31383  # 3. Pin the level-one error to a target reliability instead of setting it #    directly. The single number is the average reliability across occasions; #    the per-occasion values differ and are returned as an attribute. set.seed(113) rel <- simulate_longitudinal_polynomial(   n_per_group        = 100,   target_times       = 0:4,   fixed_coefficients = c(10, 1.5),   random_variances   = c(4, 0.25),   reliability        = 0.80 ) attr(rel, "error_variance") #> [1] 1.303557 round(attr(rel, "reliability_by_occasion"), 3)   # not constant across waves #> occasion_1 occasion_2 occasion_3 occasion_4 occasion_5  #>      0.754      0.765      0.793      0.827      0.860   # 4. Assessment-time jitter: the nominal "yearly" schedule, but subjects #    actually arrive a little early or late (SD of about six weeks on a #    one-year scale). The nominal and actual times are kept in separate #    columns so the consequences of analyzing on the nominal time can be #    studied. set.seed(113) jit <- simulate_longitudinal_polynomial(   n_per_group        = 30,   target_times       = 0:4,   fixed_coefficients = c(10, 1.5),   random_variances   = c(4, 0.25),   error_variance     = 1,   timing_sd          = 0.12 ) head(jit[, c("id", "occasion", "target_time", "time")]) #>   id occasion target_time        time #> 1  1        1           0  0.16252055 #> 2  1        2           1  0.93632062 #> 3  1        3           2  2.08847793 #> 4  1        4           3  2.70577279 #> 5  1        5           4  4.00090495 #> 6  2        1           0 -0.02811366  # 4b. Unit-specific measurement times: each of 12 children is tested #     between 40 and 90 weeks of age, five to nine times, no two on the #     same schedule. The level-one error is a single variance; the #     "schedule" attribute records the design. set.seed(113) ages <- simulate_longitudinal_polynomial(   n_per_group        = 12,   time_range         = c(40, 90),   n_occasions        = c(5, 9),   fixed_coefficients = c(10, 0.5),   random_variances   = c(4, 0.01),   error_variance     = 2 ) attr(ages, "schedule") #> [1] "unit_specific" table(table(ages$id))   # units per occasion count #>  #> 5 6 7 8 9  #> 4 1 2 4 1   # 5. A flat line (order 0): no growth, only a random subject level and #    measurement error. The coefficient vector has length one. set.seed(113) flat <- simulate_longitudinal_polynomial(   n_per_group        = 20,   target_times       = 0:4,   fixed_coefficients = 5,   random_variances   = 2,   error_variance     = 1 ) head(flat) #>   id population occasion target_time time true_score        y #> 1  1          1        1           0    0   5.188592 5.471883 #> 2  1          1        2           1    1   5.188592 6.936332 #> 3  1          1        3           2    2   5.188592 6.385949 #> 4  1          1        4           3    3   5.188592 4.852617 #> 5  1          1        5           4    4   5.188592 6.085924 #> 6  2          1        1           0    0   6.944857 8.731318  # 6. Autocorrelated measurement error: the same error variance at each wave, #    but the level-one errors decay as an AR(1) process (errors at adjacent #    occasions correlate 0.5), the kind of dependence a model assuming #    independent errors would miss. The full error covariance is returned. set.seed(113) ar <- simulate_longitudinal_polynomial(   n_per_group        = 40,   target_times       = 0:4,   fixed_coefficients = c(10, 1.5),   random_variances   = c(4, 0.25),   error_variance     = 1,   error_structure    = "ar1",   error_correlation  = 0.5 ) round(attr(ar, "error_covariance"), 3) #>       [,1]  [,2] [,3]  [,4]  [,5] #> [1,] 1.000 0.500 0.25 0.125 0.062 #> [2,] 0.500 1.000 0.50 0.250 0.125 #> [3,] 0.250 0.500 1.00 0.500 0.250 #> [4,] 0.125 0.250 0.50 1.000 0.500 #> [5,] 0.062 0.125 0.25 0.500 1.000

title: Simulate Data From a Richards Change (Growth) Model — simulate_longitudinal_richards
code: # The family in one panel: five Richards curves sharing alpha, beta, # gamma, and zeta and differing only in the shape parameter delta. # delta near 0 is the Gompertz, delta = 1 is the logistic, and # larger delta pushes the inflection later than halfway. Each curve # is its own population of size one, so a single call draws the whole panel. panel <- simulate_longitudinal_richards(   n_per_group = 1, target_times = seq(0, 12, by = 0.1),   fixed_parameters = list(     c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma = 0.9, delta = 0.02, zeta = 10),     c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma = 0.9, delta = 0.25, zeta = 10),     c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma = 0.9, delta = 1.00, zeta = 10),     c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma = 0.9, delta = 3.00, zeta = 10),     c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma = 0.9, delta = 8.00, zeta = 10)),   error_variance = 0 ) plot_trajectories(panel, id = "id", time = "time",                   outcome = "true_score", group = "population")   # Individual differences in a single parameter: only the shape # varies (a named entry leaves the other variances at zero), so the # curves agree on floor, ceiling, timing, and curvature yet turn # from acceleration to deceleration at different heights. set.seed(113) d_delta <- simulate_longitudinal_richards(   n_per_group = 25, target_times = seq(0, 12, by = 0.5),   fixed_parameters = c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma = 0.9,                        delta = 1, zeta = 10),   random_variances = c(delta = 0.04), error_variance = 0 ) plot_trajectories(d_delta, id = "id", time = "time",                   outcome = "true_score")   # Individual differences in every parameter, plus level-one error: # a late-inflecting outbreak-style curve, with delta = 3 placing the # inflection at about 63% of total change, (1 + 3)^(-1/3). set.seed(113) d <- simulate_longitudinal_richards(   n_per_group = 30, target_times = 0:12,   fixed_parameters = c(alpha = 80, beta = 6, gamma = 0.9,                        delta = 3, zeta = 10),   random_variances = c(alpha = 36, beta = 1, gamma = 0.01,                        delta = 0.04, zeta = 9),   error_variance = 16 ) plot_trajectories(d, id = "id", time = "time", outcome = "y")   # delta = 1 reproduces the logistic exactly: with no randomness and # no error, the two simulators return identical true scores. d_r <- simulate_longitudinal_richards(   n_per_group = 1, target_times = 0:5,   fixed_parameters = c(alpha = 80, beta = 3, gamma = 1,                        delta = 1, zeta = 10),   error_variance = 0) d_l <- simulate_longitudinal_logistic(   n_per_group = 1, target_times = 0:5,   fixed_parameters = c(alpha = 80, beta = 3, gamma = 1, zeta = 10),   error_variance = 0) all.equal(d_r$true_score, d_l$true_score) #> [1] TRUE

code: # Suppose the population error variance of some three-group ANOVA model # is believed to be 40. The researcher is interested in the difference # between the mean of group 1 and the average of means of group 2 and 3. # To plan the sample size so that, with 90 percent certainty, the # obtained 95 percent full confidence interval width is no wider than 3:  ss_aipe_c(true_var_error = 40, c_weights = c(1, -0.5, -0.5),           width = 3, assurance = .90) #>  term                  value #>  necessary_n_per_group 114   #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # The planning values can come from a pilot study. The posttest scores in # depression_bdi have an error variance near 40, and their residuals are # lighter tailed than the normal, as scores on a bounded inventory often # are. Thirty residuals estimate the kurtosis imprecisely, so it is a # planning value to weigh, as the error variance is. pilot <- lm(bdi_post ~ condition, data = depression_bdi) sigma(pilot)^2 #> [1] 39.61852 kurtosis(residuals(pilot)) #> [1] -0.9045304 ss_aipe_c(true_var_error = sigma(pilot)^2, c_weights = c(1, -0.5, -0.5),           width = 3, assurance = .90, true_kurtosis = kurtosis(residuals(pilot))) #>  term                  value #>  necessary_n_per_group 110   #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> The assurance allows for errors with an excess kurtosis of -0.905 (normal errors have 0).

code: # A mediation model whose research questions concern the magnitudes of # both individual paths and the indirect effect. The population model # fixes every parameter to its purported population value. true_model <- "   f1 =~ 1*y1 + 0.8*y2 + 0.8*y3   f2 =~ 1*y4 + 0.8*y5 + 0.8*y6   f3 =~ 1*y7 + 0.8*y8 + 0.8*y9   f2 ~ 0.4*f1   f3 ~ 0.5*f2 + 0.2*f1   f1 ~~ 1*f1   f2 ~~ 0.84*f2   f3 ~~ 0.7*f3   y1 ~~ 0.5*y1; y2 ~~ 0.5*y2; y3 ~~ 0.5*y3   y4 ~~ 0.5*y4; y5 ~~ 0.5*y5; y6 ~~ 0.5*y6   y7 ~~ 0.5*y7; y8 ~~ 0.5*y8; y9 ~~ 0.5*y9 "  # The analysis model labels the two paths and defines the indirect # effect; all three make up the set of interest. analysis_model <- "   f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3   f2 =~ y4 + y5 + y6   f3 =~ y7 + y8 + y9   f2 ~ a*f1   f3 ~ b*f2 + cp*f1   ab := a*b "  # Realized interval widths at N = 200, with the indirect effect held to a # narrower interval than the paths through a named vector of widths. Each # interval lands within its desired width in most of the replications, yet # all three do so together in far fewer of them: that joint proportion, # reported as composite_assurance, is what a design of this kind has to be # planned against. G = 10 keeps the example quick; a reported plan # deserves the default G = 1000 or more. ss_aipe_composite_sem(model = analysis_model, true_model = true_model,                       parameters = c("a", "b", "ab"),                       width = c(a = 0.35, b = 0.40, ab = 0.25),                       specified_N = 200, G = 10, seed = 113) #>  term                   value #>  specified_N            200   #>  composite_assurance    0.100 #>  mean_width_a           0.336 #>  mean_width_b           0.384 #>  mean_width_ab          0.212 #>  pct_ci_less_width_a    0.500 #>  pct_ci_less_width_b    0.600 #>  pct_ci_less_width_ab   0.900 #>  width_a                0.350 #>  width_b                0.400 #>  width_ab               0.250 #>  true_a                 0.400 #>  true_b                 0.500 #>  true_ab                0.200 #>  conf_level             0.950 #>  replications           10    #>  converged_replications 10    #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # Two of these planners answer a question the budget alone settles. Given # what it costs to open a cluster and what it costs to collect one more # individual, the first reports how many clusters a budget buys at a fixed # cluster size and the second reports how large each cluster can be at a # fixed number of clusters. Clusters cost nothing to open here and each # individual costs 1, so the budget buys 1000 individuals and the only # question is how to arrange them. ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_budget(budget = 1000, cluster_size = 20,   cluster_cost = 0, individual_cost = 1) #>  term                 value #>  necessary_n_clusters 50    #>  budget               1000  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_budget(budget = 1000, n_clusters = 200,   cluster_cost = 0, individual_cost = 1) #>  term                   value #>  necessary_cluster_size 5     #>  budget                 1000  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # The interval width these planners can report, and every answer that # targets a width, rests on an a priori Monte Carlo simulation: a candidate # design is evaluated by generating G data sets and reading the # likelihood-based confidence interval on the standardized effect size from # OpenMx. The calls below use G = 2 so that the page runs quickly; a # reported plan deserves the default G = 1000. Each call describes a # population standardized effect size of 0.5, with es_type = 1 putting that # effect size in individual-level standard deviation units and a quarter of # the outcome variance lying between clusters.  # Supplying G and the population values to a budget planner adds the # expected width of the interval the affordable design buys. ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_budget(budget = 1000, cluster_size = 20,   cluster_cost = 0, individual_cost = 1, true_es = 0.5, es_type = 1, true_icc = 0.25,   pr_treat = 0.5, G = 2, seed = 113) #>  term                 value #>  necessary_n_clusters 50    #>  expected_width       0.673 #>  budget               1000  #>  #> Replications: 2 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Cluster size needed for a target width, given the number of clusters. # With 250 clusters the planner settles on the smallest cluster size it # will consider, two individuals per cluster, and the expected width still # comes in under the target: for a contrast between conditions that are # assigned at the cluster level, precision is bought with clusters rather # than with what happens inside them. ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_width(width = 0.5, n_clusters = 250,   true_es = 0.5, es_type = 1, true_icc = 0.25, pr_treat = 0.5, G = 2,   seed = 113) #>  term                   value #>  necessary_cluster_size 2     #>  width                  0.500 #>  expected_width         0.473 #>  #> Replications: 2 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Once recruiting a cluster costs 5, the number of clusters and the cluster # size trade off against each other, and this planner searches the # combinations the budget allows for the narrowest expected interval. ss_aipe_crd_es_both_fixed_budget(budget = 1000, cluster_cost = 5,   individual_cost = 1, true_es = 0.5, es_type = 1, true_icc = 0.25, pr_treat = 0.5,   G = 2, seed = 113) #>  term                   value #>  necessary_n_clusters   111   #>  necessary_cluster_size 4     #>  expected_width         0.593 #>  budget                 999   #>  #> Replications: 2 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Unequal cluster sizes. Every planner accepts diff_size, which gives each # cluster's deviation from cluster_size as an integer offset or as a # multiplicative factor, recycled across the clusters; the planner prints # the resulting cluster sizes and their frequencies ahead of its table. # The budget planner shows both forms here. ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_budget(budget = 1000, cluster_size = 20,   cluster_cost = 0, individual_cost = 1, diff_size = c(-2, 1, 0, 2, -1, 3, -3, 0, 0)) #>   cluster_size freq #> 1           17    5 #> 2           18    6 #> 3           19    6 #> 4           20   16 #> 5           21    6 #> 6           22    6 #> 7           23    5 #>  term                 value #>  necessary_n_clusters 50    #>  budget               1000  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_budget(budget = 1000, cluster_size = 20,   cluster_cost = 0, individual_cost = 1,   diff_size = c(0.6, 1.2, 0.8, 1.4, 1, 1, 1.1, 0.9)) #>   cluster_size freq #> 1           12    7 #> 2           16    6 #> 3           18    6 #> 4           20   12 #> 5           22    6 #> 6           24    7 #> 7           28    6 #>  term                 value #>  necessary_n_clusters 50    #>  budget               996   #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # Textbook scenario (Kelley, 2007). A researcher plans a study to estimate the # coefficient of variation of reaction times with a 95% confidence interval no # wider than .10. They guess from prior work that the population coefficient of # variation is around .25 and apply ss_aipe_cv() to obtain a planned N.  # Question 1: how does the realized interval width behave when the planning # value is correct (well-specified case)? G = 100 keeps the example quick; # a reported sensitivity analysis deserves the default G = 1000 or more. set.seed(113) ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity(   true_cv          = .25,   supposed_cv      = .25,   width            = .10,   assurance        = NULL,   conf_level       = .95,   G                = 100,   print_iter       = FALSE ) #>  term               value #>  mean_cv            0.246 #>  median_cv          0.245 #>  sd_cv              0.021 #>  mean_ci_width      0.098 #>  median_ci_width    0.098 #>  sd_ci_width        0.009 #>  pct_ci_less_width  0.590 #>  pct_ci_miss_low    0.010 #>  pct_ci_miss_high   0.010 #>  total_type_I_error 0.020 #>  total_N            59    #>  true_cv            0.250 #>  supposed_cv        0.250 #>  width              0.100 #>  conf_level         0.950 #>  #> Replications: 100 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Question 2: what happens if the planning value is materially smaller than # the true coefficient of variation (a common direction of misspecification, # since planning values are often optimistic)? The intervals will be wider on # average than the target and the pct_ci_less_width will fall. set.seed(113) ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity(   true_cv          = .35,   supposed_cv      = .25,   width            = .10,   assurance        = NULL,   conf_level       = .95,   G                = 100,   print_iter       = FALSE ) #>  term               value #>  mean_cv            0.343 #>  median_cv          0.343 #>  sd_cv              0.030 #>  mean_ci_width      0.145 #>  median_ci_width    0.144 #>  sd_ci_width        0.015 #>  pct_ci_less_width  0.000 #>  pct_ci_miss_low    0.010 #>  pct_ci_miss_high   0.010 #>  total_type_I_error 0.020 #>  total_N            59    #>  true_cv            0.350 #>  supposed_cv        0.250 #>  width              0.100 #>  conf_level         0.950 #>  #> Replications: 100 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

title: Sample Size Planning for Polynomial Change Models in Longitudinal Study — ss_aipe_pcm
code: # The examples reproduce the tolerance-of-antisocial-thinking illustration # of Kelley and Rausch (2011, Tables 1 and 2), which draws on the National # Youth Survey data also used by Raudenbush and Liu (2001). The # within-subject (i.e., Level 1) error variance is 0.0262 and the # between-subject slope variance is 0.003. # The planner finds the sample size needed for a confidence interval on the # group-by-time slope difference that is no wider than `width`. The returned # necessary_n_per_group is per group, so the total study size is twice that. Unlike # power analysis, the value of the slope is not needed here: the confidence # interval width does not depend on it.  # (1) Expected-width planning. With five measurement occasions #     (M = frequency * duration + 1 = 1 * 4 + 1) and a target width of #     0.025, the expected 95% confidence interval is sufficiently narrow at #     278 subjects per group (Kelley & Rausch, 2011, Table 1, T = 5). ss_aipe_pcm(true_var_trend = 0.003, true_var_error = 0.0262,             duration = 4, frequency = 1, width = 0.025, conf_level = .95) #>  term                  value #>  necessary_n_per_group 278   #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # (2) More measurement occasions sharpen the estimate. Extending the study #     so that M = 10 (duration = 9, frequency = 1) cuts the expected-width #     requirement from 278 to 165 per group (Kelley & Rausch, 2011, Table 1, #     T = 10). ss_aipe_pcm(true_var_trend = 0.003, true_var_error = 0.0262,             duration = 9, frequency = 1, width = 0.025, conf_level = .95) #>  term                  value #>  necessary_n_per_group 165   #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # (3) A wider tolerated interval costs less. Relaxing the target width from #     0.025 to 0.05 at M = 5 drops the requirement from 278 to 71 per group #     (Kelley & Rausch, 2011, Table 1, T = 5). ss_aipe_pcm(true_var_trend = 0.003, true_var_error = 0.0262,             duration = 4, frequency = 1, width = 0.05, conf_level = .95) #>  term                  value #>  necessary_n_per_group 71    #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # (4) Adding an assurance parameter. Requiring 85% assurance that the #     realized confidence interval will be no wider than 0.025 raises the #     M = 5 requirement from 278 to 295 per group (Kelley & Rausch, 2011, #     Table 2, T = 5). Assurance guards against the expected-width plan being #     too small for the particular sample obtained. ss_aipe_pcm(true_var_trend = 0.003, true_var_error = 0.0262,             duration = 4, frequency = 1, width = 0.025, conf_level = .95,             assurance = .85) #>  term                  value #>  necessary_n_per_group 295   #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # (5) A higher assurance costs more. Demanding 99% assurance rather than 85% #     raises the per-group requirement further, from 295 to 316. ss_aipe_pcm(true_var_trend = 0.003, true_var_error = 0.0262,             duration = 4, frequency = 1, width = 0.025, conf_level = .95,             assurance = .99) #>  term                  value #>  necessary_n_per_group 316   #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # 1. Covariance structure path: supply the population correlation #    matrix and the population YX cross-correlations. Five predictors #    in an exchangeable structure (all pairwise correlations 0.5, #    all Y-X correlations 0.3). true_cor_YX <- c(.3, .3, .3, .3, .3) true_cor_XX <- rbind(c(1, .5, .5, .5, .5), c(.5, 1, .5, .5, .5),                 c(.5, .5, 1, .5, .5), c(.5, .5, .5, 1, .5),                 c(.5, .5, .5, .5, 1))  # Closed-form (central t) planning, targeting the first predictor's # standardized coefficient. ss_aipe_reg_coef(width = .10, which_width = "Full",                  true_sd_Y = 1, true_sd_X = 1,                  true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX, true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX,                  which_predictor = 1, noncentral = FALSE,                  conf_level = .95) #>  term        value #>  necessary_N 2184  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # With an assurance of .85: the smallest N at which the realized # interval is no wider than 0.10 with probability at least .85. The # last row is that probability at the returned N, computed exactly. ss_aipe_reg_coef(width = .10, which_width = "Full",                  true_sd_Y = 1, true_sd_X = 1,                  true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX, true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX,                  which_predictor = 1, noncentral = FALSE,                  conf_level = .95, assurance = .85) #>  term               value #>  necessary_N        2281  #>  assurance          0.850 #>  assurance_attained 0.850 #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Assurance method: analytic; assurance_attained is the exact probability that the interval is no wider than the width  # The noncentral t interval for the standardized coefficient. Required # N differs at small to moderate samples. ss_aipe_reg_coef(width = .10, which_width = "Full",                  true_sd_Y = 1, true_sd_X = 1,                  true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX, true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX,                  which_predictor = 1, noncentral = TRUE,                  conf_level = .95) #>  term        value #>  necessary_N 2190  #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # With assurance its default plan is the approximation that MBESS uses, # which does not compute the probability it attains; by simulation, the # smallest N at which the estimated probability is at least .85. G = 2000 # keeps the example quick; a reported plan deserves the default G = 20000. ss_aipe_reg_coef(width = .10, true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX,                  true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX, which_predictor = 1,                  noncentral = TRUE, assurance = .85) #>  term               value #>  necessary_N        2240  #>  assurance          0.850 #>  assurance_attained <NA>  #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Assurance method: analytic; the plan is the published approximation, which does not compute the probability that the interval is no wider than the width (assurance_attained is NA) and can attain less than the assurance. assurance_method = "simulation" computes it and returns the smallest plan that attains it plan <- ss_aipe_reg_coef(width = .10, true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX,                          true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX, which_predictor = 1,                          noncentral = TRUE, assurance = .85,                          assurance_method = "simulation",                          G = 2000, seed = 113) plan #>  term               value #>  necessary_N        2257  #>  assurance          0.850 #>  assurance_attained 0.854 #>  G                  2000  #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Assurance method: simulation; assurance_attained is estimated from G = 2000 simulated samples (Monte Carlo SE 0.008) attr(plan, "assurance_mc_se") #> [1] 0.007895695  # 2. Squared multiple correlations path: when the user has planning #    values for true_R2_Y_X and true_R2_j_X_without_j directly (e.g., #    from a prior power analysis), without specifying the full #    covariance structure. true_reg_coef_j is required on this path. ss_aipe_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = 0.30, true_R2_j_X_without_j = 0.20,                  p = 5, true_reg_coef_j = 0.25,                  width = .15, which_width = "Full",                  true_sd_Y = 1, true_sd_X = 1,                  noncentral = FALSE, conf_level = .95) #>  term        value #>  necessary_N 606   #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # 3. One predictor: its correlation matrix is matrix(1), and p and #    which_predictor follow from it. ss_aipe_reg_coef(width = .20, true_cor_XX = matrix(1), true_cor_YX = .4) #>  term        value #>  necessary_N 327   #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # Expected confidence interval width (closed form, no Monte Carlo search) # for six parallel items that correlate .6: standardized items, so # true_residual_var is 1 - true_item_covariance. ss_aipe_reliability(model = "Parallel", type = "Normal Theory", width = .1,   n_items = 6, true_item_covariance = .6, true_residual_var = .4,   conf_level = .95, assurance = NULL) #>  term        value #>  necessary_N 38    #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # The same plan when the coefficient will be estimated by full information # maximum likelihood and is expected to lose 30 percent of its information # to missing values (an FMI of .30 from a pilot study). The complete data # N minus 1 is divided by 1 minus .30, and the complete data answer prints # under the table. ss_aipe_reliability(model = "Parallel", type = "Normal Theory", width = .1,   n_items = 6, true_item_covariance = .6, true_residual_var = .4,   conf_level = .95, fmi = .30) #>  term        value #>  necessary_N 54    #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Planned for a fraction of missing information of 0.3 for the coefficient; with complete data, N = 38.  # The assurance cases run a Monte Carlo search. G_initial = 20 and # G = 100 keep the examples quick; a reported plan deserves the # defaults of 500 and 5000. The seed makes each search reproducible and # leaves the random number stream of the session where it was.  # Same population, now targeting an assurance. ss_aipe_reliability(model = "Parallel", type = "Normal Theory", width = .1,   n_items = 6, true_item_covariance = .6, true_residual_var = .4,   conf_level = .95, assurance = .85, G_initial = 20, G = 100, seed = 113) #>  term               value #>  necessary_N        54    #>  width              0.100 #>  assurance          0.850 #>  assurance_attained 0.860 #>  G                  100   #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # The assurance plan under the same FMI. The search runs at the complete # data size, the necessary N of the call above (kept as the attribute # necessary_N_complete), and maps it back. ss_aipe_reliability(model = "Parallel", type = "Normal Theory", width = .1,   n_items = 6, true_item_covariance = .6, true_residual_var = .4,   conf_level = .95, assurance = .85, G_initial = 20, G = 100, seed = 113,   fmi = .30) #>  term               value #>  necessary_N        77    #>  width              0.100 #>  assurance          0.850 #>  assurance_attained 0.860 #>  G                  100   #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Planned for a fraction of missing information of 0.3 for the coefficient; with complete data, N = 54, the size at which the assurance was simulated.  # The true score (tau equivalent) model takes true_residual_var as a # vector of length n_items (number of items) while true_item_covariance # stays a single value. Error # variances around 1 - .5 give item variances from .9 to 1.1 and # correlations near .5, and the plan is for alpha of these items as they # are, unequal variances and all. ss_aipe_reliability(model = "True Score", type = "Normal Theory",   width = .1, n_items = 5, true_item_covariance = .5,   true_residual_var = c(.4, .5, .6, .4, .6),   conf_level = .95, assurance = .85, G_initial = 20, G = 100,   seed = 113) #>  term               value #>  necessary_N        137   #>  width              0.100 #>  assurance          0.850 #>  assurance_attained 0.860 #>  G                  100   #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Congeneric model, planned from the item loadings and error variances rather # than from a single covariance. With assurance = NULL the necessary N comes # from the delta method variance of the model implied omega at the # population, the variance behind reliability_omega(denominator = # "model_implied", ci_method = "ml"). Adding an assurance to this plan fits # a one factor model at every Monte Carlo iteration and is the slow case, # so the page stops at the closed form (see Details). ss_aipe_reliability(model = "Congeneric", type = "Factor Analytic", width = .15,   n_items = 4, true_factor_loading = c(.8, .7, .7, .8),   true_residual_var = c(.4, .5, .5, .4),   conf_level = .95, assurance = NULL) #>  term        value #>  necessary_N 52    #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Planning from a presumed population correlation matrix among the items, # which plans for standardized items. pop_mat <- rbind(   c(1.0000000, 0.3813850, 0.4216370, 0.3651484, 0.4472136),   c(0.3813850, 1.0000000, 0.4020151, 0.3481553, 0.4264014),   c(0.4216370, 0.4020151, 1.0000000, 0.3849002, 0.4714045),   c(0.3651484, 0.3481553, 0.3849002, 1.0000000, 0.4082483),   c(0.4472136, 0.4264014, 0.4714045, 0.4082483, 1.0000000)) ss_aipe_reliability(model = "True Score", type = "Normal Theory", width = .15,   true_cov_matrix = pop_mat, conf_level = .95, assurance = .85,   G_initial = 20, G = 100, seed = 113) #>  term               value #>  necessary_N        113   #>  width              0.150 #>  assurance          0.850 #>  assurance_attained 0.890 #>  G                  100   #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

title: A Priori Monte Carlo Simulation for Sample Size Planning for RMSEA in SEM — ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity
code: # True data generating model: two correlated factors, each measured by # three standardized indicators. The factor correlation is 0.5 and every # loading is 0.7. The implied population covariance matrix is assembled # from the loading matrix, the factor correlation matrix, and the # residual variances. Lambda <- matrix(0, 6, 2) Lambda[1:3, 1] <- 0.7 Lambda[4:6, 2] <- 0.7 Phi   <- matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 1), 2, 2) true_cov_matrix <- Lambda %*% Phi %*% t(Lambda) + diag(1 - 0.7^2, 6) dimnames(true_cov_matrix) <- list(paste0("x", 1:6), paste0("x", 1:6))  # Proposed (misspecified) model: a single common factor. proposed <- "g =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6"  # The proposed model is fit once at a very large N to recover the # population RMSEA, the sample size is planned so that the expected width # of the 90 percent interval is 0.05, and a fresh sample of that size is # drawn and fit on every replication. Notice that true_rmsea is about # 0.20, since a single factor is a poor description of two-factor data, # that the realized widths sit close to the target, and that # pct_ci_less_width is well away from 0 and 1: planning for the expected # width aims the average width at the target, not the share of intervals # narrower than it, which is what assurance controls. G = 10 keeps # the example quick and estimates that share only roughly; a reported # sensitivity study deserves the default G = 200 or more. set.seed(113) ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity(width = 0.05, model = proposed,                           true_cov_matrix = true_cov_matrix, G = 10) #>  term               value #>  mean_rmsea         0.205 #>  median_rmsea       0.208 #>  sd_rmsea           0.017 #>  mean_ci_width      0.050 #>  median_ci_width    0.050 #>  sd_ci_width        0.000 #>  pct_ci_less_width  0.700 #>  pct_ci_miss_low    0.000 #>  pct_ci_miss_high   0.000 #>  total_type_I_error 0.000 #>  total_N            493   #>  df                 9     #>  true_rmsea         0.204 #>  width              0.050 #>  conf_level         0.900 #>  #> Replications: 10 #>  #> Confidence level: 90%

title: Sample Size Planning for Accuracy in Parameter Estimation (AIPE) of the Standardized Contrast in ANOVA — ss_aipe_sc
code: # Suppose the population standardized contrast is believed to be .6 # in some 5-group ANOVA model. The researcher is interested in comparing # the average of means of group 1 and 2 with the average of group 3 and 4.  # To calculate the necessary sample size per group such that the width # of 95 percent confidence interval of the standardized # contrast is, with 90 percent assurance, no wider than .4 (the last row # is the exact probability at that sample size):  ss_aipe_sc(true_std_contrast=.6, c_weights=c(.5, .5, -.5, -.5, 0), width=.4, assurance=.90) #>  term                  value #>  necessary_n_per_group 102   #>  assurance             0.900 #>  assurance_attained    0.964 #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Assurance method: analytic; assurance_attained is the exact probability that the interval is no wider than the width  # Asymmetric confidence interval: most of the alpha goes in the upper tail # (e.g., when a one-sided concern dominates). Pass alpha_lower and # alpha_upper instead of conf_level. ss_aipe_sc(true_std_contrast = .6, c_weights = c(.5, .5, -.5, -.5, 0), width = .4,            conf_level = NULL, alpha_lower = .01, alpha_upper = .04) #>  term                  value #>  necessary_n_per_group 108

code: # Population covariance from a fully fixed model (see cov_sem()). pop_model <- "   f1 =~ 1*y1 + 0.8*y2 + 0.8*y3   f2 =~ 1*y4 + 0.8*y5 + 0.8*y6   f2 ~ 0.5*f1   f1 ~~ 1*f1   f2 ~~ 0.75*f2   y1 ~~ 0.5*y1; y2 ~~ 0.5*y2; y3 ~~ 0.5*y3   y4 ~~ 0.5*y4; y5 ~~ 0.5*y5; y6 ~~ 0.5*y6 " Sigma <- cov_sem(pop_model)$sigma_theta  # Free analysis model with the target structural path labeled "b". analysis_model <- "   f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3   f2 =~ y4 + y5 + y6   f2 ~ b*f1 " ss_aipe_sem_path(model = analysis_model, true_cov_matrix = Sigma,                  width = 0.30, which_path = "b") #>  term        value #>  necessary_N 264   #>  path_index  5     #>  var_theta_j 0.006 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # That sample size holds the interval to the desired width on average, so # about half of the studies it plans return a wider one. Adding assurance # plans for the width to be met in 90 percent of studies instead, at the # cost of a larger sample size. ss_aipe_sem_path(model = analysis_model, true_cov_matrix = Sigma,                  width = 0.30, which_path = "b",                  assurance = 0.90) #>  term        value #>  necessary_N 293   #>  path_index  5     #>  var_theta_j 0.005 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # The planning values a researcher would bring to ss_aipe_sem_path(): two # factors, each measured by three indicators, joined by a structural path # of 0.5, with every residual variance at 0.5. planning_model <- "   f1 =~ 1*y1 + 0.8*y2 + 0.8*y3   f2 =~ 1*y4 + 0.8*y5 + 0.8*y6   f2 ~ 0.5*f1   f1 ~~ 1*f1   f2 ~~ 0.75*f2   y1 ~~ 0.5*y1; y2 ~~ 0.5*y2; y3 ~~ 0.5*y3   y4 ~~ 0.5*y4; y5 ~~ 0.5*y5; y6 ~~ 0.5*y6 "  # The population the study will actually sample from: the same structural # path, but noisier indicators than the planning values assumed, with # every residual variance at 0.8. true_model <- "   f1 =~ 1*y1 + 0.8*y2 + 0.8*y3   f2 =~ 1*y4 + 0.8*y5 + 0.8*y6   f2 ~ 0.5*f1   f1 ~~ 1*f1   f2 ~~ 0.75*f2   y1 ~~ 0.8*y1; y2 ~~ 0.8*y2; y3 ~~ 0.8*y3   y4 ~~ 0.8*y4; y5 ~~ 0.8*y5; y6 ~~ 0.8*y6 "  # The free analysis model, with the targeted path labeled "b". analysis_model <- "   f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3   f2 =~ y4 + y5 + y6   f2 ~ b*f1 "  supposed_cov_matrix <- cov_sem(planning_model)$sigma_theta true_cov_matrix <- cov_sem(true_model)$sigma_theta  # The sample size planned from the optimistic measurement quality is # evaluated against the population that actually holds. Notice that the # mean realized width (mean_ci_width) exceeds the desired 0.30, and that # pct_ci_less_width, the proportion of intervals no wider than desired, falls # well below the one half that the planned sample size would deliver if # the planning values were right. G = 10 keeps the example quick; a # reported sensitivity study deserves the default G = 100 or more. set.seed(113) ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity(model = analysis_model,                              supposed_cov_matrix = supposed_cov_matrix,                              true_cov_matrix = true_cov_matrix,                              which_path = "b", width = 0.30, G = 10) #>  term               value #>  mean_path          0.497 #>  median_path        0.502 #>  sd_path            0.053 #>  mean_ci_width      0.334 #>  median_ci_width    0.338 #>  sd_ci_width        0.032 #>  pct_ci_less_width  0.200 #>  pct_ci_miss_low    0.000 #>  pct_ci_miss_high   0.000 #>  total_type_I_error 0.000 #>  total_N            264   #>  true_path          0.500 #>  width              0.300 #>  conf_level         0.950 #>  #> Replications: 10 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # A proxy measurement costs 1% of a target measurement. Planning values # of 0.43 for the target's standard deviation and 0.55 for its # correlation with the proxy; a 90% interval no wider than 0.10. The # least costly design labels 151 units of a pool of 957 and costs 79% # of what the 202 units of the target alone would. ss_aipe_two_phase_cost(true_sd_Y = 0.43, true_cor = 0.55, width = 0.10,                        cost_ratio = 0.01, conf_level = 0.90) #>  term                     value #>  necessary_n_labeled      151   #>  necessary_n_pool         957   #>  relative_cost            0.795 #>  relative_cost_continuous 0.792 #>  expected_width           0.100 #>  necessary_n_target_only  202   #>  threshold_cor            0.198 #>  width                    0.100 #>  true_sd_Y                0.430 #>  true_cor                 0.550 #>  cost_ratio               0.010 #>  conf_level               0.900 #>  #> Confidence level: 90%  # At 10% of the cost the same proxy no longer pays: a correlation of 0.55 # is below the threshold, and the design measures the target alone. ss_aipe_two_phase_cost(true_sd_Y = 0.43, true_cor = 0.55, width = 0.10,                        cost_ratio = 0.10, conf_level = 0.90) #>  term                     value #>  necessary_n_labeled      202   #>  necessary_n_pool         0     #>  relative_cost            1     #>  relative_cost_continuous 1     #>  expected_width           0.100 #>  necessary_n_target_only  202   #>  threshold_cor            0.575 #>  width                    0.100 #>  true_sd_Y                0.430 #>  true_cor                 0.550 #>  cost_ratio               0.100 #>  conf_level               0.900 #>  #> Confidence level: 90%  # A worked example in standard deviation units: a proxy that correlates # 0.90 with the target at 5% of its cost, and a 95% interval of width # 0.20. The design is 109 labeled units in a pool of 1011, a cost of # 109 + 0.05 * 1011 = 159.55 target measurements against 387. plan <- ss_aipe_two_phase_cost(true_sd_Y = 1, true_cor = 0.90, width = 0.20,                                cost_ratio = 0.05) plan #>  term                     value #>  necessary_n_labeled      109   #>  necessary_n_pool         1011  #>  relative_cost            0.412 #>  relative_cost_continuous 0.406 #>  expected_width           0.200 #>  necessary_n_target_only  387   #>  threshold_cor            0.426 #>  width                    0.200 #>  true_sd_Y                1     #>  true_cor                 0.900 #>  cost_ratio               0.050 #>  conf_level               0.950 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # The companion planner, given that pool, returns the same number of # labeled units. ss_aipe_two_phase(true_sd_Y = 1, true_cor = 0.90, width = 0.20, n_pool = 1011) #>  term                    value #>  necessary_n_labeled     109   #>  necessary_n_target_only 387   #>  ratio                   0.282 #>  expected_width          0.200 #>  minimum_width           0.123 #>  width                   0.200 #>  true_sd_Y               1     #>  true_cor                0.900 #>  n_pool                  1011  #>  conf_level              0.950 #>  #> Confidence level: 95%

code: # A plan made with a correlation of 0.55, carried out where the # correlation is only 0.45. G = 200 keeps the example quick; a reported # evaluation deserves the default G = 1000 or more. ss_aipe_two_phase_sensitivity(true_sd_Y = 0.43, true_cor = 0.45,                               supposed_sd_Y = 0.43, supposed_cor = 0.55,                               n_pool = 20000, width = 0.10,                               conf_level = 0.90, G = 200, seed = 113) #>  term               value #>  mean_mean_Y        0.000 #>  median_mean_Y      0.001 #>  sd_mean_Y          0.032 #>  mean_ci_width      0.107 #>  median_ci_width    0.106 #>  sd_ci_width        0.007 #>  pct_ci_less_width  0.180 #>  pct_ci_miss_low    0.045 #>  pct_ci_miss_high   0.060 #>  total_type_I_error 0.105 #>  n_labeled          142   #>  total_N            20000 #>  true_mean_Y        0     #>  true_sd_Y          0.430 #>  true_cor           0.450 #>  supposed_sd_Y      0.430 #>  supposed_cor       0.550 #>  width              0.100 #>  conf_level         0.900 #>  #> Replications: 200 #>  #> Confidence level: 90%  # A fixed design, 150 labeled units in a pool of 5,000, evaluated in a # population of binary (target, proxy) pairs resampled from a pilot of # 300 units: how often is the 90% interval narrower than 0.085? set.seed(113) proxy  <- rbinom(300, 1, 0.6) target <- ifelse(runif(300) < 0.8, proxy, rbinom(300, 1, 0.6)) ss_aipe_two_phase_sensitivity(specified_n_labeled = 150, n_pool = 5000,                               width = 0.085, conf_level = 0.90,                               population = data.frame(y = target, x = proxy),                               G = 200, seed = 113) #>  term               value #>  mean_mean_Y        0.565 #>  median_mean_Y      0.565 #>  sd_mean_Y          0.024 #>  mean_ci_width      0.084 #>  median_ci_width    0.084 #>  sd_ci_width        0.009 #>  pct_ci_less_width  0.520 #>  pct_ci_miss_low    0.035 #>  pct_ci_miss_high   0.035 #>  total_type_I_error 0.070 #>  n_labeled          150   #>  total_N            5000  #>  true_mean_Y        0.567 #>  true_sd_Y          0.496 #>  true_cor           0.789 #>  supposed_sd_Y      <NA>  #>  supposed_cor       <NA>  #>  width              0.085 #>  conf_level         0.900 #>  #> Replications: 200 #>  #> Confidence level: 90%

code: # Five predictors are expected to explain .25 of the variance and four # added predictors to raise that to .30. Necessary sample size for power # .80 at alpha .01, with random predictors (the default). ss_power_R2_change(true_R2_restricted = .25, true_R2_full = .30,                    p_restricted = 5, p_full = 9, alpha_level = .01,                    desired_power = .80) #>  term              value #>  necessary_N       250   #>  actual_power      0.802 #>  noncentral_f_parm <NA>  #>  true_f2           0.071 #>  true_partial_R2   0.067 #>  true_R2_change    0.050 #>  q                 4     #>  df_1              4     #>  df_2              240    # The same plan with predictors fixed by design. ss_power_R2_change(true_R2_restricted = .25, true_R2_full = .30,                    p_restricted = 5, p_full = 9, alpha_level = .01,                    desired_power = .80, random_predictors = FALSE) #>  term              value  #>  necessary_N       242    #>  actual_power      0.802  #>  noncentral_f_parm 17.286 #>  true_f2           0.071  #>  true_partial_R2   0.067  #>  true_R2_change    0.050  #>  q                 4      #>  df_1              4      #>  df_2              232     # The effect given as the change with the full model's value, and as # Cohen's f squared. Power at a sample size of 90, fixed predictors. ss_power_R2_change(true_R2_change = .05, true_R2_full = .30,                    p_restricted = 5, p_full = 9, alpha_level = .01,                    specified_N = 90, random_predictors = FALSE) #>  term              value #>  specified_N       90    #>  actual_power      0.241 #>  noncentral_f_parm 6.429 #>  true_f2           0.071 #>  true_partial_R2   0.067 #>  true_R2_change    0.050 #>  q                 4     #>  df_1              4     #>  df_2              80    ss_power_R2_change(true_f2 = .05 / .70, p_restricted = 5, p_full = 9,                    alpha_level = .01, specified_N = 90,                    random_predictors = FALSE) #>  term              value #>  specified_N       90    #>  actual_power      0.241 #>  noncentral_f_parm 6.429 #>  true_f2           0.071 #>  true_partial_R2   0.067 #>  true_R2_change    <NA>  #>  q                 4     #>  df_1              4     #>  df_2              80     # The effect given as the restricted model's value and the change, the # way a hierarchical regression is often described. Random predictors. ss_power_R2_change(true_R2_restricted = .25, true_R2_change = .05,                    p_restricted = 5, p_full = 9, alpha_level = .01,                    desired_power = .80) #>  term              value #>  necessary_N       250   #>  actual_power      0.802 #>  noncentral_f_parm <NA>  #>  true_f2           0.071 #>  true_partial_R2   0.067 #>  true_R2_change    0.050 #>  q                 4     #>  df_1              4     #>  df_2              240    # One added predictor with fixed predictors is the test of its regression # coefficient: the two functions return the same sample size. ss_power_R2_change(true_R2_restricted = .30, true_R2_full = .40,                    p_restricted = 4, p_full = 5, desired_power = .80,                    random_predictors = FALSE) #>  term              value #>  necessary_N       50    #>  actual_power      0.806 #>  noncentral_f_parm 8.333 #>  true_f2           0.167 #>  true_partial_R2   0.143 #>  true_R2_change    0.100 #>  q                 1     #>  df_1              1     #>  df_2              44    ss_power_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = .40, true_R2_Y_X_without_j = .30, p = 5,                   desired_power = .80) #>  term              value #>  necessary_N       50    #>  actual_power      0.806 #>  noncentral_t_parm 2.887 #>  true_f            0.408  # Cohen's (1988) noncentrality for the design of the third example, # f squared times (N - w) with w = 5: four predictors and no restricted # model, with specified_N set to 90 - 5 so the noncentrality matches # Cohen's. code: # A four-group (one-way) ANCOVA with heterogeneous slopes: the a-group # generalization of the two-group composite. The conclusion needs the group # mean effect, a covariate effect, and evidence that the covariate slope # differs across the groups, so the design is planned against all three. ss_power_composite_ancova(   factor_levels = 4, slopes = "heterogeneous",   effects = list(list(type = "mean",      factors = 1, true_f = 0.30),                  list(type = "covariate",              true_f = 0.40),                  list(type = "slope",      factors = 1, true_f = 0.20)),   desired_power = 0.80) #>  term                        value  #>  necessary_n_per_cell        71     #>  total_N                     284    #>  composite_power             0.807  #>  df_error                    276    #>  power_1                     0.994  #>  power_covariate             1.000  #>  power_cov_x_1               0.812  #>  true_f_1                    0.300  #>  true_f_covariate            0.400  #>  true_f_cov_x_1              0.200  #>  df_1                        3      #>  df_covariate                1      #>  df_cov_x_1                  3      #>  noncentral_f_parm_1         25.560 #>  noncentral_f_parm_covariate 45.440 #>  noncentral_f_parm_cov_x_1   11.360 #>  cells                       4      #>  alpha_level                 0.050  #>  desired_power               0.800   # A 2 by 3 factorial ANCOVA with one common slope. Both main effects must # hold; the covariate explains 25 percent of the within-cell variance. ss_power_composite_ancova(   factor_levels = c(2, 3),   effects = list(list(factors = 1, true_f = 0.25),                  list(factors = 2, true_f = 0.20)),   true_covariate_R2 = 0.25, n_covariates = 1,   desired_power = 0.80) #>  term                 value  #>  necessary_n_per_cell 32     #>  total_N              192    #>  composite_power      0.801  #>  df_error             185    #>  power_1              0.978  #>  power_2              0.818  #>  true_f_1             0.250  #>  true_f_2             0.200  #>  df_1                 1      #>  df_2                 2      #>  noncentral_f_parm_1  16.000 #>  noncentral_f_parm_2  10.240 #>  true_covariate_R2    0.250  #>  n_covariates         1      #>  cells                6      #>  alpha_level          0.050  #>  desired_power        0.800   # The population effects can instead be a full pattern of cell means with a # common within-cell SD; plot() then draws the mean pattern itself. cell_means <- matrix(c(10, 12, 11,                        13, 12, 16), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE) fit <- ss_power_composite_ancova(   factor_levels = c(2, 3), true_means = cell_means, true_sd = 4,   effects = list(list(factors = 1, label = "A"),                  list(factors = 2, label = "B")),   specified_n_per_cell = 30) fit #>  term                 value  #>  specified_n_per_cell 30     #>  total_N              180    #>  composite_power      0.712  #>  df_error             174    #>  power_A              0.994  #>  power_B              0.717  #>  true_f_A             0.333  #>  true_f_B             0.212  #>  df_A                 1      #>  df_B                 2      #>  noncentral_f_parm_A  20.000 #>  noncentral_f_parm_B  8.125  #>  true_covariate_R2    0      #>  n_covariates         0      #>  cells                6      #>  alpha_level          0.050  plot(fit)   # A one-row broom summary of a plan. generics::tidy(ss_power_composite_ancova(   factor_levels = c(2, 3),   effects = list(list(factors = 1, true_f = 0.25),                  list(factors = 2, true_f = 0.20)),   desired_power = 0.80)) #>          term estimate     power #> 1 sample_size       43 0.8064647  # The two-group case matches the dedicated two-group planner. Here factor 1 # has two levels, so the heterogeneous one-way composite reproduces # ss_power_composite_ancova_2group with one correlation per group. ss_power_composite_ancova(   factor_levels = 2, slopes = "heterogeneous",   true_means = c(0, 0.5), true_cor = c(0.1, 0.5), true_sd = 1,   effects = list(list(type = "mean", factors = 1),                  list(type = "covariate"),                  list(type = "slope", factors = 1)),   specified_n_per_cell = 95) #> Warning: The cell correlations differ in absolute value, so the cells' residual variances differ and the shared-error composite power is an approximation whose error grows with the spread of the correlations. The powers are reported as approximate_* rows, and a planned sample size as approximate_n_per_cell, because neither is exact; confirm a final design by simulation. #>  term                        value  #>  specified_n_per_cell        95     #>  total_N                     190    #>  approximate_composite_power 0.795  #>  df_error                    186    #>  approximate_power_1         0.957  #>  approximate_power_covariate 0.993  #>  approximate_power_cov_x_1   0.837  #>  true_f_1                    0.268  #>  true_f_covariate            0.322  #>  true_f_cov_x_1              0.214  #>  df_1                        1      #>  df_covariate                1      #>  df_cov_x_1                  1      #>  noncentral_f_parm_1         13.649 #>  noncentral_f_parm_covariate 19.655 #>  noncentral_f_parm_cov_x_1   8.736  #>  cells                       2      #>  alpha_level                 0.050  ss_power_composite_ancova_2group(true_smd = 0.5, true_cor = c(0.1, 0.5),                                  specified_n_per_group = 95) #> Warning: The group correlations differ in absolute value, so the groups' residual variances differ and the shared-error composite power is an approximation whose error grows with the gap between the correlations. The powers are reported as approximate_* rows, and a planned sample size as approximate_n_per_group, because neither is exact; confirm a final design by simulation. #>  term                                 value #>  specified_n_per_group                95    #>  total_N                              190   #>  approximate_composite_power          0.795 #>  df_error                             186   #>  approximate_power_group              0.957 #>  approximate_power_covariate          0.993 #>  approximate_power_group_by_covariate 0.837 #>  noncentral_t_parm_group              3.695 #>  noncentral_t_parm_covariate          4.433 #>  noncentral_t_parm_group_by_covariate 2.956 #>  true_smd                             0.500 #>  true_cor_group_1                     0.100 #>  true_cor_group_2                     0.500 #>  true_sd                              1     #>  true_sd_X                            1     #>  alpha_level                          0.050 #>  tails                                2
