code: # A covariate correlating 0.10 with the outcome in one group and 0.40 in the # other. The correlations differ, so the slopes differ and there is an # interaction to detect; nothing had to be assumed about that in advance. # They also differ in absolute value, so the groups' residual variances # differ, the powers are approximations, and the rows are named to say so. ss_power_composite_ancova_2group(true_smd = 0.20, true_cor = c(0.10, 0.40),                                  specified_n_per_group = 100) #> Warning: The group correlations differ in absolute value, so the groups' residual variances differ and the shared-error composite power is an approximation whose error grows with the gap between the correlations. The powers are reported as approximate_* rows, and a planned sample size as approximate_n_per_group, because neither is exact; confirm a final design by simulation. #>  term                                 value #>  specified_n_per_group                100   #>  total_N                              200   #>  approximate_composite_power          0.180 #>  df_error                             196   #>  approximate_power_group              0.313 #>  approximate_power_covariate          0.957 #>  approximate_power_group_by_covariate 0.597 #>  noncentral_t_parm_group              1.478 #>  noncentral_t_parm_covariate          3.696 #>  noncentral_t_parm_group_by_covariate 2.218 #>  true_smd                             0.200 #>  true_cor_group_1                     0.100 #>  true_cor_group_2                     0.400 #>  true_sd                              1     #>  true_sd_X                            1     #>  alpha_level                          0.050 #>  tails                                2      # The covariate is nearly certain to be detected and the interaction is # better than even, but the group effect is weak, and the composite of all # three is far below any of them. No single marginal power reveals that.  # Equal correlations mean equal slopes, so the interaction is zero and its # test rejects only at the Type I error rate. Asking for a composite that # includes it therefore asks for something that cannot happen often. ss_power_composite_ancova_2group(true_smd = 0.20, true_cor = 0.10,                                  specified_n_per_group = 100) #>  term                                 value #>  specified_n_per_group                100   #>  total_N                              200   #>  composite_power                      0.005 #>  df_error                             196   #>  power_group                          0.293 #>  power_covariate                      0.293 #>  power_group_by_covariate             0.050 #>  noncentral_t_parm_group              1.421 #>  noncentral_t_parm_covariate          1.421 #>  noncentral_t_parm_group_by_covariate 0.000 #>  true_smd                             0.200 #>  true_cor_group_1                     0.100 #>  true_cor_group_2                     0.100 #>  true_sd                              1     #>  true_sd_X                            1     #>  alpha_level                          0.050 #>  tails                                2      # The composite of the two effects that are actually present. ss_power_composite_ancova_2group(true_smd = 0.20, true_cor = 0.10,                                  specified_n_per_group = 100,                                  composite_terms = c("group", "covariate")) #>  term                        value #>  specified_n_per_group       100   #>  total_N                     200   #>  composite_power             0.087 #>  df_error                    196   #>  power_group                 0.293 #>  power_covariate             0.293 #>  noncentral_t_parm_group     1.421 #>  noncentral_t_parm_covariate 1.421 #>  true_smd                    0.200 #>  true_cor_group_1            0.100 #>  true_cor_group_2            0.100 #>  true_sd                     1     #>  true_sd_X                   1     #>  alpha_level                 0.050 #>  tails                       2      # Per-group sample size for composite power of 0.80 on the group effect and # the interaction together. ss_power_composite_ancova_2group(true_smd = 0.50, true_cor = c(0.10, 0.50),                           composite_terms = c("group", "group_by_covariate"),                           desired_power = 0.80) #> Warning: The group correlations differ in absolute value, so the groups' residual variances differ and the shared-error composite power is an approximation whose error grows with the gap between the correlations. The powers are reported as approximate_* rows, and a planned sample size as approximate_n_per_group, because neither is exact; confirm a final design by simulation. #>  term                                 value #>  approximate_n_per_group              95    #>  approximate_total_N                  190   #>  approximate_composite_power          0.801 #>  df_error                             186   #>  approximate_power_group              0.957 #>  approximate_power_group_by_covariate 0.837 #>  noncentral_t_parm_group              3.695 #>  noncentral_t_parm_group_by_covariate 2.956 #>  desired_power                        0.800 #>  true_smd                             0.500 #>  true_cor_group_1                     0.100 #>  true_cor_group_2                     0.500 #>  true_sd                              1     #>  true_sd_X                            1     #>  alpha_level                          0.050 #>  tails                                2      # Composite power is not the product of the marginal powers. The tests share # one error estimate, so they are positively dependent and the composite is # larger than the product. Multiplying would understate the design. These # correlations differ in absolute value, so the rows carry the approximate_ # prefix; see the section on unequal residual variances for what that means. plan <- ss_power_composite_ancova_2group(   true_smd = 0.50, true_cor = c(0.10, 0.50), specified_n_per_group = 95,   composite_terms = c("group", "group_by_covariate")) #> Warning: The group correlations differ in absolute value, so the groups' residual variances differ and the shared-error composite power is an approximation whose error grows with the gap between the correlations. The powers are reported as approximate_* rows, and a planned sample size as approximate_n_per_group, because neither is exact; confirm a final design by simulation. plan$value[plan$term == "approximate_composite_power"] #> [1] 0.8006971 prod(plan$value[plan$term %in% c("approximate_power_group",                                  "approximate_power_group_by_covariate")]) #> [1] 0.8004597  # Correlations of equal magnitude and opposite sign leave the residual # variances equal, so this design is exact and keeps the ordinary row names, # even though the two slopes could hardly differ more. exact <- ss_power_composite_ancova_2group(   true_smd = 0.50, true_cor = c(0.40, -0.40), specified_n_per_group = 95,   composite_terms = c("group", "group_by_covariate")) exact$value[exact$term == "composite_power"] #> [1] 0.9624723  # Draw the population effects a result was planned on. The figure needs only # the effect sizes, and nothing is simulated to draw it. plot(ss_power_composite_ancova_2group(true_smd = 0.20,                                       true_cor = c(0.10, 0.40),                                       specified_n_per_group = 100)) #> Warning: The group correlations differ in absolute value, so the groups' residual variances differ and the shared-error composite power is an approximation whose error grows with the gap between the correlations. The powers are reported as approximate_* rows, and a planned sample size as approximate_n_per_group, because neither is exact; confirm a final design by simulation.   # Planning without the composite: one term returns that test's ordinary # power, and reproduces ss_power_c_ancova once the interaction is dropped. ss_power_composite_ancova_2group(true_smd = 0.50, true_cor = 0.30,                                  specified_n_per_group = 30,                                  composite_terms = "group",                                  include_interaction = FALSE) #>  term                    value #>  specified_n_per_group   30    #>  total_N                 60    #>  composite_power         0.514 #>  df_error                57    #>  power_group             0.514 #>  noncentral_t_parm_group 2.030 #>  true_smd                0.500 #>  true_cor_group_1        0.300 #>  true_cor_group_2        0.300 #>  true_sd                 1     #>  true_sd_X               1     #>  alpha_level             0.050 #>  tails                   2     ss_power_c_ancova(true_contrast = 0.50, c_weights = c(1, -1), true_sd = 1,                   true_cor = 0.30, specified_n_per_group = 30) #>  term                  value #>  specified_n_per_group 30    #>  actual_power          0.514 #>  noncentral_t_parm     2.030  # What the covariate buys, against the same design with no covariate. ss_power_smd(true_smd = 0.50, n_1 = 30) #>  term              value #>  specified_n_1     30    #>  specified_n_2     30    #>  actual_power      0.478 #>  noncentral_t_parm 1.936 #>  true_smd          0.500 #>  alpha_level       0.050 #>  tails             2      # The broom verbs summarize the plan in one row. generics::tidy(ss_power_composite_ancova_2group(   true_smd = 0.50, true_cor = c(0.10, 0.50),   composite_terms = c("group", "group_by_covariate"),   desired_power = 0.80)) #> Warning: The group correlations differ in absolute value, so the groups' residual variances differ and the shared-error composite power is an approximation whose error grows with the gap between the correlations. The powers are reported as approximate_* rows, and a planned sample size as approximate_n_per_group, because neither is exact; confirm a final design by simulation. #>          term estimate     power #> 1 sample_size       95 0.8006971

code: # A 2 by 3 factorial ANCOVA. The conclusion needs both main effects to hold, # so the design is planned against their composite. The covariate explains # 25 percent of the within-cell variance (one covariate). ss_power_composite_factorial_ancova(   factor_levels = c(2, 3),   effects = list(list(factors = 1, true_f = 0.25),                  list(factors = 2, true_f = 0.20)),   true_covariate_R2 = 0.25, n_covariates = 1,   desired_power = 0.80) #>  term                 value  #>  necessary_n_per_cell 32     #>  total_N              192    #>  composite_power      0.801  #>  df_error             185    #>  power_1              0.978  #>  power_2              0.818  #>  true_f_1             0.250  #>  true_f_2             0.200  #>  df_1                 1      #>  df_2                 2      #>  noncentral_f_parm_1  16.000 #>  noncentral_f_parm_2  10.240 #>  true_covariate_R2    0.250  #>  n_covariates         1      #>  cells                6      #>  alpha_level          0.050  #>  desired_power        0.800   # Realized composite power at 40 per cell for a main effect and the # interaction of a 2 by 2 design, effect sizes given as partial eta squared. ss_power_composite_factorial_ancova(   factor_levels = c(2, 2),   effects = list(list(factors = 1,        true_eta_squared_partial = 0.06),                  list(factors = c(1, 2),  true_eta_squared_partial = 0.04)),   specified_n_per_cell = 40) #>  term                  value  #>  specified_n_per_cell  40     #>  total_N               160    #>  composite_power       0.647  #>  df_error              156    #>  power_1               0.888  #>  power_1x2             0.728  #>  true_f_1              0.253  #>  true_f_1x2            0.204  #>  df_1                  1      #>  df_1x2                1      #>  noncentral_f_parm_1   10.213 #>  noncentral_f_parm_1x2 6.667  #>  true_covariate_R2     0      #>  n_covariates          0      #>  cells                 4      #>  alpha_level           0.050   # Naming one effect reproduces the single-effect planner exactly. ss_power_composite_factorial_ancova(   factor_levels = c(2, 3), effects = list(list(factors = 2, true_f = 0.25)),   specified_n_per_cell = 20) #>  term                 value #>  specified_n_per_cell 20    #>  total_N              120   #>  composite_power      0.675 #>  df_error             114   #>  power_2              0.675 #>  true_f_2             0.250 #>  df_2                 2     #>  noncentral_f_parm_2  7.500 #>  true_covariate_R2    0     #>  n_covariates         0     #>  cells                6     #>  alpha_level          0.050 ss_power_factorial_anova(factor_levels = c(2, 3), effect_indices = 2,                          true_f = 0.25, specified_n_per_cell = 20) #>  term                 value #>  specified_n_per_cell 20    #>  total_N              120   #>  df_effect            2     #>  df_error             114   #>  noncentral_f_parm    7.500 #>  actual_power         0.675  # The composite is not the product of the marginal powers. The tests share # one error estimate, so they are positively dependent and the composite is # the larger of the two. plan <- ss_power_composite_factorial_ancova(   factor_levels = c(2, 2, 3),   effects = list(list(factors = 1, true_f = 0.30, label = "A"),                  list(factors = c(1, 3), true_f = 0.25, label = "AxC")),   specified_n_per_cell = 15) plan$value[plan$term == "composite_power"] #> [1] 0.836889 prod(plan$value[plan$term %in% c("power_A", "power_AxC")]) #> [1] 0.836717  # A one-row broom summary of the plan. generics::tidy(ss_power_composite_factorial_ancova(   factor_levels = c(2, 3),   effects = list(list(factors = 1, true_f = 0.25),                  list(factors = 2, true_f = 0.20)),   desired_power = 0.80)) #>          term estimate     power #> 1 sample_size       43 0.8064647  # The figure of the purported population values, annotated with the power a # given sample size delivers. plot(ss_power_composite_factorial_ancova(   factor_levels = c(2, 3),   effects = list(list(factors = 1, true_f = 0.25),                  list(factors = 2, true_f = 0.20)),   specified_n_per_cell = 30))   # The effects can instead be stated as a full pattern of population cell means # with a common within-cell SD. code: # A 2 by 2 design whose conclusion needs a main effect and evidence that the # covariate slope differs across the first factor. The same design from population values: cell means, a covariate-outcome # correlation per cell (they differ across factor 1, so the slopes do), and a # common within-cell SD. plot() then draws the per-cell regression lines. cell_means <- matrix(c(10, 12,                        11, 13), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE) cell_rho   <- matrix(c(0.55, 0.55,                        0.15, 0.20), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE) fit <- ss_power_composite_factorial_ancova_het(   factor_levels = c(2, 2), true_means = cell_means, true_cor = cell_rho,   true_sd = 4, true_sd_X = 2,   effects = list(list(type = "mean",      factors = 1),                  list(type = "covariate"),                  list(type = "slope",      factors = 1)),   specified_n_per_cell = 40) #> Warning: The cell correlations differ in absolute value, so the cells' residual variances differ and the shared-error composite power is an approximation whose error grows with the spread of the correlations. The population model fixes every parameter to its purported # population value. true_model <- "   f1 =~ 1*y1 + 0.8*y2 + 0.8*y3   f2 =~ 1*y4 + 0.8*y5 + 0.8*y6   f3 =~ 1*y7 + 0.8*y8 + 0.8*y9   f2 ~ 0.4*f1   f3 ~ 0.3*f2 + 0.25*f1   f1 ~~ 1*f1   f2 ~~ 0.84*f2   f3 ~~ 0.8*f3   y1 ~~ 0.5*y1; y2 ~~ 0.5*y2; y3 ~~ 0.5*y3   y4 ~~ 0.5*y4; y5 ~~ 0.5*y5; y6 ~~ 0.5*y6   y7 ~~ 0.5*y7; y8 ~~ 0.5*y8; y9 ~~ 0.5*y9 "  # The analysis model is free; the labels name the parameters of interest. analysis_model <- "   f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3   f2 =~ y4 + y5 + y6   f3 =~ y7 + y8 + y9   f2 ~ a*f1   f3 ~ b*f2 + c*f1 "  # Realized composite power at N = 200. The probability that all three # paths come out significant in the same study is lower than the marginal # power of any one of them: the composite event sits inside each marginal # event, so the weakest parameter governs the design. G = 10 keeps the # example quick; a reported plan deserves the default G = 1000 or more. ss_power_composite_sem(model = analysis_model, true_model = true_model,                        specified_N = 200, G = 10, seed = 113) #>  term                   value #>  specified_N            200   #>  composite_power        0.500 #>  composite_power_mc_se  0.158 #>  power_a                1.000 #>  power_b                0.700 #>  power_c                0.800 #>  true_a                 0.400 #>  true_b                 0.300 #>  true_c                 0.250 #>  alpha_level            0.050 #>  replications           10    #>  converged_replications 10

title: Sample Size and Statistical Power for a Contrast in a Fixed-Effects ANOVA — ss_power_contrast
text: Let \(\psi = \sum_j c_j \mu_j\) population contrast. usual fixed-effects ANOVA model common within-group variance \(\sigma^2\) per-group sizes \(n_j\), standard error contrast estimate $$\mathrm{SE}_{\hat\psi} = \sqrt{\,\sigma^2 \sum_j c_j^2 / n_j\,},$$ test statistic \(t = \hat\psi / \mathrm{SE}_{\hat\psi}\) follows central t distribution \(N - \) degrees freedom \(H_0\!: \psi = 0\), noncentral t distribution df noncentrality parameter \(\lambda = \psi / \mathrm{SE}_{\hat\psi}\) alternative. two-sided test level \(\alpha\), $$\text{Power} = \Pr(t > t_{1-\alpha/2,\,df}) + \Pr(t < -t_{1-\alpha/2,\,df}),$$ computed exactly noncentral \(t\) distribution; one-sided test, appropriate tail contributes. Cohen's \(f\) one-df contrast reported \(f = |\lambda| / \sqrt{N}\), equivalently \(f^2 = F_{\text{pop}} / N\) (Cohen, 1988, Ch. 8); matches value pwr.f2.test expects used u = 1 v = N - .

The unstandardized slope difference is the #     standardized one times the square root of true_var_trend, -0.40 #     times the square root of 0.003, about -0.0219. Giving it as #     true_reg_coef reproduces the power of 0.61 from example (1). ss_power_pcm(true_reg_coef = -.0219, true_var_trend = .003, true_var_error = .0262,              frequency = 1, duration = 4, specified_n_per_group = 119) #>  term                  value  #>  specified_n_per_group 119    #>  total_N               238    #>  actual_power          0.612  #>  frequency             1      #>  duration              4      #>  n_occasions           5      #>  polynomial_order      1      #>  true_reg_coef         -0.022 #>  true_std_reg_coef     -0.400 #>  true_var_error        0.026  #>  true_var_trend        0.003  #>  true_var_trend_error  0.003  #>  reliability           0.534  #>  noncentral_t_parm     2.253   # (4) Longer study, same number of occasions. Doubling the duration to #     D = 8 while keeping M = 5 (so frequency = 0.5, one observation every #     two years) raises the slope reliability to 0.82 and power to about #     0.80. Spreading the same five occasions over a longer span sharply #     increases power (Raudenbush & Liu, 2001, p. 393). ss_power_pcm(true_std_reg_coef = -.4, true_var_trend = .003, true_var_error = .0262,              frequency = .5, duration = 8, specified_n_per_group = 119) #>  term                  value  #>  specified_n_per_group 119    #>  total_N               238    #>  actual_power          0.795  #>  frequency             0.500  #>  duration              8      #>  n_occasions           5      #>  polynomial_order      1      #>  true_reg_coef         -0.022 #>  true_std_reg_coef     -0.400 #>  true_var_error        0.026  #>  true_var_trend        0.003  #>  true_var_trend_error  0.001  #>  reliability           0.821  #>  noncentral_t_parm     2.795   # (5) More frequent sampling over a shorter span, same occasions. Halving #     the duration to D = 2 while keeping M = 5 (so frequency = 2) drops #     the slope reliability to 0.22 and power to about 0.31. Sampling more #     often over a shorter study does little for power (Raudenbush & Liu, #     2001, p. 393). ss_power_pcm(true_std_reg_coef = -.4, true_var_trend = .003, true_var_error = .0262,              frequency = 2, duration = 2, specified_n_per_group = 119) #>  term                  value  #>  specified_n_per_group 119    #>  total_N               238    #>  actual_power          0.305  #>  frequency             2      #>  duration              2      #>  n_occasions           5      #>  polynomial_order      1      #>  true_reg_coef         -0.022 #>  true_std_reg_coef     -0.400 #>  true_var_error        0.026  #>  true_var_trend        0.003  #>  true_var_trend_error  0.010  #>  reliability           0.223  #>  noncentral_t_parm     1.456   # (6) One-sided test. A directional test of the base design places the #     whole Type I error rate in the predicted tail, raising power from #     0.61 to about 0.73. ss_power_pcm(true_std_reg_coef = -.4, true_var_trend = .003, true_var_error = .0262,              frequency = 1, duration = 4, specified_n_per_group = 119, directional = TRUE) #>  term                  value  #>  specified_n_per_group 119    #>  total_N               238    #>  actual_power          0.727  #>  frequency             1      #>  duration              4      #>  n_occasions           5      #>  polynomial_order      1      #>  true_reg_coef         -0.022 #>  true_std_reg_coef     -0.400 #>  true_var_error        0.026  #>  true_var_trend        0.003  #>  true_var_trend_error  0.003  #>  reliability           0.534  #>  noncentral_t_parm     2.254   # (7) A higher-order trend. The same machinery plans power for the group #     difference in any polynomial change coefficient. Here the target is #     the quadratic trend (curvature / acceleration): with eight occasions #     (frequency = 1, duration = 7), a between-subject quadratic-coefficient #     variance 0.002, a within-subject (i.e., Level 1) error variance of #     0.05, and a #     standardized quadratic difference of 0.45, the design is planned for #     0.80 power. A quadratic trend needs at least three occasions; a cubic #     at least four (trend = "cubic" or trend = 3), and so on. ss_power_pcm(true_std_reg_coef = 0.45, true_var_trend = 0.002, true_var_error = 0.05,              frequency = 1, duration = 7, desired_power = .80,              trend = "quadratic") #>  term                  value #>  necessary_n_per_group 125   #>  total_N               250   #>  actual_power          0.801 #>  frequency             1     #>  duration              7     #>  n_occasions           8     #>  polynomial_order      2     #>  true_reg_coef         0.020 #>  true_std_reg_coef     0.450 #>  true_var_error        0.050 #>  true_var_trend        0.002 #>  true_var_trend_error  0.001 #>  reliability           0.627 #>  noncentral_t_parm     2.817

Had true_reg_coef_j # been the unstandardized regression coefficient, true_sd_X and true_sd_Y # would have been the standard deviation for the X variable of interest # and Y, respectively. ss_power_rc(true_R2_Y_X = 0.7826786, true_R2_j_X_without_j = 0.3652136,             true_reg_coef_j = 0.2700964, p = 5,             alpha_level = .05, true_sd_X = 1, true_sd_Y = 1,             directional = FALSE, desired_power = .80) #>  term              value #>  necessary_N       40    #>  actual_power      0.810 #>  noncentral_t_parm 2.920 #>  true_f            0.462 # Method 4 ss_power_rc(alpha_level = .05, true_f2 = 0.2130898, p = 5,             directional = FALSE, desired_power = .80) #>  term              value #>  necessary_N       40    #>  actual_power      0.810 #>  noncentral_t_parm 2.920 #>  true_f            0.462 # Power given a specified N and squared multiple correlation coefficients. ss_power_rc(true_R2_Y_X = 0.7826786, true_R2_Y_X_without_j = 0.7363697, specified_N = 25, p = 5,             alpha_level = .05, directional = FALSE) #>  term              value #>  specified_N       25    #>  actual_power      0.591 #>  noncentral_t_parm 2.308 #>  true_f            0.462  # Power given a specified N and effect size. ss_power_rc(alpha_level = .05, true_f2 = 0.2130898, p = 5, specified_N = 25, directional = FALSE) #>  term              value #>  specified_N       25    #>  actual_power      0.591 #>  noncentral_t_parm 2.308 #>  true_f            0.462  # Reproducing Maxwell's (2000, p. 445) Example Cor.Mat.Maxwell <- rbind(     c(1.00, 0.35,  0.20, 0.20, 0.20, 0.20),     c(0.35, 1.00,  0.40, 0.40, 0.40, 0.40),     c(0.20, 0.40,  1.00, 0.45, 0.45, 0.45),     c(0.20, 0.40,  0.45, 1.00, 0.45, 0.45),     c(0.20, 0.40,  0.45, 0.45, 1.00, 0.45),     c(0.20, 0.40,  0.45, 0.45, 0.45, 1.00) )  RHO.XX.Maxwell <- Cor.Mat.Maxwell[2:6, 2:6] Rho.YX.Maxwell <- Cor.Mat.Maxwell[1, 2:6] R2.Maxwell <- Rho.YX.Maxwell %*% solve(RHO.XX.Maxwell) %*% Rho.YX.Maxwell  RHO.XX.Maxwell.no.1 <- Cor.Mat.Maxwell[3:6, 3:6] Rho.YX.Maxwell.no.1 <- Cor.Mat.Maxwell[1, 3:6] R2.Maxwell.no.1 <- Rho.YX.Maxwell.no.1 %*% solve(RHO.XX.Maxwell.no.1) %*% Rho.YX.Maxwell.no.1   # Note that Maxwell arrives at N=113, whereas this procedure arrives at 111. # This seems to be the case becuase of rounding error in calculations # and tables (Cohen, 1988) used. The present procedure is correct and # contains no rounding error in the application of the method. ss_power_rc(true_R2_Y_X = R2.Maxwell, true_R2_Y_X_without_j = R2.Maxwell.no.1, p = 5,             alpha_level = .05, directional = FALSE, desired_power = .80) #>  term              value #>  necessary_N       111   #>  actual_power      0.801 #>  noncentral_t_parm 2.833 #>  true_f            0.269

code: Cor.Mat <- rbind(   c(1.00, 0.53, 0.58, 0.60, 0.46, 0.66),   c(0.53, 1.00, 0.35, 0.07, 0.14, 0.43),   c(0.58, 0.35, 1.00, 0.18, 0.29, 0.50),   c(0.60, 0.07, 0.18, 1.00, 0.30, 0.26),   c(0.46, 0.14, 0.29, 0.30, 1.00, 0.30),   c(0.66, 0.43, 0.50, 0.26, 0.30, 1.00) )  true_cor_XX <- Cor.Mat[2:6, 2:6] true_cor_YX <- Cor.Mat[1, 2:6]  # Method 1 ss_power_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = 0.7826786, true_R2_Y_X_without_j = 0.7363697, p = 5,                   alpha_level = .05, directional = FALSE, desired_power = .80) #>  term              value #>  necessary_N       40    #>  actual_power      0.810 #>  noncentral_t_parm 2.920 #>  true_f            0.462  # Method 2 ss_power_reg_coef(alpha_level = .05, true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX, true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX,                   which_predictor = 5,                   directional = FALSE, desired_power = .80) #>  term              value #>  necessary_N       40    #>  actual_power      0.810 #>  noncentral_t_parm 2.920 #>  true_f            0.462  # Method 3 # Here, true_reg_coef_j is the standardized regression coefficient. Had true_reg_coef_j # been the unstandardized regression coefficient, true_sd_X and true_sd_Y # would have been the standard deviation for the X variable of # interest and Y, respectively. ss_power_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = 0.7826786, true_R2_j_X_without_j = 0.3652136,                   true_reg_coef_j = 0.2700964,                   p = 5, alpha_level = .05, true_sd_X = 1, true_sd_Y = 1, directional = FALSE,                   desired_power = .80) #>  term              value #>  necessary_N       40    #>  actual_power      0.810 #>  noncentral_t_parm 2.920 #>  true_f            0.462  # Method 4 ss_power_reg_coef(alpha_level = .05, true_f2 = 0.2130898, p = 5,                   directional = FALSE, desired_power = .80) #>  term              value #>  necessary_N       40    #>  actual_power      0.810 #>  noncentral_t_parm 2.920 #>  true_f            0.462  # Power given a specified N and squared multiple correlation coefficients. ss_power_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = 0.7826786, true_R2_Y_X_without_j = 0.7363697, specified_N = 25,                   p = 5, alpha_level = .05, directional = FALSE) #>  term              value #>  specified_N       25    #>  actual_power      0.591 #>  noncentral_t_parm 2.308 #>  true_f            0.462  # Power given a specified N and effect size. ss_power_reg_coef(alpha_level = .05, true_f2 = 0.2130898, p = 5, specified_N = 25,                   directional = FALSE) #>  term              value #>  specified_N       25    #>  actual_power      0.591 #>  noncentral_t_parm 2.308 #>  true_f            0.462  # Reproducing Maxwell's (2000, p. 445) Example Cor.Mat.Maxwell <- rbind(   c(1.00, 0.35, 0.20, 0.20, 0.20, 0.20),   c(0.35, 1.00, 0.40, 0.40, 0.40, 0.40),   c(0.20, 0.40, 1.00, 0.45, 0.45, 0.45),   c(0.20, 0.40, 0.45, 1.00, 0.45, 0.45),   c(0.20, 0.40, 0.45, 0.45, 1.00, 0.45),   c(0.20, 0.40, 0.45, 0.45, 0.45, 1.00) )  RHO.XX.Maxwell <- Cor.Mat.Maxwell[2:6, 2:6] Rho.YX.Maxwell <- Cor.Mat.Maxwell[1, 2:6] R2.Maxwell <- Rho.YX.Maxwell %*% solve(RHO.XX.Maxwell) %*% Rho.YX.Maxwell  RHO.XX.Maxwell.no.1 <- Cor.Mat.Maxwell[3:6, 3:6] Rho.YX.Maxwell.no.1 <- Cor.Mat.Maxwell[1, 3:6] R2.Maxwell.no.1 <-   Rho.YX.Maxwell.no.1 %*% solve(RHO.XX.Maxwell.no.1) %*% Rho.YX.Maxwell.no.1  # This procedure arrives at N = 111, whereas Maxwell (2000, p. 445) # reports N = 113. The two differ because of the noncentrality # parameterization, not rounding: this function uses the fixed-predictor # noncentrality sqrt(N) * f (see Details), while the tabled value rests on # Cohen's (1988) convention. Neither is a random-predictor result; under # random predictors, where the predictor values vary across replications, # the sample size needed for the same power is larger still. ss_power_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = R2.Maxwell, true_R2_Y_X_without_j = R2.Maxwell.no.1, p = 5,                   alpha_level = .05, directional = FALSE, desired_power = .80) #>  term              value #>  necessary_N       111   #>  actual_power      0.801 #>  noncentral_t_parm 2.833 #>  true_f            0.269

Is a 90% interval with # half-width 1 reached? set.seed(113) proxy  <- rnorm(5000, mean = 50, sd = 10) target <- 20 + 0.6 * proxy + rnorm(5000, sd = 5) order  <- sample(5000) first  <- order[1:40] ss_seq_two_phase(y = target[first], x = proxy[first],                  x_unlabeled = proxy[-first], half_width = 1) #>  term                value #>  stop                0     #>  half_width_current  1.124 #>  half_width_target   1     #>  n_labeled_current   40    #>  n_labeled_projected 49    #>  n_pool              5000  #>  #> Confidence level: 90%  # Not yet; the projection suggests about 50. After labeling the next 30 # units at random: first <- order[1:70] ss_seq_two_phase(y = target[first], x = proxy[first],                  x_unlabeled = proxy[-first], half_width = 1) #>  term                value #>  stop                1     #>  half_width_current  0.896 #>  half_width_target   1     #>  n_labeled_current   70    #>  n_labeled_projected 70    #>  n_pool              5000  #>  #> Confidence level: 90%

title: Two-Sample t Test From Summary Statistics — summary_t_test
text: Pooled-variance t (Student, 1908). \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2\), pooled SD \(s_p = \sqrt{((n_1 - 1) s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1) s_2^2) / (n_1 + n_2 - 2)}\), test statistic \(t = (\bar x_1 - \bar x_2 - \mu_0) / (s_p \sqrt{1 / n_1 + 1 / n_2})\), \(df = n_1 + n_2 - 2\). Welch's t (Welch, 1947). unequal variances, \(t = (\bar x_1 - \bar x_2 - \mu_0) /   \sqrt{s_1^2 / n_1 + s_2^2 / n_2}\) Satterthwaite degrees freedom (see welch_t). Choosing pooled vs Welch. Delacre, Lakens, Leys (2017) Ruxton (2006) recommend Welch's test default. Pooled-variance t preserved primarily reproducing analyses older sources used .

code: data(teacher_expectancy) head(teacher_expectancy) #>   study                             author year weeks testing tester #> 1     1          Rosenthal, Baratz, & Hall 1974     2   group  aware #> 2     2 Conn, Edwards, Rosenthal, & Crowne 1968    21   group  aware #> 3     3                        Jose & Cody 1971    19   group  aware #> 4     4  Pellegrini & Hicks (tester aware) 1972     0   group  aware #> 5     5  Pellegrini & Hicks (tester blind) 1972     0   group  blind #> 6     6                  Evans & Rosenthal 1969     3   group  aware #>   n_experimental n_control     d p_one_tailed #> 1             77       339  0.02        0.401 #> 2             60       198  0.14        0.206 #> 3             72        72 -0.03        0.791 #> 4             11        22  0.85        0.003 #> 5             11        22  0.19        0.242 #> 6            129       348 -0.04        0.709  # The paper's central picture: effect size against weeks of prior contact. plot(d ~ weeks, data = teacher_expectancy,      xlab = "Weeks of teacher-student contact before induction",      ylab = "Effect size d")   # The study-level (18-study) data Raudenbush used for the combined tests: # merge the two Pellegrini & Hicks conditions into their study row. study_level <- teacher_expectancy[-c(4, 5), ] ph <- data.frame(study = 4, author = "Pellegrini & Hicks", year = 1972,                  weeks = 0, testing = "group", tester = "aware",                  n_experimental = 22, n_control = 22,                  d = 0.52, p_one_tailed = .010) study_level <- rbind(study_level[1:3, ], ph, study_level[4:17, ]) round(c(mean = mean(study_level$d), sd = sd(study_level$d)), 2)  # .11, .20 #> mean   sd  #> 0.11 0.20

title: Controlled Test-Market Experiment (Bryant & Bruvold, 1980) — test_market
text: benchmark ANCOVA multiple comparisons. model fitted Bryant Bruvold (Eq. 3.1) randomized-block ANCOVA, $$y_{ij} = \theta_i + \beta_j + (x_{ij} - \delta_j)\, u + e_{ij},$$ \(\theta_i\) \(\)th panel (adjusted) mean, \(\beta_j\) \(j\)th block effect, \(u\) within-cell covariate slope. point example studentized range adjusted panel means follow ordinary Tukey distribution, covariate random adjustment must estimated; correct reference distribution Bryant–Paulson generalized studentized range (bryant_paulson). Reproducible quantities. Fitting lm(brand_movement ~ panel + block + category_movement) gives covariate slope \(0.4079\) error mean square \(0.01326\) \(\nu = 14\) degrees freedom, adjusted panel means \(3.595, 3.619, 4.102, 4.515, 4.618, 4.876\), exactly values reported paper. \(q_{.05;\,1,6,14} = 4.83\) (qbryant_paulson), every pairwise simultaneous 95% interval difference adjusted panel means plus minus \(0.278\), two panels differ simultaneous 95% level exactly adjusted means \(0.278\) apart. covariate measured, error mean square \(0.2368\), roughly eighteen times larger, intervals four times wider. See data-raw/test_market.R construction script verification checks.

title: Unbiased and Adjusted Estimators of the Population Squared Multiple Correlation — unbiased_R2
text: Estimates population squared multiple correlation coefficient \(\rho^2\) observed sample \(R^2\), correcting well-known positive (upward) bias \(R^2\). Two estimators available: (essentially) unbiased Olkin Pratt (1958) estimator (default), classic Ezekiel (1930) adjusted-\(R^2\) shrinkage formula reported summary.lm adj.r.squared. inverse direction expected_R2, gives forward expectation \(E[R^2 \mid \rho^2]\).

title: Unbiased and Adjusted Estimators of the Population Squared Multiple Correlation — unbiased_R2
text: R2 Observed sample squared multiple correlation coefficient, \([0, 1]\). N Sample size. p Number predictor variables. method estimator compute: "olkin_pratt" (default) (essentially) unbiased Olkin-Pratt (1958) estimator, "ezekiel" Ezekiel (1930) adjusted \(R^2\) (value summary.lm reports adj.r.squared).

title: Unbiased and Adjusted Estimators of the Population Squared Multiple Correlation — unbiased_R2
text: 1-row data.frame (class dmar_tbl) columns   term value. term   "unbiased_population_R2" method = "olkin_pratt"   "adjusted_population_R2" method = "ezekiel"; value   corresponding estimate \(\rho^2\).

title: Unbiased and Adjusted Estimators of the Population Squared Multiple Correlation — unbiased_R2
text: sample \(R^2\) overestimates \(\rho^2\); bias larger smaller samples predictors. Two corrections offered. Ezekiel (1930) adjusted estimator $$\hat\rho^2_{\mathrm{Ezekiel}} = 1 - \frac{N - 1}{N - p - 1}\,(1 - R^2).$$ reduces bias unbiased; exactly quantity summary(lm(...))$adj.r.squared reports. Olkin Pratt (1958) estimator (essentially) unbiased: $$\hat\rho^2_{\mathrm{OP}} = 1 - \frac{N - 3}{N - p - 1}\,(1 - R^2)\;        {}_2F_1\!\left(1, 1; \frac{N - p + 1}{2}; 1 - R^2\right),$$ \({}_2F_1\) Gaussian hypergeometric function (function expected_R2 uses forward direction; see Stuart, Ord, & Arnold, 1999, section 28). estimators can fall 0 small \(R^2\); expected behavior bias-corrected estimator truncated (matching adj.r.squared, also allowed negative).

text: interval estimate alpha data see reliability_alpha reliability; sample size planning see ss_aipe_reliability. van Zyl, Neudecker, Nel (2000). multivariate normality compound symmetry, van Zyl et al. show \(n\,\mathrm{Var}(\hat\alpha)\) tends \(2J(1 - \alpha)^2 / (J - 1)\) \(n\) grows, \(n = N - 1\) degrees freedom item covariance matrix (Equation 13). asymptotic variance therefore $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\alpha) \;\approx\;   \frac{2 J (1 - \alpha)^2}{(J - 1)(N - 1)}.$$ Without compound symmetry asymptotic variance function whole item covariance matrix (Equation 21); reliability_alpha uses general form "ml" interval, compound symmetric covariance matrix equals form . Bonett (2002). Bonett (2003, Equations 2 4), citing Bonett (2002), uses \(2J / ((J - 1)(N - 2))\) large-sample variance \(\ln(1 - \hat\alpha)\) assumptions. Carried alpha scale delta method gives $$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\alpha) \;\approx\;   \frac{2 J (1 - \alpha)^2}{(J - 1)(N - 2)}.$$ Comparing two. two forms differ denominator: form \(N - 2\) form \(N - 1\) times \((N - 1)/(N - 2)\), sample size chosen reach target variance one larger \(N - 2\) denominator \(N - 1\). large-sample approximations. multivariate normality compound symmetry exact variance \(\hat\alpha\) \(N > 5\) $$\frac{2 (1 - \alpha)^2 n (nJ - 2)}{(J - 1)(n - 2)^2 (n - 4)},   \quad n = N - 1$$ (van Zyl, Neudecker, & Nel, 2000, Equation 12). larger forms, form \(N - 2\) closer two: \(J = 5\) exact variance 2.53 times form \(N = 10\), 1.27 times \(N = 30\), 1.07 times \(N = 100\).

code: # Two numeric vectors. set.seed(113) x <- rnorm(40, mean = 0.6) y <- rnorm(40, mean = 0) vargha_delaney_A(x, y) #>  A     se    ci_lower ci_upper test_statistic p_value n_1 n_2 ci_method df     #>  0.666 0.061 0.538    0.774    2.712          0.0082  40  40  logit     77.962 #>  test #>  t    #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Formula interface on the pygmalion field experiment. The first factor # level (Control) forms group 1, so A below 0.5 says a randomly drawn # control child tends to score below a child from the bloomer group. vargha_delaney_A(iq_8 ~ treatment, data = pygmalion) #>  A     se    ci_lower ci_upper test_statistic p_value n_1 n_2 ci_method df     #>  0.429 0.041 0.351    0.511    -1.718         0.0892  246 64  logit     92.478 #>  test #>  t    #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Wald (untransformed) interval rather than logit. vargha_delaney_A(x, y, ci_method = "wald") #>  A     se    ci_lower ci_upper test_statistic p_value n_1 n_2 ci_method df     #>  0.666 0.061 0.546    0.786    2.712          0.0082  40  40  wald      77.962 #>  test #>  t    #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # The studentized permutation test and the normal reference. With # 40 per group the reassignments are sampled, so a seed is given. # n_resamples = 2000 keeps the example quick; a reported p-value # deserves the default of 10,000. vargha_delaney_A(x, y, test = "permutation", n_resamples = 2000,                  seed = 113) #>  A     se    ci_lower ci_upper test_statistic p_value n_1 n_2 ci_method df   #>  0.666 0.061 0.538    0.774    2.712          0.0120  40  40  logit     <NA> #>  test        #>  permutation #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Permutation test: 2000 random reassignments vargha_delaney_A(x, y, test = "z") #>  A     se    ci_lower ci_upper test_statistic p_value n_1 n_2 ci_method df   #>  0.666 0.061 0.538    0.774    2.712          0.0067  40  40  logit     <NA> #>  test #>  z    #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # An ordinal response is supplied as an ordered factor with its levels # stated from lowest to highest. The unordered factors rating_1 and # rating_2 themselves are refused, with a message that says why: their # codes follow the alphabetical order of the labels (high, low, mid). rating_1 <- factor(c("low", "mid", "high", "high")) rating_2 <- factor(c("low", "low", "mid", "high")) lev <- c("low", "mid", "high") vargha_delaney_A(factor(rating_1, levels = lev, ordered = TRUE),                  factor(rating_2, levels = lev, ordered = TRUE)) #>  A     se    ci_lower ci_upper test_statistic p_value n_1 n_2 ci_method df test #>  0.656 0.209 0.237    0.921    0.748          0.4827  4   4   logit     6  t    #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Completely separated groups: the estimated variance is 0, the two # limits equal the estimate, and a warning says that they are not a # confidence interval. The permutation test still gives a p-value, the # share of the 252 reassignments that are also completely separated. separated <- vargha_delaney_A(6:10, 1:5, test = "permutation") #> Warning: vargha_delaney_A(): the groups are completely separated (A = 1), so the estimated variance is 0. Both confidence limits are reported equal to the estimate (1, 1). They are not a confidence interval with the stated coverage: the variance estimate is built from how much the comparisons differ from one observation to the next, and in a sample with no overlap they do not differ at all. That describes this sample, not the population. A population with some overlap often produces a sample with none when the samples are small (here 5 and 5 observations), so the limits must not be read as showing that the population value is 1. For this case Feng and Cliff (2004, Equation 8) give the limit (n_b - z^2) / (n_b + z^2) for delta = 2A - 1, with n_b the smaller group size and z the normal quantile of the level: 0.131 here at the 95% level, with the other limit 1; on the scale of A, 0.566, with the other limit 1. The permutation test is reported (test_statistic is infinite); the t and z tests are not defined here. Report the estimate with the sample sizes and say that the groups did not overlap; the randomization test (randomization_test()) gives a p-value that remains valid here. separated #>  A     se    ci_lower ci_upper test_statistic p_value n_1 n_2 ci_method df   #>  1.000 0.000 1.000    1.000    Inf            0.0079  5   5   logit     <NA> #>  test        #>  permutation #>  #> Confidence level: 95% #>  #> Limits are not a confidence interval: the estimated variance is 0. #>  #> Permutation test: all 252 reassignments results_sentence(separated) #> [1] "A = 1.00 (no confidence interval: the groups are completely separated, so the estimated variance is 0), unadjusted p = 0.0079"

title: Welch's Separate-Variance t Test — welch_t
text: Computes Welch's (1947) separate-variance t test, Satterthwaite (1946) approximation unequal-variance two-sample inference, returns test statistic, Satterthwaite degrees freedom, p-value, point estimate mean difference, confidence interval mean difference, tidy data.frame. Unlike Student's pooled-variance t test (stats::t.test(..., var.equal = TRUE)), Welch's test assume two populations equal variances, default choice applied work (Delacre, Lakens, & Leys, 2017).

title: Welch's Separate-Variance t Test — welch_t
text: Test statistic. Welch's t $$t \;=\; \frac{\bar x - \bar y - \mu_0}                    {\sqrt{s_1^2 / n_1 + s_2^2 / n_2}},$$ referred t distribution Satterthwaite (1946) approximate degrees freedom $$df \;=\; \frac{(s_1^2 / n_1 + s_2^2 / n_2)^2}                     {(s_1^2 / n_1)^2 / (n_1 - 1) +                      (s_2^2 / n_2)^2 / (n_2 - 1)}.$$ Welch default. Student's pooled-variance t assumes \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2\); assumption fails inflated deflated Type error rates depending \(n_1 : n_2\) ratio (Ruxton, 2006). scores group normally distributed, Welch's test keeps Type error rate close nominal level across combinations \(\sigma_1 / \sigma_2\) \(n_1 / n_2\), variances equal power close Student's test, little lower group sizes differ. skewed scores small groups Type error rate can depart nominal level. Delacre, Lakens, Leys (2017) Lakens (2015) recommend Welch's test default. Relation stats::t.test(). numerical results match stats::t.test(x, y, var.equal = FALSE) machine precision; function differs returning tidy data.frame composes rest DMAR.

title: Welch's Separate-Variance t Test — welch_t
code: # 1. Two groups with different variances: set.seed(113) x <- rnorm(20, mean = 100, sd = 15) y <- rnorm(20, mean = 110, sd = 25) welch_t(x, y) #>  term            value   #>  mean_difference -16.871 #>  t_value         -2.410  #>  df              28.349  #>  p_value         0.0227  #>  ci_lower        -31.204 #>  ci_upper        -2.537  #>  mean_x          100.297 #>  mean_y          117.168 #>  sd_x            14.289  #>  sd_y            27.860  #>  n_x             20      #>  n_y             20      #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # 2. One-sided test: welch_t(x, y, alternative = "less") #>  term            value   #>  mean_difference -16.871 #>  t_value         -2.410  #>  df              28.349  #>  p_value         0.0113  #>  ci_lower        -Inf    #>  ci_upper        -4.966  #>  mean_x          100.297 #>  mean_y          117.168 #>  sd_x            14.289  #>  sd_y            27.860  #>  n_x             20      #>  n_y             20      #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # 3. Side-by-side comparison with base R's stats::t.test(). # The two functions implement the same Welch / Satterthwaite test, so # the t-statistic, Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, p-value, and the # CI on the mean difference match exactly. welch_t() differs only in # what it returns: a data.frame(term, value) rather than a list- # like htest object. The return composes with dplyr / ggplot2 # pipelines and avoids stringly-typed access like $statistic. set.seed(113) a <- rnorm(15, mean = 0,   sd = 1) b <- rnorm(20, mean = 0.5, sd = 2)  # DMAR (data.frame): dmar_res <- welch_t(a, b, conf_level = 0.95) dmar_res #>  term            value  #>  mean_difference -1.156 #>  t_value         -2.288 #>  df              30.068 #>  p_value         0.0294 #>  ci_lower        -2.189 #>  ci_upper        -0.124 #>  mean_x          -0.083 #>  mean_y          1.073  #>  sd_x            1.017  #>  sd_y            1.932  #>  n_x             15     #>  n_y             20     #>  #> Confidence level: 95%  # Base R (htest list): base_res <- stats::t.test(a, b, var.equal = FALSE, conf.level = 0.95) base_res #>  #> 	Welch Two Sample t-test #>  #> data:  a and b #> t = -2.2878, df = 30.068, p-value = 0.02935 #> alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0 #> 95 percent confidence interval: #>  -2.1886355 -0.1241931 #> sample estimates: #>   mean of x   mean of y  #> -0.08317142  1.07324287  #>   # Verify the four key statistics agree numerically: pick <- function(term) dmar_res$value[dmar_res$term == term] stopifnot(   all.equal(pick("t_value"), unname(base_res$statistic)),   all.equal(pick("df"),          unname(base_res$parameter)),   all.equal(pick("p_value"),     base_res$p.value),   all.equal(pick("ci_lower"), base_res$conf.int[1]),   all.equal(pick("ci_upper"), base_res$conf.int[2]) )

title: DMAR 1.0.0
text: DMAR adds 40+ functions across families absent -developed MBESS. New families include: Mediation, halves: mediate() analyzes simple mediation model (optional covariates) percentile bootstrap, BCa, Monte Carlo, Sobel intervals indirect effect, ss_power_indirect_effect() plans study joint significance exact noncentral t component powers (Sobel power comparison), validated raw-data simulation. mediation_mbco() extends inference side arbitrary mediation structures likelihood ratio model comparison framework (see section ). Measurement invariance: measurement_invariance() fits configural, metric, scalar, strict multi-group ladder measurement model, thresholds rung ordered indicators, reports full comparison table (fit, likelihood ratio test per step, delta CFI / delta RMSEA), pinned direct lavaan fits tests. See entry top file arguments returned "fits" attribute. Construct validity: htmt() (Henseler heterotrait-monotrait ratio optional bootstrap upper bound) average_variance_extracted() (Fornell-Larcker AVE lavaan fit standardized loadings). Composite reliability needs new function; coefficient omega (reliability_omega()). Clinical behavioral endpoints: responder_analysis() (per-group responder proportions Wilson intervals, Newcombe risk difference interval, number needed treat, omnibus chi square, threshold sweep) ci_proportion(), package’s Wilson score interval single proportion. meta-analysis family. meta_es() pools effect sizes given sampling variances (REML -study variance default, Paule-Mandel, DerSimonian-Laird, fixed effect options, Hartung-Knapp adjustment default, Q-profile confidence intervals tau-squared mapped -squared, prediction interval always reported); meta_smd() (exact Hedges correction default) meta_r() (Fisher’s Z pooling, optional per-study attenuation corrections) metric front ends. combine_p() provides four classical combined significance tests meta_contrast() Rosenthal Rubin contrast among effect sizes; plot_forest() draws studies, pool, prediction interval. Validated metafor, Raudenbush (1984) line line teacher expectancy vignette; 19 effect sizes synthesis ship teacher_expectancy. Factorial ANCOVA power: ss_power_factorial_ancova() extends factorial ANOVA planner baseline covariates (error variance scaled 1 - R2, one error df per covariate), complete 2 x 4 x 3 worked example, planning, simulation, Type III analysis, interaction plots, focused complex comparisons, ancova_2x4x3_power vignette. new vignette, “Power Precision One-Way ANOVA: Model Comparison Perspective,” works one-way design comparison full model restricted model: omnibus power sample size ss_power_one_way_anova(), planned contrast ss_power_contrast(), effect size confidence intervals ci_omega_squared(), ci_pvaf(), ci_snr(), ci_srsnr(), model comparison made literal mlmr(), Type S Type M consequences design design_consequences(), accuracy parameter estimation contrast ss_aipe_c(), following Maxwell, Delaney, Kelley (2027). Bayesian t family probability statement front center: bayes_one_sample_t(), bayes_paired_t(), bayes_independent_t() report JZS posterior standardized effect (median, mean, credible interval, P(delta > 0 | data)) default Bayes factor secondary row, computed exact quadrature validated BayesFactor package. correction_for_attenuation() (renamed working name correct_attenuation()) documents demonstrates latent variable route approximates: item-level data exist, prefer two-factor model’s latent correlation plug-formula. Moments noncentral distributions: moments_nc_t(), moments_nc_F(), moments_nc_chisq() return mean, variance, standard deviation, skewness, excess kurtosis noncentral t, F, chi square distributions, NA moments whose degrees freedom conditions fail. noncentral t mean quantity behind upward bias standardized mean difference. random-coefficients polynomial growth simulator: simulate_longitudinal_polynomial() generates longitudinal data polynomial order (order 0 flat line) one several groups, ties level-one error target measurement reliability (reported per occasion), allows assessment-time jitter around nominal schedule, supports structured level-one error covariance (AR(1), compound symmetry, Toeplitz, heteroscedastic, full matrix). Monte Carlo companion ss_power_pcm(). ss_power_pcm() now plans power polynomial change coefficient (intercept, linear, quadratic, cubic, …) trend argument, carrying general Raudenbush Liu (2001) sampling variance; linear default reproduces National Youth Survey benchmark. orthogonal_polynomial() returns orthogonal polynomial trend contrast weights stored levels--trends (ready contrasts() lm()) printed Maxwell, Delaney, Kelley Table .10 layout trailing sum--squared-weights column. unbiased_R2() gives Olkin Pratt (1958) exactly unbiased estimator population squared multiple correlation alongside Ezekiel (1930) adjusted estimator (adj.r.squared summary.lm). Design consequences: design_consequences() reports chosen design delivers package’s lenses, significance lens (power, Type S wrong-sign error rate, Type M exaggeration ratio, Gelman Carlin, 2014, computed exactly rather simulation) precision lens (expected, median, standard deviation realized confidence interval width, probability realized interval beats target width, closed-form versions ss_aipe_*_sensitivity() Monte Carlo terms). Accepts standard error directly derives sd per-group n. Every ss_power_* ss_aipe_* help page points . Spearman correction attenuation: correction_for_attenuation() disattenuates correlation measurement error either variables, confidence interval sample size supplied, using reliabilities reliability_* family. New parameterization conversions: convert_d_r() / convert_r_d() (standardized mean difference point-biserial correlation, unequal-group factor) convert_d_or() / convert_or_d() (Hasselblad Hedges logistic link odds ratio). convert_F_chisq() convert_chisq_F() move test statistic F chi square metrics, returning converted statistic (value, p-value). Two conversions offered one argument, df_denominator. default, df_denominator = Inf, treats F’s error variance known returns standard scaling, df_numerator * F_value (back, chi_square / df); F chi square whose error variance estimated rather known, infinite denominator degrees freedom case known. finite df_denominator instead returns chi square value upper-tail probability (p-value) F, exact denominator degrees freedom; two conversions agree df_denominator grows, scaling default large-sample limit family. finite case computed ordinary upper-tail p-values (logarithms): upper tail used lower-tail probability rounds 1 double precision F = 500 small denominator degrees freedom, send result infinity, whereas upper-tail computation stays accurate past F = 1e20. help page states exact computation. map preserves p-value transport noncentrality parameter, noncentral work belongs ci_nc_F() ci_nc_chisq(). Display helpers extending package’s p-value convention objects DMAR produce: format_p(), print_anova(), print_summary(). DMAR longer requires GSL system library: Gauss hypergeometric function behind exact squared multiple correlation moments computed base R (remains accurate squared multiple correlation approaches 1, previous route lost precision). Installation now system prerequisites. Plot functions plot_* family: plot_smd(), plot_ci(), plot_R2(), plot_trajectories(), plot_trajectories_fitted(). built ggplot2 colored default neutral, colorblind-safe palette; accepts palette argument ("okabe_ito" "tableau") , applicable, colors override full manual control. Plot colors come base R. plot_* family colors base R’s Okabe-Ito colorblind-safe palette default, base R’s Tableau 10 available plot’s palette argument. DMAR defines palette adds color dependency; user wants colors adds ordinary ggplot2 scale plot. Ordinal non-parametric effect sizes: cliff_delta(), vargha_delaney_A(), probability_of_superiority_paired(), cles(), proportion_of_superiority() (sometimes called Cohen’s U3). Agreement reliability extensions: bland_altman_loa(), lin_ccc(), cohen_kappa(), fleiss_kappa(), gwet_ac(), krippendorff_alpha(), icc(), icc_lmer(), reliability_omega_categorical(), reliability_omega_h(), reliability_H(), reliability_kr20(), plus var_* family asymptotic variance utilities. Within-subjects, mixed, multivariate ANOVA: anova_within(), anova_within_two_way(), mixed_anova(), manova_split_plot(), mauchly_test(), epsilon_corrections(), pairwise_within(), simple_effects_AB(). Sample size planning broadened, particularly ss_power_* family, now covers -subjects, within-subjects, mixed, multi-level designs across chapters Maxwell, Delaney, Kelley (2027). Parameterization conversions convert_* family (convert_R2_f, convert_f_R2, convert_lambda_R2, convert_R2_lambda, convert_r_Z, convert_Z_r, convert_delta_lambda, convert_lambda_delta, convert_cor_cov). Every conversion exact-invertible inverse direction shipped sibling function makes sense. worked simulation study AIPE family reports expected realized CI widths, realized coverage, assurance-achievement rates across 10,000 Monte Carlo replications per cell. establishes methods perform rather used, maintained alongside package rather shipped .

title: DMAR 1.0.0
text: ss_aipe_reliability() longer embeds vendored copy MBESS 3.2.0’s ci.reliability() Monte Carlo assurance search. interval candidate sample size now comes DMAR’s reliability internals (single-factor delta method interval factor analytic type; van Zyl, Neudecker, Nel closed form normal theory type). --grid covering every model interval type combination confirmed computed interval widths, therefore every planned sample size, unchanged. icc_lmer() now reads grouping factor lme4’s grouping list, interaction groupings (1 | school:teacher) work; mlmr_mv gained tidy() / glance() methods documentation promised (one row per coefficient per outcome, response column). test suite runs warnPartialMatchArgs, warnPartialMatchDollar, warnPartialMatchAttr enabled, internal reliance partial matching fails loudly, display layer (dmar_tbl print methods, format_p(), print_anova(), print_summary()) covered testthat snapshots. seed argument defaults NULL everywhere exposed, meaning function uses caller’s current RNG state seed; user wants reproducibility passes explicit integer, supplied seed restores caller’s RNG state exit. value 113 used @examples tests, never baked function default. cluster-randomized design helpers ss_aipe_crd* consolidated single set shared internals (R/ss_aipe_crd_internals.R); difference effect size families now call .find_*_crd_*() back end. ss_aipe_pcm() typo cubic change coefficient constant (K_3 coded 1/1000800, one tenth correct 1/100800). constant sits denominator slope variance, inflated cubic variance, hence resolved sample size, roughly tenfold trend = "cubic". constant now matches closed form K_p = (p!)^2 / [(2p)! (2p+1)!] Raudenbush Liu (2001, p. 392), regression test recovers directly OLS fit. linear (1/12) quadratic (1/720) constants already correct. ss_aipe_pcm() now honors documented contract user may supply either error_variance converted variance variance_true_minus_estimated_trend. Previously error_variance effectively required, consistency check two used round(..., 3), mishandled small variances typical slope-change designs. cross-check now uses .equal(), supplying neither argument raises informative error. ss_aipe_pcm() now scales within-subject contribution slope variance frequency^(2p), matching ss_power_pcm() Raudenbush Liu (2001, p. 392). change coefficient per-unit-time rate, sampling variance error_variance * frequency^(2p) / (sum squared polynomial weights); factor previously omitted. Every Kelley Rausch (2011) benchmark uses frequency = 1, factor 1, tabled sample sizes unchanged; correction affects designs frequency != 1, now agrees direct OLS slope variance actual time grid. ss_aipe_pcm_sensitivity() now simulates estimand planner targets: -group difference mean slopes (group--time change parameter), using two independent groups, pooled standard error, 2n - 2 degrees freedom. previous simulator built one-group mean-slope interval, whose width systematically 1/sqrt(2) planned target every frequency. realized mean CI width now tracks planned width. schema terms mean_slope / median_slope / sd_slope renamed mean_slope_diff / median_slope_diff / sd_slope_diff reflect difference estimand.
